verses.2: Al-Mizan: Allah alone is the Ever-living, Self-subsisting God by Whom all subsist.
verses.3: Al-Mizan states that God revealed the Book with truth, confirming the Torah and Injīl, which were earlier guidance for the people, and sent down al-Furqān. Those who disbelieve in His signs will face severe chastisement, for He is Mighty and the Lord of retribution.
verses.4: Al-Mizan states that God revealed the Book with truth, confirming the Torah and Injīl, which were earlier guidance for the people, and sent down al-Furqān. Those who disbelieve in His signs will face severe chastisement, for He is Mighty and the Lord of retribution.
verses.5: Al-Mizan affirms that nothing in the earth or heaven is hidden from Allah.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan presents the chapter as a coherent, probably single revelation of two hundred interconnected verses. It addresses believers when Islam had spread in Arabia but had not gained a firm footing beyond Medina, urging them to remain united in religion and to defend it with patience, forbearance, and determination. It refers to Uḥud, the planned imprecation with the Christians of Najrān, the Jews, and the struggle against the polytheists. Jews and Christians sought internal sabotage through arguments and schemes to demoralize the Muslims, while the polytheists were enemies in an ongoing war; the Byzantines and Persians beyond Arabia had the same design. The chapter recalls religious realities that remove doubt and satanic suggestion, guard believers against the People of the Book’s deceptions, and show that God never ceases to govern His kingdom or grows weary of His creatures. He has chosen the religion and guided some servants through His established order of cause and effect. Both belief and unbelief occur within that order; apparent victory alternates between them, because this world is a place of trial and action whose outcome will be known later, not now.

The commentary treats verses 1–6 as a prologue containing the chapter’s message in brief. The opening declaration of God’s oneness introduces the basic truth, verses 5 and 6 give the reason for what precedes, and the central theme lies in the revelation of the Book, the distinction between truth and falsehood, and retribution. God’s management encompasses the entire universe and all its actions and reactions. Unlike unconscious physical and natural causes, it is a living management, entailing comprehensive knowledge and power: nothing is hidden from Him, and nothing occurs unless He intends and permits it. Believers should therefore recognize that the One God, whom none can overcome, revealed the Book to guide to truth and sent the distinction between right and wrong. In this sphere too, He has established causation and granted human beings freedom of choice: belief brings reward and disbelief chastisement, while neither is independent of His will and decree.

Al-Mizan maintains that al-tanzīl signifies sending down gradually, whereas al-inzāl signifies sending down all at once. Verses that use forms of al-tanzīl while speaking of a revelation all at once, food from heaven, or a sign do not overturn this distinction. A composite thing may be considered as one whole, as rain may be described by al-inzāl, or according to its successive parts, as its drops may be described by al-tanzīl; succession does not require long intervals. Thus, the demand that the Qur’an be revealed all at once can mean that its verses be revealed successively in one continuous stretch without considerable gaps. The proposed gloss that it means merely sending after sending is an arbitrary invention of meaning and does not solve the objection. Descent is an appropriate description of revelation because God is High, the Book is from Him, and it settles in the Messenger’s heart.

The commentary distinguishes al-ḥaqq from al-ṣidq. Al-ḥaqq concerns an established reality to which information relates, while al-ṣidq concerns information’s conformity to that reality. Here al-ḥaqq is an established fact that cannot be invalidated; bi al-ḥaqq means that the Book was revealed accompanied by truth, so falsehood cannot mingle with it. Al-taṣdīq means acknowledging truth, and what is before the Qur’an means the Torah and Injīl. The Old and New Testaments contain some revelation given to Moses and Jesus, but they also contain omissions and alterations. The Torah and Injīl existing in the Prophet’s time were the same Pentateuch and four Gospels known today; the Qur’an confirms them only partially, not wholly. Its use of the singular, divinely sent Injīl, despite the existence of several Gospels, shows that there was one Gospel revealed to Jesus which was later altered and deleted. Their early mention also alludes to the Jews and Christians, including the story of Jesus, whose affairs the chapter will discuss.

Al-Furqān is that which distinguishes one thing from another; in guidance, it distinguishes truth from falsehood in belief and knowledge and distinguishes a servant’s duties from what is not duty. It can therefore denote all basic principles and subsidiary matters revealed to prophets, whether in a book or otherwise. It has the same function as al-mīzān, the balance: religion judges people equitably, contains true knowledge, and explains their duties toward their Lord. The commentary records proposals that al-Furqān means the Qur’an, a proof separating right from wrong, the Prophet’s argument against those disputing about Jesus, divine help, or wisdom, but regards its broader meaning as fundamental.

Al-intiqām is punishment of a wrongdoer for his wrongdoing, not necessarily the emotional redress sought in human retaliation. God neither gains nor loses from His servants’ acts; rather, His true promise is to judge them with truth and repay good with good and evil with evil. His might is absolute invincibility. The severe chastisement threatened for disbelief may extend to this life as well as the hereafter. Al-Mizan says that people commonly restrict chastisement to bodily pain, loss of wealth or relatives, sickness, and weakness, whereas the Qur’anic conception is different.

Joy and sorrow depend on what one regards as fortune or misfortune, and comfort and discomfort differ according to their subject: the spirit has its own happiness and pain, the body its own, and animal and human experience are not on the same level. One who forgets his Lord lives a straitened life even amid luxury, and even wealth and children may be chastisement. A materialist, lacking divine character and treating worldly possessions, prestige, and domination as complete felicity, is distressed before obtaining them and disappointed after obtaining them. Each acquisition brings its own afflictions, and because he has no connection with the Real Cause beyond apparent causes, he finds neither solace in adversity nor peace in prosperity; his pursuit of ever further goals repeats the same frustration.

Human beings consist of an eternal spirit and a body subject to change and decay until their return to God. What blesses the spirit, such as knowledge, is real felicity. Wealth and children may also be felicity when they bless spirit and body together, provided they do not distract from God or bind one to materialism. Conversely, bodily loss or even destruction that brings spiritual blessing is a blessing, while bodily comfort that harms the spirit is the true suffering, chastisement, and evil reward. What harms both body and spirit is also chastisement, but the Qur’an calls it so because of the harm to the spirit, whereas unbelievers judge it by bodily harm. Since pleasure and pain depend on perception, people need training to perceive real happiness and unhappiness. The Qur’an trains them not to attach their hearts to other than God, to know Him as the Real Owner on whom everything depends, and to seek things only for His sake. Such a person finds either spiritual happiness or the happiness of spirit and body together; one attached to worldly pleasure eventually finds that apparent good fortune has become misfortune, with every pleasure mixed with worry and distress. The outlook of the people of God and the Qur’an thus differs from that of others, although believers occupy countless degrees between the extremes.

The Qur’an can also call bodily pain ʿadhāb, but this bodily discomfort is distinct from the real, spiritual chastisement. Thus Job speaks of Satan’s toil and torment, while Pharaoh’s people’s severe punishment is described as a trial from their Lord, though it was torment in itself and not from God.

The statement that nothing is hidden from God prevents the thought that the Mighty Lord of retribution might fail to notice someone’s disbelief and so leave it unpunished. Possibly, what is in the earth refers to actions performed by bodily organs, while what is in heaven refers to ideas settled in the mind.

Al-taṣwīr means giving form. The shaping of human beings in the wombs carries the argument beyond divine knowledge and retribution: one who rejects God’s signs has no independent power even to disbelieve, but acts through the power God has given him. He neither overpowers God’s decree nor disrupts His system, and his will cannot prevail over God’s will. God has granted people latitude to choose belief and obedience or disbelief and disobedience so that the test may be meaningful; they do not will except as God wills. Everything, including belief and disbelief, is within the all-encompassing divine decree by which each thing proceeds toward its intended end. Human rebellion itself remains within the system of free will and choice. From foetal life, human existence is set upon the path God has opened by granting freedom of will, not by compelling a particular choice.

The verse confines itself to the divine decree as it concerns human beings and also hints against Christian belief about Jesus: Christians do not deny that he developed in the womb and did not make himself. The shift from the singular, revealed to thee, to the plural, shapes you, shows that believers’ faith, no less than disbelievers’ unbelief, is not independent of the decree. Recognizing this should make believers rejoice in God’s mercy and bounties rather than be depressed by the retribution of disbelievers. The closing assertion of divine oneness condenses the argument: guidance after creation, revelation of the Book, the criterion between right and wrong, and punishment of those who disbelieve all require a god to administer them. Since there is no god but Him, He alone guides, reveals, distinguishes, and chastises, doing all by His might and wisdom.
verses.7: Al-Mizan states: The Book contains decisive verses, its basis, and ambiguous verses. Those with perversity pursue the ambiguous to mislead and impose their own interpretation; only Allah knows its interpretation. Those firmly rooted in knowledge believe that all of it is from their Lord, and only people of understanding take heed.
verses.8: Al-Mizan gives a prayer that God preserve hearts from deviation after guidance and grant His mercy, as the most liberal Giver.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan treats the prayer in (3:9) as the completion of the preceding description of those firmly rooted in knowledge. The discussion of (3:7) begins with the use of al-inzāl rather than al-tanzīl: al-inzāl is appropriate because the verse regards the Book as a complete whole and describes the characteristics of that whole. It divides the Book into decisive verses, the muḥkamāt, and ambiguous verses, the mutashābihāt, whose intended import is known by returning them to the decisive verses.

The commentary explains that muḥkamāt are protected and made precise so that ambiguity cannot enter them. This differs from passages that call the entire Book confirmed or call it conforming in its parts. The confirmation of the whole Book refers to its stable, undivided condition before its revelation and division into particular verses, while its conformity refers to the consistency of its style, eloquence, disclosure of realities, and guidance. Neither meaning is the same as the decisiveness and ambiguity that divide the revealed verses into two categories.

The decisive verses are called umm al-kitāb because al-umm is that to which something returns or in which it takes refuge. The basis of the Book is not something outside the Book; it is a part of it to which another part returns. The singular form indicates that the decisive verses are united and mutually connected. An ambiguous verse is one whose connotation cannot be settled merely on hearing it, because the hearer is left between possible meanings. When it is returned to a decisive verse, its true semantic value is fixed; it then becomes clear through the aid of the decisive verse, whereas a decisive verse is clear by itself.

Thus, wording about God’s sitting firmly upon the Throne cannot be understood bodily when it is returned to the decisive principle that nothing is like Him; it signifies mastery and firm power over the kingdom, not occupation of a place. Likewise, looking to the Lord cannot mean optical sight when returned to the declaration that visions do not comprehend Him. An abrogated command is also clarified when returned to its abrogating verse, which shows that its ruling had a limited duration. The commentary holds that the verse distinguishing decisive from ambiguous is itself decisive: to declare it ambiguous would make the entire Qur’an ambiguous, empty its own division and remedy of meaning, and undermine the Qur’an’s descriptions of itself as clear guidance, light, explanation, and a discourse free of discrepancy.

No Qur’anic verse is without meaning. Its true meaning is either the sole meaning apparent to an Arabic speaker or one of its possible meanings, and it cannot conflict with the Qur’an’s established principles: the Creator, His Oneness, prophethood, law, and resurrection. These principles determine the true meaning of a verse capable of more than one reading. In this sense, decisive verses contain the governing principles of religion, while ambiguous verses are those whose intended meanings must be determined through those principles.

Al-Mizan identifies two chief sources of such ambiguity. First are elevated spiritual and metaphysical realities. Physical-sounding expressions about God, such as His being on watch or coming, initially suggest bodily meanings to an ordinary mind, until they are returned to Qur’anic principles that deny bodily attributes and material action and reaction to God. This difficulty belongs generally to discourse about realities beyond matter, not to the Qur’an alone. Second are social laws and rules revealed piecemeal, some of which were abrogated when the circumstances for which they had been legislated ended. Their ambiguity is removed by returning the abrogated ruling to the abrogating one.

The verse accordingly separates people into two groups. Those with al-zaygh, a deviation marked by inward disturbance, act upon ambiguous verses without returning them to the decisive ones; they seek al-fitnah, which here means misleading people, and seek to impose their own interpretation. Had they referred such verses to the decisive ones before acting, their action would in effect have been an action upon the decisive verses and would not be blameworthy. Their deeper aim is to derive everything from ambiguous verses independently of the decisive foundation, a course that would destroy the foundation of religion. By contrast, those firmly rooted in knowledge act upon the decisive verses, believe in the ambiguous ones without being shaken by them, refrain from acting on them independently, and pray that their hearts not deviate after guidance.

The commentary distinguishes this return of an ambiguous verse to a decisive verse from al-taʾwīl. Derived from al-awl, returning, al-taʾwīl is a special returning base or source from which the realities of the Qur’an derive; final interpretation is only an imperfect translation. It cannot simply mean the future event with which a statement conforms. That account might cover statements about divine acts or the Day of Resurrection, but it cannot encompass laws, rational and ethical teachings, or stories whose events have already occurred. Nor is it enough to call al-taʾwīl the fact on which a statement depends, or the social benefit of a legal command. The benefit of honest measuring, for example, follows from actual honest conduct, not from the mere wording of the command. Both the benefit and the conduct are real facts; al-taʾwīl is not a property of speech as such.

The Qur’anic accounts of Moses and al-Khiḍr show the relevant kind of return. The damaging of a boat, the killing of a boy, and the repairing of a wall appeared objectionable to Moses because their purposes were hidden: preserving the boat from a king who seized sound boats, protecting believing parents from the boy’s future unbelief and oppression, and safeguarding an orphaned boys’ treasure until maturity. Their al-taʾwīl was the underlying purpose and reality of the acts, not merely the correspondence of a report to a fact. Likewise, Joseph returned dream-images to the events they represented: the dream forms were outward figures, and their interpretations were the realities behind them. The manifestation of the Qur’an’s information on the Day of Resurrection is also not merely the fulfillment of a worldly prediction, because the perception of that Day and its governing reality are unlike worldly perception.

Al-Mizan therefore concludes that a verse’s al-taʾwīl differs from its being ambiguous and from its return to a decisive verse. Al-taʾwīl belongs to the whole Qur’an, decisive and ambiguous alike, and is not a word-meaning but an external reality to which the verse points through the reality it describes. The later convention that calls a meaning contrary to a word’s apparent sense al-taʾwīl is rejected as misuse of language and misinterpretation; it was not the Qur’anic sense of the term.

In the clause that none knows its interpretation except Allah, the pronoun may apparently refer to the ambiguous part, though it may also refer to the Book as a whole. In either case, this verse apparently restricts knowledge of interpretation to God. The following and, introducing those firmly rooted in knowledge, begins a new sentence rather than joining them to God as possessors of that knowledge. The point is to contrast those whose hearts deviate with those who say that they believe in the ambiguous verses because all are from their Lord. The commentary further argues that, had the verse intended to include those firmly rooted in knowledge with God, the Messenger would have been separately named before them, as the Qur’an ordinarily names him separately when praising a group that includes him. The fact that the Book was revealed to him does not remove the force of this argument.

This restriction is, however, limited to what this verse establishes. Other verses may qualify an apparent restriction, just as Qur’anic declarations that God alone knows the unseen are qualified by the disclosure of some unseen matters to chosen apostles. Thus, this verse does not itself prove that those firmly rooted in knowledge know the Qur’an’s interpretation, but neither would other evidence showing knowledge of the Qur’an’s reality in some of them contradict it, because the verse is describing their conduct toward ambiguous verses, not comprehensively defining their knowledge.

Firm rootedness, al-rusūkh, means fixed and established knowledge of God and His signs, immune to doubt. Such people believe in and act on decisive verses; when faced with an ambiguous verse, they retain faith in it but do not act on an interpretation that conflicts with the decisive verses. Their declaration that all is from their Lord is both premise and conclusion: all verses must be believed in because all come from God; the clear verses must be followed; and the ambiguous ones must be believed in but, for action, returned to the decisive ones. Their tadhakkur, or mindful recollection, is the movement from premises to conclusion. As people of al-albāb, sound understanding free from defect, they continually remember God, ponder His signs, acquire true knowledge, turn to Him, and follow the best of what they hear.

Their prayer in (3:8) displays this rooted knowledge. They know that all authority over themselves belongs to God and that even after guidance their hearts may be made to deviate. They therefore seek protection from deviation and ask for mercy from Him. Freedom from deviation alone would not ensure firmly rooted knowledge: a person might be neither deviant nor knowledgeable, but remain in a state of ignorance and weakness. Moreover, they are still traveling toward their end and require forms of divine mercy that they cannot enumerate or even know. The first petition wards off misfortune; the second seeks the greatest good, mercy that keeps the heart alive and advances it on the straight path. By asking for an unspecified mercy from God, they admit that they know only their complete dependence on it and look directly to the Real Cause rather than to intermediary causes.

The prayer in (3:9) gives the reason for asking mercy. Creation, the call to religion, and human striving are all preliminaries to the gathering on the Day of Resurrection. On that Day no one will avail another, and no one will be helped except through divine mercy. The believers therefore leave the details of mercy to God’s discretion so that it may truly benefit them. Their assertion that the Day is beyond doubt expresses their urgent concern for that mercy, and their certainty rests on its cause: God has promised it, and God does not fail His promise. Firm knowledge requires knowledge of the cause from which the known matter proceeds.

The entire invocation uses the form of a proposition followed by its reason. Their belief is grounded in the fact that all is from their Lord; their request not to deviate is qualified by the guidance already given; and their request for mercy from God is grounded in His being the uniquely liberal Giver. The prayer does not ask for just any mercy but mercy from Him. Its restrictive second-person forms and definite predicate emphasize that He alone gives; hence only His mercy is sought. The closing shift from direct address to the divine name Allah is also meaningful: the promise of resurrection is not a private promise to the speakers but a universal promise, and the divine name expresses His sovereignty over all things. Their words and deeds therefore proceed from knowledge, which is why the Qur’an calls them firmly rooted in knowledge and people of understanding.

Al-Mizan then argues that later disputes became confused because interpreters mixed the question of decisive and ambiguous verses with that of al-taʾwīl. It insists that decisive and ambiguous cannot bear, in this context, the same meanings as the descriptions of the entire Book as confirmed or conforming. Instead of deriving the distinction from the Qur’an’s own account of verses returning to their basis, many exegetes advanced incompatible classifications.

It rejects the view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās that only three commands near the end of the Chapter of the Cattle are decisive and the initial letter-symbols are ambiguous. The view lacks proof, would leave nearly all the Qur’an in an unmentioned third category, and misstates the reports: the reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās identify those verses, and other passages as well, merely as examples of decisive verses. The converse view, attributed to Abū Fākhitah and similarly reported from Saʿīd b. Jubayr, makes the letter-symbols decisive because the Qur’an is composed from the letters and makes all other verses ambiguous. It rests on an unproved theory of the symbols and would imply that only symbols may be followed, although there is nothing to follow in them and the Qur’an commands adherence to the revealed light.

The commentary also rejects defining ambiguity as ordinary vagueness or unspecified wording. A genuinely vague expression is followed only after another expression has clarified it; what is then followed is the formerly vague expression as clarified, not merely the clarifying expression. Neither the perverse nor the rooted would follow a vague expression before clarification, whereas the verse condemns a distinctive following of ambiguous verses. It likewise rejects the restriction of ambiguity to abrogated verses and decisiveness to abrogating ones, an opinion ascribed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and others. At most abrogation is one instance of the distinction; this account leaves most verses outside either class and ignores non-abrogated verses on divine attributes and acts that are also liable to distortion. A fuller report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, which includes laws, limits, duties, parables, oaths, juxtaposition, abrogation, and action, confirms that abrogating and abrogated verses were not meant as an exhaustive division.

The definition of decisive verses as those with self-evident rational proof and ambiguous verses as those requiring thought fails either because legal injunctions would become ambiguous and acting upon them blameworthy, or because every verse has support within the coherent Book and all would become decisive. The opposing definition, which makes decisive what can be known by proof and ambiguous what is altogether unknowable, such as the time of resurrection, confuses ambiguity with al-taʾwīl. A Qur’anic verse, being a sign, must be understood either independently or through other verses; matters that are truly unknowable, such as the precise time of resurrection, are not disclosed by a verse in a way that leaves its intended meaning unknowable.

The view attributed to Mujāhid, that legal verses are decisive and other verses ambiguous because they affect one another, is defective in both directions. Legal verses too require mutual qualification and contextual clarification; yet if only legal verses were decisive, the Qur’an’s teachings about divine and spiritual realities would have no decisive verses to which they could return and would remain unknowable. Al-Shāfiʿī’s definition of decisive as admitting one interpretation and ambiguous as admitting several merely restates the terms, and becomes erroneous if interpretation is taken to mean word-meaning, since word-meanings are understood by believers and unbelievers alike and cannot be restricted to God. Restricting the two classes to detailed and repeated stories has no basis in the verse and cannot explain why following the ambiguous is connected with misleading people.

The definition attributed to Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, that ambiguous verses need explanation while decisive ones do not, is neither inclusive nor exclusive: decisive legal verses needed prophetic explanation, while abrogated verses, although treated as ambiguous, require no explanation for present action. The formulation attributed to Ibn Taymiyyah, that decisive verses are believed and acted upon while ambiguous ones are believed but not acted upon, mistakes the duty that follows the classification for the criterion by which verses are classified. It also would make every non-legal verse ambiguous and deprive the Qur’anic realities of decisive bases, while abrogated legal verses remain a counterexample.

Ibn Taymiyyah is also said to have confined ambiguous verses to descriptions of divine and prophetic attributes. Al-Mizan accepts that such verses can be ambiguous, especially for those who materialize attributes, but denies that they are the sole class. The related claim that the meanings of attributes are known but their hidden reality is known only to God is treated later under al-taʾwīl. The division of verses into what reason can reach and what it cannot is likewise unsupported, does not match the Qur’anic distinction, and excludes legal verses that are decisive although unaided human reason cannot independently discover them.

The later definition that an ambiguous verse has an interpretation contrary to its apparent wording, while a decisive verse accords with that wording, is dismissed as a new terminology alien to the verse. Ambiguity concerns more than one possible meaning, one of which is intended; its intended meaning is not its al-taʾwīl. No Qur’anic verse has a true connotation contrary to its apparent linguistic sense. When other decisive verses and the Qur’an’s own context settle an initially misleading appearance, that settled meaning is not contrary to the apparent meaning of a Book whose parts are declared to explain one another. Defining decisiveness by scholarly unanimity, ascribed to al-Aṣamm, would make every verse ambiguous because every verse has occasioned some dispute; the claim that the entire Qur’an is ambiguous is self-defeating because it relies on at least one decisive verse to prove itself.

Al-Rāghib’s extensive account is treated as the most comprehensive of the rejected theories. He includes difficult rare or polysemous words, omissions, additions, altered word order, divine attributes, resurrection matters, general and particular wording, obligatory and recommended commands, abrogation, occasions of revelation, and conditions affecting validity. He then divides ambiguity into what no one can know, what ordinary people can know through linguistic means, and what some rooted scholars can know. Al-Mizan replies that lexical, grammatical, and syntactical difficulties are solved by dictionaries, grammar, and other linguistic methods, not by returning verses to decisive verses. Nor do such difficulties normally furnish a way to mislead people through private interpretation. Al-Rāghib’s account also wrongly makes interpretation peculiar to ambiguous verses.

The commentary’s own conclusion is that an ambiguous verse permits more than one meaning, but its more immediately apparent meaning is doubtful because it conflicts with the semantic force of a decisive verse, not because of an ordinary linguistic defect. Its intended meaning can only be fixed through the decisive verse. The initially attractive but unintended meaning will often be the one most easily accepted by common minds. Al-Mizan traces many doctrinal schisms to neglect of this rule: materializing God, asserting complete determinism or complete human independence, imputing sins to prophets, denying or separating divine attributes, and similar claims. It also traces to the same tendency claims that religious law can be abandoned after attaining a supposed goal, replaced whenever people judge another law more beneficial, or reduced to obsolete social arrangements; it includes the reinterpretation of prophetic miracles as merely ordinary events among such distortions. It holds that the later suspension and alteration of religious laws proceeded through this kind of self-directed interpretation. The root of such perversity is attachment to the material world and surrender to desire; its remedy is remembrance of the Day of Reckoning. This is why the prayer ends by affirming the certain gathering and God’s unfailing promise.

The commentary further distinguishes three explanations of the decisive verses being the basis of the Book. The first makes them merely the foundation of religious beliefs and deeds, so that they are believed and acted upon while ambiguous verses are only believed. The second says that ambiguous verses are believed but, for action, returned to a relevant decisive verse, as an abrogated command is returned to its abrogating command. Al-Mizan accepts a third and fuller explanation: decisive verses are the basis because they clarify ambiguous ones and remove their ambiguity. Al-umm signifies not a bare foundation but the return of a branch to its root or of a part to its whole. Ambiguous meanings thus branch from and return to decisive meanings. Their ambiguity does not arise from possessing al-taʾwīl, since decisive verses also have al-taʾwīl.

The interpretation of looking to the Lord is reinforced, in this account, by Qur’anic descriptions of the Prophet’s heart seeing great signs. The commentary infers that the heart has a kind of sight distinct from bodily vision and from discursive thought, which joins subject and predicate. It is a direct orientation of the heart toward its object. The same principle applies to all other ambiguous verses: decisive verses disclose what an ambiguous expression actually signifies.

Al-Mizan surveys four principal theories of al-taʾwīl. The first identifies it with exegesis, explanation, or the meaning of a sentence, particularly the meaning of ambiguous verses. The second identifies it with a meaning contrary to the apparent wording. The third treats it as a series of hidden or successive meanings behind the manifest wording, whether as concomitants or as an esoteric meaning contained within the outward one. The fourth treats it as an external reality upon which speech rests: the purpose behind a command, the event narrated in a story, or the reality of present and future matters, while reserving full knowledge of divine attributes and resurrection matters to God. Several subsidiary distinctions—between tafsīr and taʾwīl as word and sentence explanation, certain and selected meaning, clear and difficult meaning, transmitted explanation and rational inference—are regarded as variations of the first theory.

All these accounts share the mistake of treating al-taʾwīl as a meaning, an ordinary event, or a cause referred to by the verse. For Al-Mizan, it is a particular external reality related to the verse as the purpose of a proverb is related to its outward form, or as an interior is related to an exterior. The first theory would make some Qur’anic verses unintelligible despite the Qur’an’s declaration that it is understandable to ordinary minds; confining such unintelligibility to letter-symbols has no proof and cannot explain actual doctrinal misguidance. The second would make Qur’anic verses genuinely contradictory unless their clear linguistic meanings were arbitrarily discarded; such a procedure could reconcile any contradictory writing and would deprive the Qur’an’s freedom from discrepancy of evidential force. The third correctly recognizes levels of meaning but confuses such levels of word-meaning, which depend chiefly on intelligence, with al-taʾwīl, whose knowledge is connected with purification.

The fourth theory rightly says that interpretation belongs to the whole Qur’an and is not word-meaning, but it wrongly identifies every fact mentioned by a verse with its interpretation and restricts ambiguity to divine attributes and the Resurrection. If the interpretation of the entire Book were simply its narrated and practical facts, those facts could be known by many people, including people with perversity of heart. If the restriction applied only to ambiguous verses, then misguidance would still arise from misinterpreting laws and prophetic narratives as well as attributes and resurrection matters. The commentary consequently repeats that al-taʾwīl is the sublime reality to which a verse points, a reality for which the Qur’anic expressions provide an intelligible likeness rather than a verbal definition.

The debate over whether anyone besides God knows interpretation is thus also partly misframed. Some early exegetes, some Shāfiʿites, and most Shīʿites treated the conjunction before those firmly rooted in knowledge as joining them to God in knowledge of interpretation; most early exegetes and the Ḥanafites treated it as beginning a new sentence. Al-Mizan says both sides commonly confuse knowing al-taʾwīl with returning ambiguous verses to decisive ones. The context aims to praise the rooted for their faithful conduct toward the Book, not to establish that they share God’s knowledge of its interpretation. Thus, in this verse, the absolute restriction remains intact.

Reports used in the dispute do not alter that result. Sunni reports that the Prophet prayed for Ibn ʿAbbās to receive knowledge of religion and interpretation, and reports that Ibn ʿAbbās claimed to be among the firmly rooted and to know interpretation, use interpretation in the sense of intended meaning and are irrelevant to the Qur’anic sense established here. Uncommon recitations attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ubay b. Kaʿb, and Ibn Masʿūd, which separate God’s knowledge from the rooted, have no probative value; even if accepted, they would show only that the verse does not prove the rooted know interpretation, not that they do not. A narration transmitted by al-Ṭabarānī from Abū Mālik al-Ashʿarī warns that a believer may seek to interpret the Book when none knows its interpretation except God, but it concerns ordinary believers and does not decide the case of those firmly rooted in knowledge. Reports commanding adherence to decisive verses and belief in ambiguous ones concern practical conduct rather than the disputed knowledge. A marfūʿ report cited by al-Ālūsī through Ibn Jarīr from Ibn ʿAbbās, which says that only God knows the ambiguous, is also challenged because names are omitted from its chain, it conflicts with other reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, and it treats interpretation as the meaning of ambiguity rather than as the Qur’an uses it.

Nevertheless, Al-Mizan maintains that other Qur’anic evidence establishes the possibility that someone besides God may know interpretation. Because people differ widely in their ability to understand what lies beyond sensory experience, while guidance addresses all people, these realities must be expressed through familiar images, parables, and forms analogous to what people already know. Al-Mizan explains that these verses address a Muslim community beset by internal hypocrisy and hostile external forces. Following warnings against manipulating the ambiguous Qur’anic passages, they call the Muslims to unity, firmness, and patience, and turn to the unbelievers and polytheists who imagine that wealth, children, and worldly power can make them independent of Allah. The verses refute this illusion through the fate of Pharaoh’s people and promise that such enemies will be overcome. Believers, meanwhile, are warned not to be ensnared by worldly desires, but to seek felicity and Allah’s enduring pleasure.

The commentary says that human beings first recognize their dependence through such intermediate causes as food and offspring. Desire for food develops into attachment to wealth, which is taken to solve every difficulty; wealth and children then appear to be the sources of felicity. Forgetting that these are not independent causes blinds one to the Lord and His signs and leads to disbelief. Wealth is mentioned before children because dependence on wealth, or food as a kind of wealth, comes first, even though love for children may sometimes exceed love of wealth. The continuing wont of Pharaoh’s people and earlier peoples was the same persistent rejection of divine signs. Al-Mizan holds that being caught bi-dhunūbihim does not merely mean being punished because of sins; the juxtaposition strongly suggests that sins themselves are the instrument of punishment. Divine requital is therefore all-encompassing: a person’s own sin remains with him inwardly and outwardly, becoming a fire from which neither flight nor stillness can provide refuge.

The return to the divine name then displays His universal authority and the ease with which He catches those who rebel against Him. The wider subject includes people’s purposes, acts, obedience, and disobedience. Allah’s comprehensive lordship is not weakened by disbelief or sin: all things occur within the decreed systems of causation and trial, while recompense in the next world follows good and evil. Likewise, the view that only commendable acts may be attributed to Allah is correct only as regards direct attribution. Indirect attribution through permission is necessary if He is truly the Lord, Creator, and Owner of everything.

The universe is one interrelated system in which events and causes affect one another and all proceed toward Allah. Divine wisdom therefore requires this world of opposites. In creation generally, all making and unmaking are directly Allah’s; in human action, virtuous deeds are directly attributed to Him as guidance, while Satanic whispering, domination by desires, and oppression may be attributed to Him indirectly through permission. The unrestricted power that people mistakenly seek in hoarded wealth is thus found only through Allah’s pleasure.

It agrees that worldly bounties adorn this brief life, but says that the objection wrongly removes the very human being who is to endure. Resurrection gives this same human entity eternity and removes change and death; it does not replace it with a different entity. Accordingly, its joys and pains must be akin to those a human being knows in this life, though eternal rather than transitory. A tradition of the Messenger of God states that as one lives, so one dies, and as one dies, so one is raised.

Worldly life together with the good or evil a person earns is itself provision for the hereafter. Natural pleasures first serve bodily survival, but for a being of perception and will they become real perfections only insofar as they are known and desired. A person finds felicity in what he consciously recognizes and wishes for, and misery in what he recognizes but does not wish for. Paradise is the eternal attainment of the pleasures desired by the believer, with more besides; Hell is the enduring deprivation and punishment corresponding to evil.

Those who guard against evil call Allah their Lord, thereby confessing servitude and seeking His mercy. Their declaration that they believe is not an attempt to establish a claim over Him, since faith itself is His grace. Rather, it is an appeal to His promise to forgive believers; the word therefore links their firm declaration of faith to their plea for forgiveness. Forgiveness by itself does not necessarily entail release from punishment. Protection from the Fire and admission to the Garden are divine grace, not a servant’s independent right, although Allah has mercifully promised forgiveness, protection, and the Garden to those who believe. The commentary nevertheless infers that deliverance from punishment is, in this connection, forgiveness together with entry into the Garden.

The five qualities named are essential to piety. Patience includes steadfastness in obedience, abstinence from disobedience, and forbearance in calamity. Truthfulness is apparently truthfulness in speech, since a broader conformity of inward and outward life would encompass the other virtues; Allah knows better. Devoutness is humility before Allah and includes worship and obedience. Benevolent spending gives money to those entitled to it. Seeking forgiveness before dawn entails prayer in the last part of the night; traditions identify it with the voluntary prayer after midnight and seeking forgiveness in its al-qunūt invocation.

Al-Mizan explains al-shahādah as both seeing or knowing by presence and describing that knowledge so as to preserve truth from denial, concealment, or forgetfulness. Allah’s witness that there is no god but He confirms the preceding teaching: nothing, including wealth, children, or worldly adornment, can avail against Him; if it could, it would itself be a god or depend on another god. Allah bears this verbal witness while maintaining creation with justice. He administers a created system of cause and effect whose causes, effects, and relations all return to Him, and He has placed worldly bounties on humanity’s road so that they may be used for the hereafter rather than treated as a permanent settlement.

Allah’s justice is both self-evidencing and evidence of His Oneness. Human testimony is accepted from a just witness, one who follows the straight path of nature and puts things in their proper places. Therefore the natural system that establishes such justice is itself pure justice, and it is Allah’s work. When people object to events in nature, later inquiry may reveal their reasons; if it does not, this proves only ignorance of the reason, not its absence. Were there other gods, each could at most govern a separate sphere, and the universe could not display an all-encompassing justice. The justice of creation thus proves that its Creator is One.

The witness in this verse is verbal testimony, not merely evidence supplied by divine acts, even though the unity of the created order also evidences the Creator’s Oneness. The angels bear witness because they are Allah’s honoured servants who act only by His command and declare His glory. Those possessed of knowledge bear witness after contemplating the signs in the universe and within themselves. The phrase maintaining His creation with justice is a circumstantial description of Allah as He bears witness; it is not itself an object jointly witnessed to by Allah, the angels, and those possessed of knowledge.

The commentary rejects the claim that verbal divine testimony would create a vicious circle because belief in Allah would be needed before accepting His word. A report from one whose truthfulness is established can produce certainty equal to, or stronger than, independent rational proof, and Allah cannot utter falsehood. His declaration therefore truly establishes both His own witness and His report of the angels’ and knowledgeable persons’ witness. It also refutes polytheism. Those who assign partners to Allah generally regard them as intercessors or links whom Allah has taken to Himself; hidden polytheists likewise seek worldly benefit, prestige, or others’ approval through acts ostensibly directed to Allah. If Allah had any such partner, He would know it; the angels who execute His commands would know it; and knowledgeable people would perceive signs of its creative or governing role. Their shared witness that no such god exists therefore decisively denies every partner.

The repeated declaration that there is no god but He is not a further element of the preceding argument but a parenthetical praise demanded by Allah’s sublimity whenever His lack of partners is affirmed. He alone is the Mighty, whose absolute power admits no partner to diminish it, and the Wise, whose wisdom allows no one to interfere in creation or the management of affairs.
