Natural pleasures first serve bodily survival, but for a being of perception and will they become real perfections only insofar as they are known and desired. A person finds felicity in what he consciously recognizes and wishes for, and misery in what he recognizes but does not wish for. Paradise is the eternal attainment of the pleasures desired by the believer, with more besides; Hell is the enduring deprivation and punishment corresponding to evil.

Those who guard against evil call Allah their Lord, thereby confessing servitude and seeking His mercy. Their declaration that they believe is not an attempt to establish a claim over Him, since faith itself is His grace. Rather, it is an appeal to His promise to forgive believers; the word therefore links their firm declaration of faith to their plea for forgiveness. Forgiveness by itself does not necessarily entail release from punishment. Protection from the Fire and admission to the Garden are divine grace, not a servant’s independent right, although Allah has mercifully promised forgiveness, protection, and the Garden to those who believe. The commentary nevertheless infers that deliverance from punishment is, in this connection, forgiveness together with entry into the Garden.

The five qualities named are essential to piety. Patience includes steadfastness in obedience, abstinence from disobedience, and forbearance in calamity. Truthfulness is apparently truthfulness in speech, since a broader conformity of inward and outward life would encompass the other virtues; Allah knows better. Devoutness is humility before Allah and includes worship and obedience. Benevolent spending gives money to those entitled to it. Seeking forgiveness before dawn entails prayer in the last part of the night; traditions identify it with the voluntary prayer after midnight and seeking forgiveness in its al-qunūt invocation.

Al-Mizan explains al-shahādah as both seeing or knowing by presence and describing that knowledge so as to preserve truth from denial, concealment, or forgetfulness. Allah’s witness that there is no god but He confirms the preceding teaching: nothing, including wealth, children, or worldly adornment, can avail against Him; if it could, it would itself be a god or depend on another god. Allah bears this verbal witness while maintaining creation with justice. He administers a created system of cause and effect whose causes, effects, and relations all return to Him, and He has placed worldly bounties on humanity’s road so that they may be used for the hereafter rather than treated as a permanent settlement.

Allah’s justice is both self-evidencing and evidence of His Oneness. Human testimony is accepted from a just witness, one who follows the straight path of nature and puts things in their proper places. Therefore the natural system that establishes such justice is itself pure justice, and it is Allah’s work. When people object to events in nature, later inquiry may reveal their reasons; if it does not, this proves only ignorance of the reason, not its absence. Were there other gods, each could at most govern a separate sphere, and the universe could not display an all-encompassing justice. The justice of creation thus proves that its Creator is One.

The witness in this verse is verbal testimony, not merely evidence supplied by divine acts, even though the unity of the created order also evidences the Creator’s Oneness. The angels bear witness because they are Allah’s honoured servants who act only by His command and declare His glory. Those possessed of knowledge bear witness after contemplating the signs in the universe and within themselves. The phrase maintaining His creation with justice is a circumstantial description of Allah as He bears witness; it is not itself an object jointly witnessed to by Allah, the angels, and those possessed of knowledge.

The commentary rejects the claim that verbal divine testimony would create a vicious circle because belief in Allah would be needed before accepting His word. A report from one whose truthfulness is established can produce certainty equal to, or stronger than, independent rational proof, and Allah cannot utter falsehood. His declaration therefore truly establishes both His own witness and His report of the angels’ and knowledgeable persons’ witness. It also refutes polytheism. Those who assign partners to Allah generally regard them as intercessors or links whom Allah has taken to Himself; hidden polytheists likewise seek worldly benefit, prestige, or others’ approval through acts ostensibly directed to Allah. If Allah had any such partner, He would know it; the angels who execute His commands would know it; and knowledgeable people would perceive signs of its creative or governing role. Their shared witness that no such god exists therefore decisively denies every partner.

The repeated declaration that there is no god but He is not a further element of the preceding argument but a parenthetical praise demanded by Allah’s sublimity whenever His lack of partners is affirmed. He alone is the Mighty, whose absolute power admits no partner to diminish it, and the Wise, whose wisdom allows no one to interfere in creation or the management of affairs.
verses.19: Al-Mizan states that Islam alone is the religion with Allah; those given the Book differed only after knowledge came to them, from mutual envy, and disbelief in Allah’s signs brings His swift reckoning.
verses.20: Al-Mizan says that, if they dispute, the Prophet and his followers affirm complete submission to Allah and summon the People of the Book and the unlearned to submit. Submission is right guidance; if they refuse, the Prophet need only deliver the message, while Allah sees His servants.
verses.21: Al-Mizan announces a painful chastisement for those who disbelieve in Allah’s signs, unjustly kill prophets, and kill people who enjoin justice.
verses.22: Al-Mizan says that their deeds are nullified in this world and the hereafter, and they will have no helpers.
verses.23: Al-Mizan describes those given a portion of the Book who, when invited to Allah’s Book for judgment, partly turn away and withdraw.
verses.24: Al-Mizan says that they claim the Fire will touch them only for a counted number of days, while their own forgeries deceive them in religion.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan identifies these verses as concerning the People of the Book—the Jews and Christians—the last and most important of the three groups discussed in the chapter, much of which was revealed about them.

Al-Mizan takes al-Islām here, apparently, in its literal sense of surrendering oneself to God. The religion ordained by God is one shariah: the religion described in the Books revealed to the prophets and indicated by the Divine signs. It is willing surrender to the truth through correct belief and sincere deeds, accepting all the knowledge and commandments God has sent down. Although the laws of the prophets differed in quality and quantity, and in degrees of perfection suited to their nations’ capacities, they contained no discrepancy or contradiction: all summoned people to submit to God’s will and to the commands conveyed by His prophets. One must therefore accept what has been clearly explained and stop at doubtful matters, submitting to God rather than interpreting them according to desire and personal thought.

The People of the Book knew from their revealed Book that religion was one, but differed through envy and injustice. Though they continued to believe in God, this made them disbelieve in His signs and in the Book that had explained religion’s reality. God’s quick reckoning includes this world, where they receive disgrace and ignominy, and the hereafter, where they receive the painful chastisement of the Fire; the later statement that their works are null in both worlds confirms this scope. Here, religion means shariah, not a created instinct to believe in God; and al-āyāt means the verses of the Divine Books, not signs in creation leading to belief in one God. The verse thus threatens the People of the Book for their envy and rebellion. Al-Mizan says this probably explains why the following verse joins them to the polytheists, and why its question about submission also carries a threat.

Al-Mizan understands the People of the Book’s dispute as a claim that their religious differences arose from sincere intellectual inquiry rather than envy, injustice, arrogance, or rebellion, and that the Prophet’s call was likewise merely another conclusion of thought. The command that the Prophet declare his and his followers’ total submission to God, then ask the People of the Book and the unlearned whether they too submit, is a direct rebuttal. The Divine Books and untainted wisdom agree that religion is submission, so no objection can be made to the Prophet’s submission. If they submit, they will be rightly guided, accept what was revealed to the Prophet and the earlier prophets, and their difference will end. If they turn away, he should not pursue a dispute about a self-evident truth, but only deliver the message.

The phrase literally rendered as submitting one’s face to God signifies complete, willing obedience, because al-Wajh, the face or front, contains most of the senses and organs of perception. The inclusion of the Prophet’s followers demonstrates his excellence and elevates their rank by joining them to him. Al-Mizan identifies the unlearned, al-Ummiyy, with the polytheists, contrasting them with the People of the Book and noting that the latter used this designation for them. It adds that al-Ummiyy means one who does not read or write; an editor’s note expressly qualifies this by saying that it does not mean not knowing how to read and write. The two groups are joined because both believed in religion and God, despite their respective monotheism and polytheism.

The statement that, if they turn back, the Prophet need only deliver the message and Allah sees the servants has three implications. It forbids needless disputation with one who denies a self-evident truth, because it produces obstinacy. It assigns total authority over people and their affairs to God: the Prophet is a messenger who conveys the revelation, not a guard over people. And it threatens the People of the Book and the polytheists: their refusal is obstinate opposition and heedlessness of truth, and God will deal with and punish them as they deserve. Al-Mizan therefore rejects the view of some exegetes that the verse establishes freedom of religious belief or absence of compulsion; in its reading, it threatens disbelievers with chastisement if they do not submit. Calling them servants reminds them that they are wholly dependent on God, whether or not they consciously submit, and cannot escape His judgment.

Al-Mizan applies the threat of (3:21-22) to the People of the Book, especially the Jews. The verbal forms indicate persistent, habitual disbelief in Divine communications, rejection of revealed truth through envy and arrogance, murder of prophets, and murder of compatriots who enjoined justice and sought to restrain injustice and rebellion. It says Jewish history confirms this as a national characteristic, and that Christians followed in their footsteps by killing many good Christians. The painful chastisement manifests divine wrath in both worlds: the Fire in the hereafter, and in this world slaughter, dispersion, loss of lives and property, and enmity and hatred among themselves continuing to the Day of Resurrection. The nullification of works further shows that one who kills a person solely for enjoining good and forbidding evil forfeits his good deeds, and that intercession will not avail such a killer, for they have no helpers.

Their refusal, when invited to the Book of God to decide their disputes, further displays their envy and rebellion. They turn away because they are deluded that the Fire will touch them only for a few days and because their own forgeries deceive them. Al-Mizan says that being given only a portion of the Book indicates that Jews and Christians possess only portions of the revealed Scriptures: they have altered, changed, and edited them so extensively that most of the original has been lost. Thus, God knows better, they reject the Book’s judgment through their claims and their forgeries, behaving as though they had no need of God’s Book.

Al-Mizan explains how people may be deceived by what they themselves forged: the forgery may have originated with an earlier generation, while later generations are treated as one nation because they approve their ancestors’ act. It also says it is not improbable that the People of the Book, particularly the Jews, knowingly succumbed to or even boasted of their deception. Ingrained psychological traits can override knowledge, as people persist in harmful habits despite knowing their harm. Their perennial indiscipline produced arrogance, envy, rebellion, and an overpowering attraction to base desires. They forged religious falsehoods, repeatedly taught them while knowing them to be lies, and eventually believed them themselves; repeated falsehood displaced truth in their minds and deceived whole nations, leading them to refuse submission to God and the truth revealed in His Book.

For (3:25), Al-Mizan says the omitted expression governed by how is understood from the context as asking how they will fare. The verse continues the threat: those who turn away from the Book cannot defeat God’s judgment. On the certain, approaching Day of Reckoning, they will be gathered and become fully submissive, in contrast to their worldly arrogance; this contrast explains the wording We shall gather them together rather than raise them or make them alive. Its final synthesis, qualified by God knows better, is that their forged religion and arrogant refusal to submit lead them to turn from the Book, yet on that certain Day judgment will be decisively, truthfully, and justly pronounced, each soul will receive in full what it earned, and none will be wronged. Knowing this, they must not turn away as though they could frustrate God’s purpose or overrule His decrees: all power belongs to God, and this life is only a trial.
verses.26: Al-Mizan presents God as the sole Master of the Kingdom: as He pleases, He grants or removes rule and honor; all good is in His hand, for He has power over all things.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan relates these verses to the preceding warning directed especially at the Jews, whose worldly chastisement included the loss of kingdom and enduring abasement. More centrally, they express the chapter’s theme that creation and all its affairs lie wholly in God’s hand: He grants and removes kingdom, honor, good, and sustenance as He pleases.

The commentary says that the verse teaches believers to seek refuge humbly with God, rather than be misled by hypocrites, polytheists, and the People of the Book, who imagined that dominion and honor were independently in their own hands. Such an illusion destroys those who hold it, whereas God alone bestows every good and sustenance.

It distinguishes real possession from conventional possession. Real possession is an inherent, untransferable relation by which a possessor can dispose of a thing that depends on him for its existence and cannot be separated from him without perishing. God possesses the universe and all its affairs in this real sense. Conventional possession, by contrast, is a transferable social institution, devised so that people may obtain benefits from worldly things; it exists only through convention. Kingdom is a form of possession: an ownership over the ownership of a people, by which the ruler manages what they possess without their management conflicting with his. Both possession and kingdom have real and conventional forms.

God is the absolute real Owner because everything depends upon Him in its essence and existence, and nothing can prevent His disposal of it. He is also the absolute real King: throughout creation, causes possess their effects, things possess their faculties, and faculties possess their acts; since God owns every owner and every possession, He is King over all kingship. Conventional ownership and kingship also belong to Him. His bestowal of ownership presupposes that He owns what He gives, and as Lawgiver and Ruler He regulates what people hold. He owned all things before they came into human hands, remains their Owner while people hold them, and inherits them when their holders are gone.

Thus, “O Allah, Master of the Kingdom” means that every kingdom belongs to God and is bestowed by Him; that His being God is the basis of His mastery; and, “And God knows better,” that “the Kingdom” includes both real and conventional kingdom. The first verse concerns God’s management of conventional kingdom, while the next concerns His management of real kingdom.

The grant and removal of kingdom is unrestricted: it includes kingdoms acquired lawfully or unlawfully, justly or unjustly. Kingdom itself is a Divine bounty capable of benefiting and improving society. It is condemned in an unworthy ruler not for being kingdom as such, but because he has usurped it or governs through injustice and oppression. For a good, capable, just ruler it is a bounty; for an undeserving ruler it is an affliction and trial. In either case it is attributed to God and tests both ruler and ruled. God’s doing what He pleases does not mean purposeless or irrational action: it affirms that no one compels Him, while all His acts and decrees aim at His servants’ good and welfare.

Exaltation means being difficult to subdue, while abasement is the opposite, being susceptible to subjugation. True might and honor belong inseparably to God’s absolute kingship. Any honor possessed by another is His gift; the honor granted to the Messenger and the believers is real, whereas the self-exaltation of unbelievers is humiliation disguised as might. Everything other than God is inherently abased unless He exalts it.

Al-khayr denotes what is selected as suitable for attaining an end; the ultimate good is what is desired for itself. Although the word carries a sense of selection and is often used where English would say “better,” it is not grammatically a comparative. God is absolute good because He is the ultimate destination of all things, yet the Qur’an does not use “the Good” as an independent Divine name, since that would suggest a general comparison with beings wholly subject to Him. It can, however, describe Him or occur in relational descriptions such as the best of sustainers.

“In Thine hand is the good” restricts every desired good exclusively to God’s management and control. It explains why He gives or removes kingdom and honor: these are among the goods that He alone dispenses. The removal of kingdom and abasement are also related to good, because evil at the level of creation is the absence or withholding of a good, just as removal is the non-bestowal of what could have been given. Such withholding may be attributed to God, who acts for the welfare of the whole order and cannot be compelled or questioned by His creatures. Yet sins, errors, and improprieties must not be said to emanate from Him.

The commentary therefore distinguishes the level of creation from that of legislation. At the former, good is a positive reality and evil is its privation; gain and loss, good and evil, all issue from the Divine good. At the latter, obedience and disobedience are human acts freely chosen, so their moral quality and responsibility belong to human beings. God may be said to assist good deeds or to withhold His assistance from evil ones according to the reasons requiring either, but evil acts themselves are not ascribed to Him. Al-Mizan rejects an exegete’s attempt to supply an unstated “and evil” after “in Thine hand is the good.” Although it regards the Muʿtazilite refusal to attribute evil to God even indirectly as mistaken, that does not license additions to the Qur’anic wording. God’s absolute power explains the exclusivity of good in His hand: any power appearing in another is received through His authority.

Apparently, the entering of night into day and day into night refers to the continual variation in the lengths of day and night through the year according to latitude and the earth’s position in relation to the sun. In one hemisphere day lengthens while night shortens during one half of the year, and the reverse happens during the other half; the opposite occurs in the other hemisphere. Changes occur even at the poles and equator, despite their apparent equality of day and night.

The bringing forth of living from dead and dead from living is explained first as the emergence of a believer from an unbeliever and of an unbeliever from a believer, since belief is called life and light, and disbelief death and darkness. It may also be understood generally as the production of living plants and animals from insentient earth and their return to it through death. Al-Mizan reports the view of some scientists that life merely developed from one germ into another and did not arise from senseless matter, connecting this with their belief that the universe arose by itself. It replies that living germs too succumb to death, thereby establishing the correlation of life and death.

This verse displays God’s management of His real possession, as the preceding verse displays His management of conventional possession. Its four changes correspond to the four acts previously mentioned. The giving and taking of kingdom are paralleled by night’s entering day and day’s entering night: rule imposes authority over people and curtails some of their freedom, like night’s dominance over part of the day, while the removal of rule is its converse. Exaltation resembles the bringing forth of life from death, because honor brings one from obscurity into recognition; abasement corresponds to bringing forth death from life. The Qur’anic depiction of day as manifest and night as blotted away, and of life as the source of knowledge and power, reinforces these correspondences. Might and respect mirror life, while humiliation and abasement mirror death.

The final clause, “and Thou givest sustenance to whom Thou pleasest, without measure,” explains the preceding acts through the more general fact that God is the Sustainer. It stands parallel to the earlier declaration that all good is in His hand. Al-Rizq originally referred to food supplied by one person to another, then broadened to every useful thing received by someone, including wealth, prestige, family, supporters, beauty, knowledge, and prophethood.

In reality, God alone provides sustenance. When people are called sustainers, they are only means through which His gift reaches His servants; they possess no independent sustaining power. Whatever good a person receives, uses, and benefits from in existence is his sustenance and is bestowed by God.

A benefit obtained through sin is not sustenance at the level of legislation, because God neither enjoins indecency nor could He forbid a thing while making a servant’s provision depend on it. At the level of creation, however, even such a benefit is sustenance, since religious obligation does not extend to that level. God’s giving kingdom and wealth to tyrants such as Nimrod, Pharaoh, and Korah is likewise a trial and a completion of proof against them, allowing them to pursue their chosen error. What seems harmful in a Divine gift is harmful only relatively: it may serve a wider good within the universal order, or a person may himself misuse it.

For practical purposes, sustenance, good, and creation coincide: every sustenance is good and created, and every created thing can be sustenance and good. Yet they differ in meaning. Sustenance presupposes a recipient who needs and benefits from it; good presupposes one who selects it as fitting; creation does not require any actual or imagined prior thing, because each created thing is itself the direct object of creation.

Every sustenance and good comes gratuitously from God, not as payment for something supplied by the creature, for everything that could be offered already belongs to Him. Although He has undertaken to sustain every creature, so that sustenance is in this sense a right established by His own promise, no creature possesses an independent claim against Him. Hence one who acquires provision unlawfully must originally have been allotted lawful provision: it is inconceivable that God would oblige a person to obtain his provision unlawfully and then punish him for doing so.

The commentary distinguishes a general mercy and sustenance, encompassing every creature’s preservation and survival, from a special mercy and sustenance reserved for those who follow the path of felicity and righteousness and remaining within lawful limits. Both are foreordained and measured. Guidance is a special mercy decreed for every person at the legislative level through the sending of prophets and books; lawful sustenance is likewise determined at that level. Strictly, a person’s sustenance is only what he actually uses and benefits from, not necessarily all the wealth placed in his possession.

Finally, “without measure” means that Divine sustenance has no price or exchange demanded from its recipient, not that it is unlimited or unmeasured in amount. All things are created according to measure, and sustenance too is measured according to God’s pleasure. The verses therefore establish that possession and kingdom belong exclusively to God; every good comes from His hand; sustenance is His uncompensated gift; and kingdom, might, honor, wealth, prestige, and other social goods are forms of the sustenance He gives His servants.
verses.28: Al-Mizan states that believers must not prefer unbelievers to believers as friends; whoever does so has no bond with Allah, except in guarding against them from fear. Allah warns them of Himself, to whom all return.
verses.29: Al-Mizan states that Allah knows all that hearts conceal or reveal, everything in the heavens and earth, and has power over all things.
verses.30: Al-Mizan states that every soul will find its good and evil deeds present, and will wish its evil far distant. Allah warns them of Himself while remaining Compassionate to His servants.
verses.31: Al-Mizan: If you love Allah, follow the Messenger; Allah will love you and forgive your sins; He is Forgiving, Merciful.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan treats these verses as connected to the preceding admonition of the People of the Book and the polytheists. If “unbelievers” includes the People of the Book, the command forbids friendship with both them and the polytheists; if it denotes only the polytheists, it forbids friendship with them and summons believers to God's party, loving Him and His Messenger.

It explains al-Awliyā as a term first denoting guardianship—the authority to manage another's affairs—and then love, through which the beloved gains influence over the lover's life. Here, taking unbelievers as friends means forming a psychological rapport with them. Preferring them to believers as one's loved ones and models corrupts vision, thought, character, and conduct; the nearer one comes to them, the farther one moves from believers. Qur'anic prohibitions on such friendship contain qualifications specifying the forbidden kind, and this verse concerns friendship that prefers unbelievers over believers. The wording also places believers above them in rank.

Belief and disbelief are irreconcilably opposed in thought, deed, and the journey toward God, whereas friendship requires unity and rapport. Such preference first spoils the fruits of faith, then its branches, and finally its roots. Thus, one who does it has nothing to do with Allah: he no longer belongs to God's party, and his thoughts and deeds become those of Islam's enemies.

The exception is a disjoined one: taqiyyah is an outward display of attachment compelled by fear, without real love, and fear and love have opposite effects on the heart. Al-Mizan holds that the verse clearly permits taqiyyah, as do traditions of the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt and the verse concerning one compelled while his heart remains at rest in faith. Qur'an, sunnah, and reason support it, because maintaining outwardly good relations with enemies of religion may in some circumstances preserve the truth, while abandoning taqiyyah serves no purpose.

The warning that Allah cautions people of Himself is exceptionally severe. The one who gives such friendship preference is left directly before Allah's chastisement, with no veil, protector, helper, or intercessor. Al-Mizan calls this friendship a transgression that rejects God's guardianship, joins His enemies, and destroys religion from within. Unlike an open enemy, an inwardly accepted enemy gradually reshapes Muslims' manners, deeds, and thoughts until disbelief displaces belief and Islam's tenets and symbols are discarded. The threatened punishment is firmly decreed and cannot be averted; the return to Allah reinforces this threat. The commentary also regards this admonition as a prediction, expressed as warning, of developments that would later occur in the ummah, while deferring its fuller explanation.

On (3:29), Al-Mizan relates the verse to the earlier statement that Allah calls people to account for what they disclose or conceal. There, disclosure precedes concealment because accounting is usually manifest; here concealment precedes disclosure because the subject is Allah's knowledge, especially of hearts. The Messenger is ordered to convey the warning because Allah does not directly address those whom He knows will disobey by befriending unbelievers; this itself displays divine displeasure. Allah's knowledge encompasses heaven and earth, and His power encompasses all things.

For (3:30), it says that “On the day” apparently remains part of the message to be conveyed: it may imply “remember” or “describe,” or it may qualify the preceding statement that Allah knows. On the latter reading, it does not mean that Allah only then knows hidden matters; rather, servants will then plainly witness the effects of His all-encompassing knowledge, just as they will plainly witness His exclusive kingdom, power, and command.

Finding deeds “present” means that good and evil deeds already exist and are preserved by Allah, then brought forth on the Day of Judgment; this supports the embodiment of deeds. Every good deed, however slight, and every evil deed, however insignificant, will be found. The evildoer's wish for a long interval from his evil shows his sorrow, just as the presence of good entails the good-doer's happiness. He wishes for separation in time rather than the deed's disappearance because, seeing it preserved by Allah, he knows that wishing it away is futile. The repeated warning may specifically concern punishment on the Day of Judgment, whereas the first warning may concern the worldly result of the offense or both lives. Allah's compassion does not soften the warning; it is compassion that warns servants beforehand, because the offense would bring punishment without an intercessor or protector.

On (3:31), Al-Mizan says that sincere religion requires a heart detached from everything besides Allah—not only other deities and worldly aims, but even desire for the Garden or escape from the Fire—and attached exclusively to Him. This is the love of Allah. Love binds the lover to the beloved and seeks reciprocal love; yet not every claimed love is true. True love of Allah requires loving all connected to Him and accepting all that comes from Him.

Such love is attained through the monotheistic religion, Islam, brought by the prophets and consummated in Muḥammad's final shariah. That shariah, comprising beliefs, moral teaching, practical laws, and the Prophet's sacred life as a model, is the path of sincere invitation to Allah, total submission, and God's straight path. Therefore, following the Prophet is the means by which a servant's love reaches its desired end: Allah's requital of that love. In this context, love of Allah cannot coexist with following unbelievers in their vain views, worldly attractions, honor, or wealth; friendship and following correspond because each shapes thought and action. The verse mentions God's love rather than His guardianship because guardianship rests on love, and love of the Prophet and believers is, in reality, part of Allah's love rather than an independent love.

Allah's mercy is unrestricted and available to all; any limitation lies in the servant's capacity to receive it. Sin is the impediment and veil preventing nearness to Allah and the resulting divine bounties. When Allah loves a servant, He removes that veil by forgiving sins, opening the way to divine bliss, honor, and enduring bounty.

For (3:32), Al-Mizan explains that following the Messenger means proceeding along the straight path belonging to Allah: the shariah ordained for the Messenger and conveyed through him, including his commands, prohibitions, mission, and guidance. Following him is therefore obedience to Allah and the Messenger in one and the same shariah. It rejects the interpretation that the command separates obedience to Allah in the Book from obedience to the Messenger in the sunnah: the verse explains the preceding command to follow the Messenger, and the single occurrence of “obey” shows that the two obediences are one, unlike a formulation that repeats the command for distinct objects. Turning away from this obedience identifies the offenders as unbelievers whom Allah does not love.

The commentary concludes that taqiyyah is allowed in certain circumstances, but the punishment for preferring unbelievers as friends is not waived and this disobedience is not forgiven. The divinely ordained shariah resolves into sincerity toward Allah, sincerity into love of Allah; conversely, love produces sincerity and sincerity leads to the shariah. From another angle, religion resolves into submission, and submission into monotheism. Taking unbelievers as friends is disbelief pertaining to the branches of religion rather than its roots, like disbelief through refusing zakāt or prayer. Alternatively, the person may be called an unbeliever because this friendship is the ultimate destination to which it leads.
verses.33: Al-Mizan says Allah chose Adam, Noah, and the descendants of Abraham and ʿImrān above all worlds.
verses.34:
Al-Mizan introduces these verses as the link between the preceding discussion of the People of the Book and the coming account of Jesus, son of Mary. That account will distinguish truth from the falsehoods surrounding his life and person, while also arguing against the People of the Book.

Al-Mizan explains al-iṣṭifāʾ as taking the choicest part of a thing and purifying it of impurity. In relation to the stages of al-wilāyah, it corresponds to Islam: the servant’s complete surrender to the Lord’s will and contentment with His decree. An editor’s note adds that, although friendship of God is one sense of al-wilāyah, it here means God’s guardianship, or His management of believers’ affairs. Yet this is not the sense of selection intended in the verse. Had it said that God chose these persons from among the worlds, it would imply that Islam and complete surrender belonged exclusively to them, which is untenable. By saying that He chose them above all the worlds, it instead gives a comparative meaning: they received special excellences and precedence over others. Mary’s verse 3:42 illustrates the distinction: her first choosing concerns her own virtues without comparison, while her choosing above the women of the worlds exalts her over others.

Adam was first among those named because he was the first human vicegerent appointed for the earth, the first to open the door of repentance and divine forgiveness, and the first for whom God ordained the religion. These exclusive virtues suffice for his excellence. Noah was the first of the five ūlū al-ʿazm messengers given a Divine Book and a new shariah. He was also the second father of the human race; God made his offspring the survivors, perpetuated his praise among later generations, and sent peace upon him in all the worlds.

Al-Mizan takes āl, rendered here as descendants, to mean a person’s close family members and those exclusively attached to him. At first, āl Ibrāhīm could seem to include all Abraham’s purified descendants—Isaac, Israel, the Israelite prophets, Ishmael, Muḥammad and his progeny—as well as those attached to them through stages of the friendship of God. But the separate mention of āl ʿImrān shows that this scope cannot include all of Abraham’s purified descendants. Whether ʿImrān is taken as Mary’s father or Moses’s father, he and his descendants belong to Abraham’s line; naming them separately therefore restricts āl Ibrāhīm to only some of that line.

The commentary reads verse (4:54), together with supporting verses, as condemning the Israelites’ envy of Muḥammad. It concludes that the descendants of Abraham mentioned here exclude Isaac, Jacob, and Jacob’s progeny, who are generally called the Israelites. An author’s note says that it will later prove that the people mentioned in verse (4:54) are the Prophet and that he certainly belongs to Abraham’s descendants intended there. Further support is found in verses concerning Abraham’s nearest followers and Abraham and Ishmael’s prayer for a messenger from their offspring. Thus, the descendants of Abraham in this verse are Ishmael and his purified descendants, including the Prophet and his progeny.

This selection is not exclusive. The verse’s silence concerning Abraham himself, Moses, and other Israelite prophets does not deny their excellence, nor does it conflict with verses that exalt the Children of Israel. To affirm one excellence is not to negate another. Excellence over the worlds means precedence over those below in some worldly or otherworldly virtue; it neither prevents others from receiving similar excellence nor prevents some from being exalted above those already exalted. Likewise, the fact that all those named were chosen above the worlds does not conflict with some among them being made more excellent than others.

Al-Mizan holds that ʿImrān apparently means Mary’s father. The immediately following account concerns ʿImrān’s wife and daughter, Mary, and the Qur’an repeatedly names Mary’s father, whereas it does not identify Moses’s father in the same way. Accordingly, āl ʿImrān means Mary and Jesus, either alone or together with ʿImrān’s wife. Although Christians are reportedly not agreed that Mary’s father was named ʿImrān, the Qur’an is not bound by their view.

Dhurriyyah originally meant small children but later came to mean all offspring, which is its meaning here; its accusative form functions as an explanatory conjunction. The words one from the other mean that, viewed in any member, this group begins from and returns to the others: its parts are alike and do not differ in their attributes and qualifications. They therefore share the qualities of excellence for which Allah selected them; such divine selection is not haphazard or reckless. Allah hears their speech, which reveals their inward thoughts, and knows what is in their minds and hearts. Thus His being Hearing and Knowing gives the reason for their selection, while their being offspring one from another explains why the whole group was worthy of it: they are alike in spiritual sublimity, surrender of heart, and the established truth of their speech.
verses.35: Al-Mizan says that the woman of ʿImrān vowed her unborn child to devoted service to God and asked the Hearing, Knowing One to accept it.
verses.36: Al-Mizan says that after bearing a girl, the woman of ʿImrān named her Mary and commended her and her offspring to Allah’s protection from accursed Satan; Allah knew best what she bore, and the male was not like the female.
verses.37: Al-Mizan says that Allah graciously accepted Mary, raised her well, and placed her in Zachariah’s charge. Whenever he entered her sanctuary, he found food with her; Mary said it was from Allah, who sustains whom He pleases without measure.
verses.38: Al-Mizan relates that Zachariah prayed that his Lord grant him good offspring, for He hears prayer.
verses.39: Al-Mizan says angels told Zachariah, praying in the sanctuary, that Allah gave good news of John: a verifier of a word from Allah, honorable, chaste, and a prophet among the good.
verses.40: Al-Mizan recounts Zachariah’s wonder at having a son despite his old age and his wife’s barrenness; the reply affirms that Allah does what He pleases.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan explains that a vow, al-nadhr, makes binding an act that had not previously been obligatory. The woman of ʿImrān’s vow during pregnancy suggests that ʿImrān had already died, for she could then independently release her child for God. This release, taḥrīr, is not emancipation from slavery but freedom from parental authority and claims: the parents neither train nor use the child for themselves, nor require the usual obedience. A child released for God comes under divine protection and serves a place of worship until the period of ordinary parental guardianship ends; it is reported that such a child served in the synagogue until puberty, then could remain or leave. Her request that God accept from her most probably concerns the child rather than merely the vow, because the following verse says that Mary herself was accepted.

The unqualified vow and the masculine muḥarraran show that she firmly expected a male child. Her later disappointment at giving birth to a girl confirms this reading. Because the sex of what is in the womb belongs to the unseen, and because the Qur’an does not leave a false assertion unmarked, the commentary infers that her certainty rested on some divine revelation rather than conjecture. Her equally assured commendation of Mary’s offspring to God likewise indicates revealed knowledge of the future. It reconstructs the matter as follows: she knew that she would receive from ʿImrān a righteous son; when she conceived after his death, she thought the unborn child was that promised son; and when she bore Mary, she recognized that the promise would be fulfilled through Mary’s offspring.

Her statement that she had borne a female is therefore an exclamation of disappointment, not bare information. Al-Mizan holds that both parenthetic clauses—Allah knew best what she bore, and the male is not like the female—are God’s words, not the woman’s. Their order shows that the particular male she had hoped for was not like the particular female God had given. The commentary rejects the widespread attribution of the latter clause to the mother, since that view cannot adequately account for its reversed syntactic arrangement. God knew that through this daughter He would fulfil her hopes more perfectly than through a direct son: Mary would bear Jesus without a father; Mary and her son would together be a sign for the people; and Jesus would speak in the cradle, be a spirit and a word of God, and resemble Adam before God. Even a son directly given to her could not have accomplished this divine purpose.

The commentary reports that Mary means worshipper or servant in her language. On that reported meaning, the mother’s immediate naming of the girl signified a transfer and renewal of her vow: she dedicated Mary to worship and to service of the synagogue. A translator’s note, however, records a dictionary derivation of Hebrew Miryām as “obstinacy, rebellion,” contrary to that reported meaning. The mother then entrusted Mary and her offspring to God’s protection from Satan so that her dedication would be realized. Her confidence shows, according to Al-Mizan, that once she understood the promised son would come through Mary, she transferred to the daughter the vow originally intended for the son she expected.

“Good acceptance” stresses the excellence of God’s reception. The two clauses in the next verse answer the mother’s two requests: God’s acceptance answers her naming and dedication of Mary, while her good growth answers the plea for protection. Thus it was Mary, not simply her mother’s vow, that was accepted. Her acceptance means that God chose her for sincere worship and sanctuary service, a choice entailing total surrender to Him; her good growth means that He gave her and her offspring guidance, sanctity, and a purified life untouched by Satan’s misleading suggestions. Her being chosen and purified answers her mother’s prayer, and Mary and her son becoming a sign verifies that the male she expected was not like the female she received.

Zachariah obtained Mary’s custody when his name was selected by lot after those contending for the privilege agreed to decide it in that way. The food he found in her sanctuary was unexpected and unusual, not merely ordinary provisions always kept there. Mary’s answer—that it came from Allah, who sustains whom He pleases without measure—and Zachariah’s immediate prayer show that he recognized it as a miraculous sustenance and as a sign of her standing with God. The unconnected wording of his question further indicates that he asked only once; once she answered, he was satisfied and turned to God for an extraordinary offspring of his own.

A good thing is one suitable to its purpose; accordingly, “good offspring” means a child whose qualities and conduct fulfil a father’s hopes. Overwhelmed by the grace and distinction he witnessed in Mary, Zachariah asked for a child resembling her in divine prestige. His request was granted in John, whom Al-Mizan presents as the prophet who most nearly resembled Jesus and, through him, Mary. God Himself named John before his conception. John was given, to the greatest extent possible, the qualities bestowed on Mary and Jesus; yet Jesus necessarily preceded and surpassed him, because Jesus’ creation and birth had been firmly decreed before Zachariah’s prayer. Jesus was therefore an ūlū al-ʿazm messenger with a new shariah and a new Book.

John’s verification of a Word from Allah means that he was the harbinger of Jesus, the Word. The parallel accounts of John and Jesus show their likeness: both received wisdom and the Book while still young; both are described through purity, tenderness, dutifulness, and peace at the decisive stages of existence; and both are prophets among the righteous. John’s being honorable denotes noble, leading distinction, while his chastity means total abstinence from women through renunciation of worldly desire and ascetic self-denial. These qualities answer Zachariah’s request for a good heir with whom God would be pleased.

Zachariah’s question about having a son despite old age and his wife’s barrenness was not doubt or despair. He had already invoked those very impediments when praying, and his question expresses awed joy and a desire to know how and when each hindrance would be removed. Having prayed while overwhelmed by the mercy shown to Mary, he now responded to the granted prayer as though awakened to the marvel of it; the causes of his former sorrow intensified his happiness. Al-Mizan compares this to Abraham’s joyful questioning of similar glad tidings, which did not imply despair of divine mercy. Zachariah’s wording also observes the propriety of the purified servants: he alludes discreetly to his own loss of sexual capacity, while his wife had both old age and a barrenness that had existed from the beginning.

The answer, “Even so,” affirms that the matter is certain and firmly decreed, while “Allah does what He pleases” gives the reason. The immediate speaker may have been the angel, though the speech is attributable to God because it was conveyed by His command; the commentary also infers that Zachariah heard the voice from the place where he had previously heard angelic voices.

Zachariah’s requested sign was that he would be unable to speak to people for three days except by signs, while remaining able and commanded to remember and glorify God abundantly. Al-Mizan notes a further resemblance between John and Jesus in the silence Jesus instructed his mother to observe after his birth. It considers two explanations for Zachariah’s request: that he sought confirmation that the tidings came from God rather than Satan, or that he wished to know the time of his wife’s conception. The context favors the first. Although prophets are protected by ʿiṣmah and distinguish angelic inspiration from satanic whispering, this knowledge is granted by God; asking God for a sign to bring certainty to tranquillity does not conflict with their protection.

The nature of the sign itself confirms this explanation. Satan may afflict prophets bodily, hinder their missions, lead people away from their path, and strengthen their enemies, but cannot gain power over their persons. Zachariah’s divinely caused inability to speak ordinary speech was therefore beyond Satan’s power and decisively showed that the message was from God. His earlier dialogue does not invalidate this: certainty has degrees. He may first have known that the voice was angelic, then asked about the extraordinary birth, and finally sought a sign so that his certainty would reach tranquillity. The angels’ calling may also mean that he heard their voices without seeing them.

Al-Mizan rejects another exegete’s account that God merely prohibited Zachariah from speaking for three days as a voluntary regimen of gratitude, whose completion would signal conception and allow him to inform his wife. The verses contain no indication that Zachariah asked for such worship, that the three days marked conception, that silence was simply an order rather than an imposed inability, or that he sought the sign in order to announce the news to his wife.

The commentary then explains that “speech” is whatever conveys a speaker’s intended meaning, whether voiced or communicated through signs, symbols, or other soundless means. For this reason, the Qur’an describes the ideas Satan puts into human minds as his commands, promises, threats, whisperings, and suggestions, even though they are not heard as vocal speech. Angels and Satan thus speak to people by placing ideas in their minds. Angelic inspiration brings expansion of the breast, forgiveness, abundance, wisdom, light, tranquillity, and adherence to the divine Book and prophetic sunnah. Satanic whispering constricts the breast, incites desire, threatens poverty, enjoins abomination, and drives one contrary to the Book, the sunnah, and sound human nature.

Apart from speech sent through an angelic messenger, God speaks either by direct revelation without a veil or from behind a veil. Direct revelation needs no outside confirmation, for no doubt can enter speech in which there is no barrier between God and its recipient. Other modes require supporting evidence that ultimately rests on direct revelation. Prophets and their close followers may sometimes see and recognize angels or Satan directly, making further identification unnecessary. When they do not see the speaker, however, they need a God-given means of knowing whether the communication is truly from God, just as other believers do.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan connects this verse to the prayer of the wife of ʿImrān and the divine selection of her descendants. Mary was one of those to whom angels spoke and whose speech she heard; the appearance of the Spirit to her in human form further establishes this.

Her being chosen means that God accepted her for His worship, while her purification means that she remained under His protection and was therefore protected from sin. The alternative explanation that she was a virgin who did not menstruate, and hence did not have to leave the synagogue, is possible, but the commentary considers protection from sin more suitable to the context.

To be chosen above others means more than mere selection: it is precedence through an excellence exclusively bestowed. Mary’s exclusive precedence over all women lies in her miraculous conception and birth of Jesus. Her purification, obedience, acceptance of God’s words and books, and being spoken to by angels are virtues found in others as well. Because the verse is unconditional, her precedence cannot be restricted to the women of her own time.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan explains al-Qunūt as obedient perseverance marked by submission and humility; al-Sajdah is prostration, and al-rukūʿ is bowing or humility. Mary is called again by name so that she will heed a further message. The preceding announcement concerned the rank God granted her; this one states the service she owes in gratitude and as required by servitude.

Thus, because she was chosen, purified, and preferred above the women of the worlds, she is commanded to remain obedient to her Lord, prostrate, and bow with those who bow. Each of the three commands may correspond to one of the three preceding excellences, although their precise respective connection is not clear.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan calls this account a tiding of the unseen because reports found in the scriptures of the People of the Book cannot be relied on, having suffered alteration, deletion, and interpolation; Qur’anic details of Zachariah’s story are absent from the Bible. The Prophet’s and his people’s being unlettered is another possible reason for calling it unseen news, but the first explanation better fits the context.

Here al-Qalam, besides meaning a pen, can mean an arrow used for casting lots. The contenders disputed Mary’s guardianship until they agreed to cast such arrows; the lot favored Zachariah, who took charge of her. Some take the verse to concern a later guardianship after Mary grew up and Zachariah became weak, because it follows the earlier mention of his guardianship. Al-Mizan instead holds that the Qur’an may repeat or allude to an earlier part of an event in order to establish its point, as it does when later recalling Joseph’s brothers’ earlier conspiracy.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan identifies the angels’ annunciation with the event in which the Spirit appeared to Mary. Whether “the angels” refers to Gabriel alone or to Gabriel with other angels, the difference is resolved by the ordered ranks of angels: the acts and speech of leaders and followers may be attributed to one another and, ultimately, to God. Gabriel, a chief angel near to God, therefore announced the good news together with the angels under his authority. Mary was consequently one of those spoken to by angels, and she also saw the Spirit in the form of a well-made man.

In Qur’anic usage, a word attributed to God is that which manifests His will, whether a creative command, revelation, or inspiration. The commentary rejects the explanations that Jesus is a “Word” merely because earlier prophets foretold him, because he interpreted the Torah, or because the Word is simply the annunciation to Mary. The first conflicts with the Qur’an’s presentation of Jesus as announcing Aḥmad and with the phrase naming the Word itself as the Messiah; the second lacks Qur’anic support; and the third does not fit the same naming phrase. The best interpretation is that Jesus is God’s creative Word, “Be”: unlike ordinary human conception, his coming into being bypassed the usual intervening causes, so he himself is called the Word communicated to Mary.

Exegetes have offered several derivations of al-Masīḥʾ, including anointing with blessing, purification from sins, anointing with holy oil, Gabriel’s touch, or Jesus’ healing touch. Al-Mizan instead notes that the name is the Arabicised form of the Biblical Meshiha. Since Israelite kings were anointed so that their rule might be blessed, it may mean king or blessed; the commentary considers “the blessed” not unlikely. Jewish expectation of a promised kingdom led Jews to deny Jesus when no temporal kingdom appeared, while Christians, followed by some Muslim exegetes, interpreted it as spiritual. Calling him “Jesus son of Mary,” although the address is to Mary, emphasizes his birth without a father and makes mother and son jointly the sign.

His worthiness of regard denotes esteem and acceptability in this world and the hereafter, and he is certainly among those brought near to God. Nearness is the goal toward which all things proceed to God; for human beings it is attained through striving, while for angels it is a divinely bestowed rank.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan takes al-Kahl to mean middle age, the period between youth and old age when bodily strength is complete. The verse therefore gives Mary further good news that Jesus would live to maturity, but not to old age. It notes the tension with Gospel reports that he lived only about thirty-three years: some say his mature-age speech will occur after his descent from heaven, while others claim he lived about sixty-four years.

Speaking while ordinarily in a cradle would not itself be extraordinary, since children begin to speak at that age. The verse means rather that Jesus would address people from the cradle with complete, thought-provoking speech of the kind heard from a mature man; this is a miracle. The account in the Chapter of Mary shows that he did so in the very first hour of life, when Mary brought him to her people, and such speech on the day of birth is undoubtedly miraculous.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan explains that Mary addressed her question to her Lord, although the Spirit or angels were speaking, because their speech was in reality God’s speech. Her words may alternatively be read as a cry for help.

“Even so” is a complete sentence: the matter announced to her has been decreed and cannot be averted. “Allah creates what He pleases” removes any thought that the birth lies beyond His power. “When He has decreed a matter, He only says to it: ‘Be,’ and it is” removes the supposed difficulty, for difficulty belongs to effects dependent on numerous and powerful preliminary causes, whereas God does not need such causes to create.
verses.48:
Al-Mizan takes “the Book” generically as revelation that removes human differences, and “the Wisdom” as useful knowledge concerning belief and action. Their definite articles do not mean that Jesus was taught every book or all revelation. The Torah and Injīl, though themselves books containing wisdom, are separately named because of their particular importance.

The Torah is the revelation given to Moses on the tablets. The Torah possessed by the Jews in the Prophet’s time was not wholly different from the original, but had undergone extensive alteration and interpolation; its own transmission also contains a major historical gap. The Injīl, meaning good news, was one book revealed especially to Jesus, unlike the present Gospels attributed to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, which were composed long after him.

The Law belonged to the Torah. The Injīl brought no wholly new shariah, though it abrogated some Torah rules and apparently contained some affirmative rulings. Like the Torah, it also contained good news of the advent of the Messenger Prophet, the ummī.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan holds that Jesus was specifically a messenger to the Children of Israel, yet, like Moses, was among the ulu al-ʿAzm prophets sent to the whole world. A prophet conveys what benefits people in this world and the hereafter, whereas a messenger brings a decisive message to a particular people, whose acceptance brings everlasting felicity and whose rejection brings destruction. Thus, being messenger to a specified nation does not confine a prophet’s mission to it. Moses’ call reaching Pharaoh’s people and the acceptance of the Pharaoh’s magicians’ faith illustrate this distinction; likewise, non-Israelites entered Jesus’ religion and Qur’anic statements about Christians are not confined to Israelite Christians. A translator’s note objects that Gospel reports restrict Jesus’ mission to Israel and attribute the spread to Gentiles to Paul; a publisher’s note qualifies that objection as resting on the correctness of reports in the present Gospels.

Here “create” means assembling a thing’s parts and can be attributed to a creature. Jesus formed a bird from dust, healed the blind and leper, raised many dead—as the plural at least suggests—and disclosed what people ate and stored. The repeated qualification “with Allah’s permission” for creation and resurrection denies that these signs arose from any independent power in Jesus and guards against deifying him; this is why he concludes by calling people to worship Allah alone. The wording, together with God’s later address to Jesus on the Day of Resurrection, establishes that these miracles actually occurred, not merely that Jesus could have performed them if asked.

His disclosure of food and household stores was another unambiguous miracle: knowledge of the unseen belongs to God and to His messengers through revelation. It lacks the explicit qualification of divine permission because informing is Jesus’ own speech, whereas creation and resurrection are truly God’s acts and can be attributed to another only by His permission. Those latter signs also posed a greater danger of misleading people into deifying him; ordinary people may imagine information about the unseen to be an art learned through magic. Healing was sufficiently covered by the initial description of all the signs as from their Lord, and the final condition, “if you are believers,” addresses people claiming faith.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan explains that Jesus verified the Torah originally revealed to Moses and taught to him by God; this does not attest that the Torah held by the Jews of his time was unaltered. He upheld its law except for some burdensome prohibitions imposed upon the Jews, allowing again part of the good things forbidden to them because of their iniquity. In this sense, the Injīl did not introduce an entirely new shariah.

His coming with a sign from God is repeated to show that the command to fear God and obey Jesus rests on his divine sign, not on his relaxation of some prohibitions. The wording that he came “that I may allow” expresses the purpose of abrogating those particular hard rules.
verses.51: Al-Mizan explains that Jesus’ declaration that Allah is both his Lord and theirs was meant to preclude any excuse for believing in his divinity, whether he perceived such a tendency or was informed of its future occurrence by revelation. Like his repeated qualification that miracles occurred by God’s permission, it removes grounds for misunderstanding. His words on the Day of Judgment indicate that he made this declaration in obedience to God’s command and revelation.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan resumes Jesus’ story after his mission and miracles, when he encountered resistance. His perception of unbelief means either that it was outwardly manifest or that he detected the plot, born of unbelief, to harm and kill him. Seeing that most of the Children of Israel would not accept faith and fearing that the mission might fail if they destroyed him, he sought a select, wholly dedicated core through which religion could be strengthened, distinguished from disbelief, and spread.

“My helpers to Allah” means helpers in proceeding toward God and nearness to Him, not helpers “with” God. The preposition conveys movement toward God, and the disciples’ reply confirms this meaning. The alternative has no evidence, improperly places God alongside other helpers, and would have required them to say that they were Jesus’ helpers with God. The disciples are Jesus’ close companions, and their declaration, “We are helpers of Allah,” is explained by their belief in God.

Their belief was not their first entry into faith, but belief after belief. The Qur’anic statement that God revealed to the disciples that they should believe shows, according to Al-Mizan, that they were prophets. Their submission is unconditional surrender to whatever God requires and therefore belongs to sincere believers, not merely to those who profess the basic testimony. The use of a verb for their newly declared belief and an adjective for their established submission likewise indicates a higher rank.

Al-Mizan distinguishes successive ranks: initial islām is general submission and testimony, followed by heartfelt īmān; a second islām is sincere acceptance of faith’s demands, free from resentment and put into practice, followed by an īmān in which deeds and servitude become sincere; a third islām is surrender of love and will to God, so that one loves and wills only for Him, followed by an īmān that permeates all action.

Jesus had first called people to fear God and obey him because God was Lord of both messenger and people; this becomes the command to worship God, the straight path leading to Him. When the general call failed, he sought helpers on that same path of piety and obedience. The disciples accepted it by professing belief and submission, that is, obedience and following. In their later prayer, they extend their belief to all God revealed, including what Jesus was taught of the Book, Wisdom, Torah, and Injīl; this is among the highest ranks of faith. They ask Jesus to witness their submission and following so that his testimony may stand as proof when they address God.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan notes that the disciples’ prayer is quoted directly, allowing the hearer to receive their words without a narrator. They ask to be recorded among the witnesses on the basis of both their īmān and islām.

Apparently, these witnesses testify that the messenger truly conveyed God’s message. A messenger conveys it in teaching and practice, and followers can testify to this only by learning it from him and following his shariah, thereby showing that he himself practised what he taught. This differs from witnessing to the truth of a messenger’s mission. Alternatively, since the disciples had asked Jesus to witness their submission, they may probably be asking to be enrolled among those who will bear witness concerning deeds.
verses.54: Al-Mizan identifies those who planned against Jesus as the Children of Israel, as indicated by the preceding mention of their unbelief. Its explanation of planning when attributed to God is given elsewhere.
verses.55:
Al-Mizan explains al-tawaffī as taking something completely. Though it is used at death because the soul is taken from the body, its primary force is taking and preserving, not death itself: the soul is preserved for its return at resurrection. Where this preservation is not at issue, the Qur’an uses al-mawt for death. Thus al-tawaffī does not necessarily mean that Jesus died.

The Qur’an’s denial that the Jews killed or crucified Jesus, together with its statement that the People of the Book will believe in him before his death, indicates that he is alive near God and will not die until that belief occurs. In this verse, therefore, al-tawaffī apparently means that God would take Jesus completely away from the Jews, although the wording does not state this explicitly.

“Cause you to ascend unto Me” first appears to mean a spiritual ascension, since God has no physical location, just as the later return to Him is not spatial. If al-tawaffī were read as causing death, ascension would mean raising Jesus’ rank and bringing him near to God. Another possible interpretation is that Jesus was raised alive, body and soul, to the physical heaven, which Qur’anic appearances may present as the abode of nearness, angels, and descending divine favor. His purification from the unbelievers is spiritual: God removes him from their unbelieving and truth-rejecting society.

The verse promises that Jesus’ followers will be made above those who disbelieved in him until the Day of Resurrection. The usual exegetical view confines the true followers to Christians who remained on his path before Islam and to Muslims thereafter, and takes their superiority as superiority of proof. Al-Mizan rejects this: the whole statement is future good news, while Jesus’ proofs were already victorious during his life and after his ascension; moreover, a true proof does not need a time limit ending at the Resurrection. Nor can the verse be made a promise of eventual popularity, political triumph of true believers, or numerical majority, since its wording and the facts do not support these readings.

Rather, the verbal descriptions can extend an ancestor’s accepted action to a whole nation that identifies with it. On this reading, “those who disbelieve” includes the Jewish nation through its identification with the disbelief and conspiracy of its forebears, while “those who follow you” includes Christians because their early forebears truly followed Jesus, even though God was not pleased with trinitarian belief or with continued adherence to Jesus’ religion after Islam. The promised domination of Christians over Jews thus manifests divine wrath against the latter. The best reported interpretation extends “those who follow you” to all Christians and Muslims: the Jews remain under the domination of those who believe in, and recognize the obligation to follow, Jesus. The later shift to “those who believe and do good deeds” confirms that the earlier phrase does not itself identify those saved in the hereafter.

The final return and judgment address Jesus, his followers, and his disbelievers together, giving their ultimate result on the Day of Resurrection and ending the narrative of Jesus’ earthly life.
verses.56: Al-Mizan explains that the punishment of the disbelievers unfolds from both their being placed beneath Jesus’ followers and their final return for judgment. They are punished in this world through the power and rule of those made dominant over them, and in the hereafter through the Fire. This supports reading the earlier promised predominance as actual domination, not merely victory in argument. Their having no helpers means that no intercession can protect them from this unalterable decree.
verses.57: Al-Mizan holds that full reward belongs only to those among Jesus’ nominal followers who themselves truly believe and perform good deeds. Being included in a community’s name is not the same as personally possessing its faith and conduct. The closing statement that Allah does not love the unjust therefore concerns those who claim to follow Jesus but lack true belief and righteous deeds; they receive no reward.
verses.58: Al-Mizan takes this as the close of the story. The wise reminder is the Qur’an: it reminds people of God, is firm and wise in its verses and descriptions, and admits neither falsehood nor frivolous speech.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan presents this verse as the summary of the argument with the Christians of Najrān: Jesus’ exceptional birth establishes only that he was a created human being, like Adam, created without a father. God gathered Adam from the earth and commanded him to be, and he became a man.

The verse independently refutes Jesus’ divinity in two ways. First, God created him as a man, and a created man is God’s servant, not a god. Second, Adam’s creation was no less extraordinary than Jesus’ creation; if birth without a father made Jesus divine, Adam should also be called divine, which Christians do not claim. Both creations were physical and worldly, though contrary to the ordinary manner of conception.

The use of fa-yakūn describes the past here. The instant divine command, “Be,” does not conflict with the gradual formation of Adam and Jesus: things are gradual when viewed through their created causes, but, in relation to God, there is no interval between His command and their being. The point is that God needs no causes at all; possibilities, difficulties, distance, and nearness arise only from the conditions of intermediary causes, while all things stand equally related to His creative command.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan says that this confirms the preceding account in order to reassure the Prophet that he possesses the truth and to strengthen him in argument. “The truth is from your Lord” uses “from” to mark God as truth’s point of origin; saying that truth is merely “with” God would suggest that God needs it and would hint at polytheism.

Unalterable true propositions are discovered from things that really exist, and all existence is from God. Therefore all truth is from Him. A creature’s correct action only accords with truth, whereas God’s action is existence itself and thus truth itself; consequently, God is not questioned about what He does, while human beings are questioned.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan explains that the offer of al-mubāhalah follows the preceding, decisive teaching about Jesus son of Mary. The word "this" in the dispute may refer either to Jesus or to the truth just mentioned. What had come to the Prophet was knowledge in two respects: it was Divine Revelation, and it contained the rational proof comparing Jesus with Adam. Thus, even one who did not accept its revealed source could not reasonably doubt its subject; this may explain why the verse speaks of knowledge rather than merely of what had been explained to the disputants. Recalling this Divine knowledge also assures the Prophet that, by Allah’s support, he will overcome his adversaries.

The plural in "let us call" embraces both disputing parties, whereas "our sons," "our women," and "our selves" belong respectively to the Islamic side, just as the corresponding expressions belong to the Christian side. The sense is that each party should summon its own sons, women, and selves. Al-Mizan rejects the inversion that would make each side summon the other’s family, since that would make the inclusion of sons and women pointless; it would also require an unwarranted authority by each side over the other’s family.

Al-mubāhalah and al-mulāʿanah mean mutual cursing; al-ibtihāl, originally connected with a curse, came to be used for earnest prayer. Although the immediate disputants were the Messenger of God and Christian men, the challenge includes their nearest family members in order to display complete certainty in the claim. A person naturally guards his family even at personal risk, and sons are named before women because of the greater love he has for them. The challenge means that each whole group should earnestly invoke Allah’s curse upon the lying party, so that its sons, women, and selves would share its chastisement and the enemies of truth would be utterly removed. Its force therefore does not depend on the number of persons in each category.

The commentary reports the unanimous statement of exegetes, supported by traditions and history, that the Messenger of God brought only ʿAlī, Fāṭimah, al-Ḥasan, and al-Ḥusayn for the imprecation. Thus the Islamic side consisted of two selves, two sons, and one woman, yet the command was fully carried out. The general meaning of a Qur’anic expression must be distinguished from the persons to whom it is applied in a particular event: plural wording may be applied in an occasion involving only one person, as occurs in Qur’anic rulings and statements concerning recurrent cases.

The words "bring about the curse of Allah," rather than merely ask Him to curse, indicate that the prayer would certainly be granted, because it was then the means of separating truth from falsehood. "The liars" means neither all liars in the world nor a class of liars; it means the particular side in this dispute whose claim was false. The Prophet’s claim was that Allah is One and that Jesus was His servant and messenger, whereas the Christians claimed that Jesus was God, God’s son, and one of three persons.

Al-Mizan argues that everyone who came forth for the imprecation was a partner in the claim made by his respective side. Had the confrontation been between the Prophet alone and the Christian delegation, a form covering both singular and plural, such as whosoever lies, would have been required. The plural "liars" shows that a plurality of persons in one side were claimants and therefore capable of being called liars. While plural language may be used for a singular in statements concerning recurrent kinds of cases, the proposed imprecation was a unique and nonrepeatable event; consequently, "the liars" cannot here be reduced to one person. It requires a plurality of claimants in each summoned party. On this basis, ʿAlī, Fāṭimah, al-Ḥasan, and al-Ḥusayn were partners in the Messenger’s claim and Mission, and their designation as his selves, woman, and sons is an exclusive excellence.

The objection that they were merely samples of the sons, women, and selves, while all believers shared the same belief, is rejected. If they had been mere samples, the Prophet would have had to bring persons sufficient to meet the ordinary plural forms; instead, he brought only one man, one woman, and two sons. This shows, according to the commentary, that no others were worthy of these designations. The Christians had come to dispute with the Prophet himself about Jesus, not with the believers generally, as the verse’s singular address to him makes clear. The other believers had no part in that dispute and no reason to be exposed to the curse. The Prophet, however, had to expose himself because he was a party to the claim; bringing those four shows that his claim depended upon them as it depended upon himself, rather than that they were illustrative examples.

Their partnership extends to the Mission because the Christians had not come merely to contest the Prophet’s personal belief about Jesus. They came because he had called them to accept what he said was revealed to him. When he brought those four to the imprecation, he did so in connection with both his claim and that call. The fact that taking one’s nearest relatives into danger ordinarily proves confidence in one’s truth does not exhaust the verse’s meaning: the plural "liars" additionally establishes that those present with him were claimants and partners in the Mission. This does not make them partners in prophethood. Call and propagation are among a prophet’s divinely bestowed responsibilities and concomitants, but are not identical with prophethood; nor are they identical with Imamah, though they may accompany it.

Al-Mizan takes "this is the true story" to refer to the preceding accounts of Jesus: the stories Allah has related concerning him are true, unlike those related by the Christians. Its repeated forms of emphasis strengthen the Prophet for the coming imprecation, fortifying his certainty in the revelation. The accompanying assertion that there is no god but Allah confirms the truth of those accounts. Allah is then described as the Mighty, who can aid the side of truth, and the Wise, who cannot neglect that aid through ignorance or forgetfulness; unlike the false gods of the opponents, only He is Mighty and Wise.

Finally, the commentary holds that the proper aim of argument and imprecation is the manifestation of truth. A genuine seeker of truth, knowing that Allah guards truth, could not turn away from such an imprecation. If the Christians turned back, it would show that they sought outward victory, preservation of their position and inherited beliefs, and the continuance of familiar customs, rather than truth, reform, and the good life. Their turning away would thus disclose their mischief-making: the verse names its cause, corrupting the life founded on truth, in place of its effect, refusal to let truth be manifest. The emphatic declaration that Allah knows the mischief-makers indicates that this disposition was ingrained in them and that Allah knew they would refuse; their subsequent refusal confirmed the Divine statement.
