verses.64:
Al-Mizan explains that the call to come to a common word addresses all the People of the Book and summons them to unite upon its meaning by believing, acknowledging, propagating, and acting upon it. Its being common means that both sides are equally bound by the acknowledgment and action which its meaning requires; the unity, the word, and its commonness are all rhetorical expressions for this shared obligation.

Although one interpretation makes the common word the monotheism jointly taught by the Qur’an, Torah, and Injīl, the commentary holds that the ending of the verse supports the primary interpretation: the common word is the practical commitment that none shall be worshipped but Allah, nothing shall be associated with Him, and no human beings shall be taken as lords besides Him. The call is therefore to practical rather than merely theoretical monotheism, which is demanded by Islam, total submission to God. The first clause rejects worship of other than God; it does not aim to establish God’s existence, which the Qur’an treats as self-evident. Since worship is not truly for God unless it is accompanied by faith purified of polytheistic beliefs, the later clauses exclude such beliefs as divine sonship and trinity, as well as the worship of alleged partners or human religious authorities.

Al-Mizan presents this pure monotheism as the comprehensive purpose of prophethood. Prophethood awakens humanity to religion, whose reality is balance in social life: justice and equity give each person his due place and permit individual freedom except where it harms society. Humanity’s natural course requires that individual and collective conduct be founded on submission to God, equal rights, and freedom of good intention and action. This cannot be attained while the strong exploit or enslave the weak, or while some dominate others and compel them to serve their interests. There is no lord and no rule except God.

The command to worship God alone follows from Godhead itself. All things seek their perfections from God and are joined in one ordered system; their interconnected creation and management therefore require one Creator, Owner, and Lord, without partner. Likewise, human beings are similar parts of one human reality and consequently possess equal rights in the affairs common to them, while particular advantages belong only where nature and circumstances require them. No person may impose his will upon another without undertaking a corresponding burden for him. To surrender to a human equal as an arbitrary master is to raise him into lordship, negate human nature, and contradict the submission due to God alone.

If the People of the Book turn away, the Prophet and the believers are to call them to witness that they are Muslims, following the religion with which God is pleased. This declaration ends dispute by identifying their religion with the truth, and shows that monotheism in worship is inseparable from Islam.
verses.65:
Al-Mizan says that the verse may be governed by the preceding command to say, making it an instruction to the Prophet, although its connection with the later verse about those nearest to Abraham may indicate that it is direct divine speech.

The People of the Book disputed over Abraham, apparently beginning with rival attempts to claim him as proof of their own truth and then degenerating into bigotry: the Jews called him a Jew and the Christians a Christian. But Judaism and Christianity arose only after the Torah and Injīl, which were revealed long after Abraham. He could therefore be neither a follower of Moses’ religion nor of Jesus’ law. The commentary concludes that Abraham was sincerely upon truth, uprightly avoiding falsehood, and submitting himself to God.
verses.66:
Al-Mizan rejects two common explanations of the knowledge affirmed and denied in the verse. The People of the Book had not disputed Abraham’s existence or prophethood, and their disputes over Jesus cannot simply be called knowledgeable disputes because neither side was wholly right in its beliefs about him.

The commentary’s preferred explanation, offered with the qualification that God knows better, distinguishes the particular matters in which each side had knowledge. Christians knew that Jesus was a prophet sent by God when disputing this with the Jews; Jews knew the falsity of his alleged godhead, sonship, and trinity when disputing these claims with Christians. Their ignorant contention was that Abraham was a Jew or a Christian.

Their ignorance was not failure to know that Abraham preceded the Torah and Injīl, nor failure to see that an earlier man cannot follow a later one. Rather, they failed to draw the consequence: Abraham could be neither Jew nor Christian, but must have followed the divine religion, submission to God. Each group assumed that there could be only one true religion and identified it with its own later form.

Al-Mizan maintains that God’s religion is one: Islam, meaning submission to God. It has advanced through stages toward perfection in accordance with humanity’s progress, while Judaism and Christianity are branches or stages in the perfection of that root religion. Abraham founded this basic Islam and remained an upright Muslim; the root is not named after its later branches, but the branches are related to the root. Calling Abraham Muslim does not make him a follower of the Prophet or of the Qur’anic law. Islam as applied to Abraham means humbling oneself before God’s Lordship, whereas Islam as the name of the Qur’anic dispensation is a later usage. The People of the Book did not understand this graduated reality of the one religion, though God knows it.
verses.67: Al-Mizan reports an explanation that the verse answers not only Jewish and Christian claims that Abraham belonged to their respective religions, but also the idol-worshipping Arabs’ claim to follow al-dīn al-ḥanīf, the upright religion of Abraham. Since al-ḥanīfiyyah had thereby come to be misconstrued as idol-worship, the description of Abraham as upright is clarified by calling him a Muslim and denying that he was a polytheist. He followed Islam, submission to God, and was not like the polytheists of the days of Ignorance.
verses.68:
Al-Mizan explains that nearness to Abraham cannot mean that Abraham was a follower of later generations; it means likeness to him in following the truth and accepting the religion he brought. Those who followed Abraham in his own time, this Prophet, and the believers are nearest to him because they follow the Islam for which God chose Abraham. The Jews and Christians are thus indirectly told that they are not nearest to him, because they did not follow him in submission to God.

The separate mention of this Prophet and those who believe, rather than treating the Prophet merely as Abraham’s follower, manifests his exalted rank. The concluding statement that Allah is the Guardian of the believers completes the reasoning: Abraham was a waliyy, a friend of God, and his al-wilāyah, friendship and guardianship, belonged to God’s guardianship. God is Guardian of believers, not of those who disbelieve in His signs and mix truth with falsehood.
verses.69:
Al-Mizan explains that the desire to turn believers away from truth is itself a depravity of the soul, a sin and transgression against truth. Thus, even before such people mislead anyone, their desire to lead believers into falsehood has led them astray, though they do not perceive it.

Even if they plant doubts in a believer and succeed in misleading him, they have first misled themselves. Every good or evil deed belongs to its doer; one who goes astray through another’s deception does so principally through his own wrongful choice and sin, by God’s permission. The commentary treats this as a consequence of al-Tawḥīd, monotheism, of action, grounded in the realities of Lordship and Kingdom. It alone explains why the verse exclusively says that they lead astray only themselves; other explanations do not account for that exclusiveness.
verses.70:
Al-Mizan distinguishes disbelief in God’s communications from open disbelief in God Himself. The latter is a direct rejection of monotheism, whereas the former is rejection of clarified divine knowledge. The People of the Book acknowledge one God, but reject such communicated truths as Muḥammad’s prophethood, Jesus’ being God’s servant and messenger, and Abraham’s being neither Jew nor Christian.

When another verse describes some People of the Book as not believing in God and the latter day, the commentary takes this as an attribution through consequence: rejection of God’s communications entails such disbelief, even if they do not realize it. It does not mean that they openly and directly deny God.

Their witnessing in this verse refers specifically to their rejection of the Prophet despite seeing that the signs and descriptions of the promised Prophet in the Torah and Injīl fitted him completely. Al-Mizan therefore rejects the view that communications here is an unrestricted reference to every true sign of God.
verses.71:
Al-Mizan explains confounding truth with falsehood as presenting truth in the form of falsehood. The words while you know indicate, or at least allude, that the People of the Book were concealing and confusing religious knowledge and realities, rather than merely altering, hiding, or misinterpreting the written verses of scripture.

Together with the preceding verse, this completes the discussion of the party among the People of the Book that sought to mislead believers. The whole community is reproached for acts committed by some of its members because of their shared race, tribe, and character, and because they accepted what those members did; the Qur’an commonly speaks in this manner.
verses.72:
Al-Mizan explains wajh al-nahār, literally the face of the day, as its first part, in contrast to its end. It holds that the phrase in the first part of the day qualifies what was revealed, not avow belief: an early revelation agreed with the People of the Book’s practice, while a later revelation opposed it. Disbelieve at the end of it consequently means disbelieve in what was revealed at the day’s end, an expression in which the time is put for the event occurring at that time.

The commentary accordingly follows narrations from the Imams of the Ahl al-bayt concerning the change of qiblah. The Messenger of God prayed the morning prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis, the Jewish qiblah, and then, during the noon prayer, the qiblah was changed to the Kaʿbah. A group of Jews urged one another to accept the former revelation and reject the latter, hoping that believers would return from their religion. Their following instruction to trust only those of their own religion aimed to keep secret the foretold sign that the promised Prophet would change the qiblah toward the Kaʿbah.

Al-Mizan considers it possible in itself that they planned to feign belief in the morning and renounce Islam by day’s end in order to cast believers into doubt, but judges this inconsistent with the wording. Two further readings—affirming prayer toward the Kaʿbah early and rejecting it later, or first acknowledging and then denying the Prophet’s foretold signs—are said to lack proof. The commentary nevertheless regards the verse as unambiguous.
verses.73:
Al-Mizan reads this verse as continuing the People of the Book’s speech from the preceding verse. Their instruction not to believe except one who follows their religion means not to trust anyone outside their group with their secret. The words about another being given what they were given, and about opponents arguing before their Lord, also continue their speech. Surely the guidance is the guidance of Allah is a parenthetical divine reply to their whole scheme, while the declaration that grace is in Allah’s hand answers their fear that others might receive what they had received.

The commentary explains, with the qualification that God knows better, that the Jews urged one another to acknowledge the believers’ morning prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis but reject their afternoon prayer toward the Kaʿbah. They sought to conceal that the change to the Kaʿbah was foretold as a sign of the promised Prophet. They feared both that the believers would acquire a qiblah of their own and thereby end Jewish precedence in that matter, and that believers would argue before God that the Jews knowingly rejected a truth they had witnessed.

God’s answer is that the believers require God’s guidance, not Jewish guidance; the Jews’ disclosure or concealment cannot alter that. Their attempt to prevent an argument before God is so plainly false that it receives no direct reply, since God knows what people conceal and proclaim. Grace cannot be reserved by the Jews for themselves.

Al-Mizan treats grace, al-faḍl, as a voluntary and gratuitous divine bestowal. The statement that it is in God’s hand is an abbreviated argument: revelation and divine bestowal are grace, not something mortals can impose upon God; therefore He gives them to whom He pleases. The commentary further excludes every basis for monopolizing grace. No other power can divert God’s will, because grace is in His hand; grace cannot be exhausted, because He is Ample-giving and all-powerful; and no claimant can be hidden from Him, because He is Knowing. It regards alternative divisions of the speech between God, the Jews, and the believers, as well as alternative meanings assigned to grace, as remote from the context.
verses.74:
Al-Mizan explains that because grace is in God’s hand and He is Ample-giving and Knowing, He may select some servants for particular favors. The unrestricted character of His bounty and the absence of any external restraint do not oblige Him to distribute it indiscriminately; such an obligation would itself restrict His absolute power. He manages His own property as He pleases.

Allah’s being Lord of mighty grace explains this selection. Grace is great, belongs in His hand, and is bestowed by One who knows the condition of His servants and which favor suits each of them. The replacement of grace with mercy in the verse shows that grace, as a free and discretionary gift, is a branch of mercy.
verses.75:
Al-Mizan notes that the verse fairly distinguishes among the People of the Book: some return even a great trust, while others will not return even a small one without urgent and insistent pressure from the claimant. Al-qinṭār and al-dīnār are used respectively for a great and a small amount, and the singular addressee is indefinite, making the statement generally applicable. Remaining standing over the debtor denotes urgency and insistence.

The commentary attributes the dishonest attitude to the claim that there is no way of reproach against them in dealings with the unlearned people, meaning gentiles or non-Israelites. They called themselves the People of the Book and treated others as unlearned; they held that no gentile had a claim against an Israelite, and represented this conduct as religiously authorized. The verse refutes this as a lie against Allah knowingly told.

Al-Mizan says that they believed, and continue to believe, that they were the chosen people, uniquely entitled to divine grace, prophethood, the Book, and kingdom, and therefore superior to other races and entitled to subjugate them. On this basis, they limited social and financial duties, including protection of property and rights, to their own circle, while treating gentiles as having no such claims and as no better than animals. The commentary says this conception was not contained in books regarded as revealed, but was taken from rabbis and blindly followed. Since the religion of Moses was meant for the Children of Israel alone and did not admit others, it became a racial religion and produced the notion that Israelite birth itself gave absolute precedence. Such racial arrogance leads to mischief and destroys humanity’s social foundation.

The commentary adds that rights may sometimes be withheld from those who negate the rights of others or damage society. In its stated Islamic criterion, rights belong through acceptance of Islam or protection under the Islamic State; one who is neither Muslim nor dhimmī has no right in life. It holds that this accords with nature and with the general social principle of depriving aggressors of rights.

The wording among the People of the Book, rather than among them, prevents the verse from being confined to the previously mentioned party, while also intensifying the rebuke: possessing the Book means they knew it gave no permission to consume gentile property. Al-Mizan allows that this may refer either to the contrast between trustworthy and untrustworthy people, as an ethical disparity generated by their false premise, or only to the untrustworthy group, with the trustworthy group mentioned for completeness and justice. The pronouns may accordingly refer to all the People of the Book or to the specified subgroup. In every case, their claim is refuted as a knowing attempt to give their conduct the authority of divine revelation.
verses.76:
Al-Mizan explains that fulfilment of the promise means acting upon it and guarding it from breach. It primarily refers to God’s covenant that His servants believe in and worship Him, though it may extend to all promises, including that covenant. The verse answers the claim that there is no reproach for wrongdoing against non-Israelites: divine honor comes through God’s love for those who fulfil the covenant and guard against evil, not through permission to deceive, exploit, or oppress others.

The statement that Allah loves those who guard against evil contains an abbreviated syllogism: He loves the one who fulfils the promise because he is pious, and God loves the pious. Divine dignity is thus conditional on piety and covenant-keeping, not verbal affiliation or racial and national supremacy. It consists in God’s love, friendship, and guardianship, bringing divine help, a happy and prosperous life in this world, and elevation in the hereafter. It cannot authorize a supposed master race to claim exemption from accountability, exclusive friendship with God, or divine sonship and belovedness, and thereby spread corruption.

The following verse explains why this dignity is restricted to the pious. Those who break God’s covenant and their own oaths sell them, along with piety, for the small and immediate provision of this world in preference to everlasting happiness. They have exchanged the covenant for the world itself and consequently have no honor or portion in the hereafter.

Their punishment is the reverse of the nearness granted to the pious. The distal demonstrative used for them indicates their remoteness from God, whereas the pious are near through His love. Since they chose the worldly share, they receive no share in the hereafter. God will neither speak to them nor look upon them on the Day of Resurrection, denying them every degree of intimate honor; speech is mentioned before looking because it signifies the greater intimacy. Nor will He purify them, and they will have a painful chastisement. Al-Mizan takes these unrestricted statements to mean that they remain unpurified and under chastisement in both this world and the hereafter.

verses.78:
Al-Mizan explains that distorting the Book with the tongue means reciting lies invented against God in the tone and style used for revelation, so that hearers mistake them for part of the Book. The three occurrences of Book distinguish their forged writing from the Book actually revealed by God, and then repeat the latter in order to eliminate ambiguity and emphasize that the lofty divine Book cannot contain such forgeries.

Likewise, the repeated divine name in the assertion that their words are not from Allah stresses that they are not from the true God, who speaks only truth. The successive denials refute both their deceptive recitation and their claim of divine authority. They further show that lying against Allah is their ingrained and persistent trait, and that they do it knowingly rather than through confusion or ignorance.
verses.79:
Al-Mizan explains that li in li-basharin conveys ownership: it does not belong to such a man, and he has no right, to tell people, “Be my servants rather than Allah’s.” The verse’s wording is decisive. Had it merely said that it was not meet for a man to make this claim, it could mean that he had no right to do so but might nevertheless transgress through insolence. Instead, by making Allah’s giving of the Book, the Judgment, and Prophethood part of the statement, it teaches that a recipient of these favors—of knowledge, gnosis of reality, and Divine upbringing—cannot cross the limits of servitude or dispose of what is not his. Divine guidance necessarily achieves its end; therefore, combining these favors with a summons to one’s own worship is impossible, not merely forbidden. Jesus’ reply in (5:116), that it did not befit him to say what he had no right to say, illustrates this reality.

In this respect, the verse resembles the statement that the Messiah and the near angels do not disdain to be Allah’s servants (4:172–173). Their high rank makes disdain for worship impossible, especially since such pride entails painful chastisement, which cannot befit honored prophets or near angels. The objection that thumma, “then,” indicates delay does not alter the argument: the combination of Divine favor and calling people to unbelief may consist in simultaneous or successive acts.

The qualification “rather than Allah’s” is necessary because worship is accepted only when it is exclusively for Allah. Worshipping others alongside Him, even as alleged intermediaries or intercessors intended to bring one nearer to Him, is rejected. Worship in fact presupposes some independence for the object worshipped; but absolute Lordship and Godhead belong only to Allah. His Lordship and worship are complete only when every other independence is negated, so worshipping another with Allah remains worship of other than Allah.

Rather, a prophet given this station calls people to be al-Rabbānī—those specially related to the Lord, who devote their lives to His service and worship—through teaching and reading the Book. Al-dirāsah particularly denotes study of a book through reading, recitation, and memorization. Such a prophet calls people to faith in the Book’s fundamental Divine knowledge, to the noble traits it teaches, and to the good deeds they themselves urge upon others, so that they attach themselves solely to their Lord and become divine scholars. The past tense in bi-mā kuntum indicates that the audience had already been teaching and reading the Book.

This apparently alludes to the Christians, who claimed that Jesus had told them he was the son and Word of God. The Children of Israel had received a revealed Book but differed over it, with textual changes and alterations. Jesus was sent to clarify part of their disagreements, permit some things formerly forbidden to them, and call them back to their obligation to learn and teach the Book in exclusive attachment to their Lord. Although the verse may in some way apply to the Messenger of God, whose mission included the People of the Book, it applies more fittingly to Jesus because he preceded the Prophet and was sent exclusively to the Children of Israel. It plainly does not apply to the other ulu al-ʿAzm prophets with Books—Noah, Abraham, and Moses.
verses.80:
Al-Mizan explains that verse (3:80) denies that a man granted the Book, Judgment, and prophethood could command people to take angels or prophets as lords, and then command unbelief after they had submitted to God. Some People of the Book took angels as lords: the Sabaeans worshipped them under religious authority, while Arabs claiming Abraham’s religion called them God’s daughters. Likewise, Jews are quoted as calling ʿUzayr God’s son, although Moses and the Torah taught only monotheism; had Moses permitted this, he would have enjoined it, which is unthinkable.

The commentary distinguishes this verse from the preceding statement, “Be my servants rather than God’s.” The preceding verse concerns openly worshipping another besides God and alludes to Christians’ worship of Jesus, which they ascribe to Jesus’ own call. The present verse concerns taking angels and prophets as lords, a violation of monotheism by implication rather than an explicit declaration of godhood; hence it says “lords,” not gods. The preceding expression addresses “men” in the third person because “saying” ordinarily implies a face-to-face conversation, and the Prophet’s contemporaries were not present when Jesus was allegedly to have spoken. “Enjoining,” however, need not occur in the presence of those enjoined: a command associated with ancestors may be applied to descendants who identify with them. Thus the basic form is direct address, with the earlier third-person wording required by its particular context.

The final question addresses those who followed a prophet, such as the People of the Book, and those who claimed Abraham’s religion, such as the Arabs of the Days of Ignorance. If they truly followed the prophet given the Book, Judgment, and prophethood, they had already submitted to God; that prophet could not then divert them into unbelief from the path to which God had guided them. Here Islam means the monotheistic religion brought by every prophet, as in Surely the religion with Allah is Islam (3:19) and the surrounding verses, not merely the communal designation that arose after revelation. The commentary therefore rejects an exegete’s view that these verses refer specifically to the Messenger of God because a report says Abū Rāfiʿ al-Quraẓī and a Najrānite Christian asked Muḥammad whether he wanted them to worship him. That exegete confuses Qur’anic Islam, the universal religion of monotheism, with the later technical use of “Islam” for the Muslims’ religion.

The commentary then recounts the Qur’anic story of Jesus and Mary. Mary, daughter of ʿImrān, was dedicated by her mother to Temple service before her birth. Her father had died, and the priests disputed over her custody until Zachariah was chosen by lot. He protected her in a sanctuary, where he found provision with her from God. Mary was truthful, protected from sin, purified, chosen, addressed by angels, obedient to her Lord, and a sign for the worlds.

When Mary withdrew behind a curtain, God sent His Spirit to her in the form of a well-made man. He announced a pure son without a father, whose future miracles, support by the Holy Spirit, knowledge of the Book, Wisdom, Torah, and Injīl, and mission to the Children of Israel were disclosed to her. He breathed the Spirit into her, and she conceived Jesus. She withdrew to a remote place, endured childbirth beside a palm-tree, and was comforted by her child’s call to eat, drink, and remain silent before people. When her people reproached her for bearing a child unmarried, she pointed to Jesus. Speaking in the cradle, he declared himself God’s servant, recipient of the Book and prophethood, blessed wherever he was, commanded to pray and give zakāt, dutiful to his mother, and granted peace at birth, death, and resurrection.

This speech foreshadowed Jesus’ mission: to oppose oppression and injustice, revive and reform the shariah of Moses, restore obscured revealed knowledge, and clarify matters disputed by his people. Jesus and his mother nevertheless ate and drank and lived with the normal conditions of human life. Jesus was sent to the Children of Israel, called them to monotheism, and performed such signs as forming a bird from clay, healing the blind and leper, reviving the dead, and informing people of what they ate and stored, all by God’s permission. He confirmed the Torah while abrogating some prohibitions imposed upon the Jews as punishment, clarified part of their disputes, and announced a messenger to come after him named Aḥmad. When he recognized the obstinacy, hostility, and priestly arrogance of his people, he selected apostles from the small body of believers as helpers to God. The Jews then sought to kill him, but God took him away completely and raised him; they were left confused, some thinking they had killed him and others that they had crucified him, although it had only been made to appear so.

Al-Mizan lists Jesus’ Qur’anic stations: he was God’s servant, prophet, messenger to the Children of Israel, and one of the five ulu al-ʿAzm prophets, bringing a new shariah and the Injīl. He was named the Messiah, Jesus; was the Word of God and a Spirit from Him; an Imam; a witness over deeds; a bearer of good news of the Messenger of God; honored in this world and the next and brought near to God; among the chosen, selected, and righteous; blessed, purified, a sign and mercy to people, dutiful to his mother, and taught the Book and Wisdom. These characteristics belong either to acquired stations, such as servitude, righteousness, and nearness, or to special Divine bestowals.

The Qur’an, in the commentary’s view, establishes that Jesus was God’s servant and messenger and never claimed what Christians ascribe to him. His answer in (5:116–119) expresses complete servitude: he did only what his Lord ordered and told people only to worship Allah, his Lord and theirs. His role toward his people was to witness their deeds while he was among them; whether God forgave or punished them was wholly God’s affair. This does not deny Jesus’ intercession. The commentary holds that the Qur’an expressly or nearly expressly makes him an intercessor through the conjunction of his witnessing, his knowledge, and the exception in And those whom they call upon besides Him have no authority for intercession, but he who bears witness of the truth and they know (43:86). But this differs completely from atonement: Jesus’ words refute the claim that he controls his people’s fate, while neither affirming nor denying the intercession that God permits.

The Qur’an focuses on Christian claims about Jesus and Mary because they affect monotheism, rather than on every subsidiary disagreement. Its descriptions—calling the Messiah God’s son, identifying God with the Messiah, calling God the third of three, and saying “Three”—all point, according to the commentary, to a common doctrine of trinity in unity, despite the many divisions among Christians. The Torah and Gospels affirm divine oneness, while Gospel language concerning sonship and union with the Father led Christians to formulate the Trinity as one substance with three Persons: existence, knowledge or Word, and life or Spirit; that is, Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. The commentary notes that some Gospel passages use “Father” for God in relation to Jesus and others in a sense of distinction and honor, while other passages are taken to suggest union. It regards trinitarian formulas as an attempt to reconcile sonship with Christ’s teaching of one God, but as unintelligible in themselves. The Qur’an addresses their common result rather than their differing explanations because the same refutation applies to each.

Al-Mizan presents two Qur’anic arguments against trinity. First, God cannot take a son in any sense. Natural sonship entails a material body, separation of matter, likeness of offspring to parent, and gradual development. God transcends matter, motion, time, space, and gradual action; He possesses absolute Lordship, while all else is dependent on Him. Thus no being can share His identity, attributes, independence, or species. Even if sonship is made allegorical so that it no longer implies physical separation or graduality, it still entails a similar and independent divine being. If the Son is dependent on God, he is not God; if independent and similar to God, God’s oneness is negated. This is the force attributed to And they say: Allah has taken to Himself a son. Glory be to Him; rather, whatever is in the heavens and the earth is His, all are obedient to Him. The Originator of the heavens and the earth; and when He decrees an affair, He only says to it, Be , and it is (2:116–117), and to and say not, Three . Desist, it is better for you; Allah is only one God; far be it from His glory that He should have a son; whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth is His; and Allah is sufficient for a Protector (4:171). The description of God as Originator may also indicate that creation has no prior model; begetting a son of His own likeness would contradict that originality.

Second, Jesus specifically cannot share Godhead because his condition was human. He was conceived and born from Mary, raised through ordinary stages of life, and subject to hunger, thirst, eating, drinking, sleep, fatigue, pleasure, pain, joy, and sorrow. His miracles and fatherless birth are extraordinary only because rare, not impossible; Adam had no father, and other prophets performed miracles without ceasing to be human. The special mention that Jesus and Mary ate food in (5:73–75) especially proves need and material dependence, which cannot belong to a self-sufficient God. Jesus’ real human acts and conditions, recorded also in the Gospels, cannot be explained away as illusion. His prayers and worship demonstrate that he sought nearness to God in humility, rather than merely teaching others how to pray; no being can be both servant of itself and self-sufficient God. Likewise, the angels’ worship proves that they are not God’s daughters, and the obedience of the Holy Ghost to God and His messengers excludes its divinity. Jesus’ call to worship Allah, his Lord and the Lord of his people, likewise disproves his godhood. If his reported saying, “I and my Father are one” (John, 10:30) is accepted, the commentary says that, in light of the rest of his teaching, it can only mean that obedience to him is obedience to God, like Whoever obeys the Messenger, he indeed obeys Allah (4:80).

The commentary next distinguishes the Qur’anic doctrine of intercession from the Christian doctrine of atonement. It reports that Christians hold Adam’s eating from the forbidden tree to be an inherited original sin deserving unavoidable eternal perdition; that mercy and justice allegedly required Christ, who was both complete God and complete man, to enter Mary’s womb; and that the sinless Christ accepted crucifixion and the Divine curse in order to redeem believers, indeed the whole world, from punishment. Al-Mizan maintains that Christianity makes this crucifixion and atonement the foundation of its call, notwithstanding Gospel exhortations to believe in and love one God.

The commentary rejects the premise of Adam’s punishable sin. The prohibition concerning the tree was advisory, like a physician’s direction, intended for Adam’s worldly well-being; its consequence was exclusion from the Garden, not an otherworldly judicial punishment. Moreover, Adam was a prophet, and prophets are protected from sins and transgression of God’s binding commands. It also rejects the claim that Adam’s act remained permanently attached to him: God chose Adam, turned mercifully to him, and guided him. Forgiveness is a real aspect of a master’s authority, just as punishment is; if a sin cannot be removed after repentance, forgiveness loses its meaning.

The inheritance of Adam’s sin by descendants is also rejected as punishing those who did not commit it, apart from descendants who might approve of the act. The Qur’anic principle is: That no bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another: and that there is not for man (aught) except what he strives for (53:38–39). Nor are all sins alike. The Qur’an distinguishes grave and lesser sins and teaches that God forgives what is less than association with Him for whom He pleases; therefore, a violation concerning a tree cannot reasonably be placed with disbelief or polytheism and made the cause of eternal ruin.

According to Al-Mizan, the proposed conflict between Divine mercy and justice also imputes to God a human-like will and knowledge governed by external considerations. Such a God would deliberate, discover advantages and disadvantages, err, forget, regret, be overcome, and undergo change. A being subject to bodily conditions, change, limitation, and gradual completion is created and transient, not the self-existent Creator. The Qur’an instead affirms God’s absolute existence, power, knowledge, and life, all free of weakness, ignorance, death, change, bodily conditions, error, repentance, uncertainty, defeat, and need. It declares: Glory be to Allah (for freedom) from what they describe (37:159).

The incarnation thesis is therefore unintelligible: an eternal, unlimited, changeless Being beyond time, space, and bodily properties cannot be united with a body that develops from sperm to foetus and bears all physical accidents. The commentary connects the rejection of rational argument by Paul and other Christian leaders to the inability of this doctrine to stand before reason. It further says that speaking of God as “protected from sin” is misplaced: the imagined deity is said to err in perception and action, while sin in the sense of disobeying a superior cannot apply to God at all.

If God could become man while retaining full divinity, the commentary argues, there would be no reason He could not become any created species, combine multiple species, perform all creaturely acts, or possess contradictory attributes such as knowledge and ignorance, power and powerlessness, life and death. The claim that God suffered crucifixion and curse is equally impossible. Curse means exclusion from Divine mercy and honor, yielding poverty, disgrace, or privation; it cannot reach the Self-sufficient God. If the suffering and curse were real, the contradiction remains; if merely metaphorical, the alleged reconciliation of mercy and justice fails, because God Himself would not have furnished the required ransom.

The commentary then explains the Qur’anic account of deeds, law, and requital. Human social laws and penalties are mentally posited for social welfare and deterrence. Qur’anic teaching goes further: obedience to the God-given shariah forms noble traits in the soul, while disobedience forms evil ones. These real inner qualities prepare the person for Paradise or Hell, whose realities are nearness to God and distance from Him. Divine legislation completes creative guidance: it reforms human society and directs human beings toward nearness to God, producing both worldly well-being and preparedness for Divine bounty in the hereafter. Thus religion, conduct, and worship have an actual role in human perfection.

If eternal ruin were unavoidable until Christ’s atonement and no deed or repentance could remove it, the sending of prophets, revealed books, laws, promises, warnings, and earlier shariahs would have been futile. It would also leave unresolved the fate of the righteous prophets and believers who died before Christ. If atonement subsequently redeemed everyone, religious law and good deeds would become equally futile afterward; if it benefits only believers in Christ, as an objection proposes, this contradicts the claim of atonement for the whole world and confines salvation to a very small group, while calling into question the missions and books of the earlier prophets. Claims that previous books merely gave good news of Christ do not resolve the futility of their laws or explain why people were still commanded to obey them and cultivate virtue.

By contrast, God gives every being its creation and then guides it, including through religious guidance for mankind: Our Lord is He Who gave to everything its creation, then guided it (to its goal) (20:50). The guidance given after Adam’s descent already contained clear legislation, promise, and warning. God does not alter His word, forget, discover a defect in His plan, abandon what He wills, or suffer hindrance from another. He rewards each soul according to what it earns, without injustice. Hence neither a ransom nor a redemption can override His ownership; intercession itself occurs only by His permission.

Atonement, properly understood, is a human transaction in which something less valuable is offered to transfer a claimant’s right away from a person threatened by loss, captivity, or punishment. Such a transfer is conceivable in human social rights, which are conventional and alterable, but not in God’s real authority and ownership over created beings. Accordingly, the commentary reads So today ransom shall not be accepted from you nor from those who disbelieved; your abode is the fire (57:15), as well as the Qur’anic denials of compensation, bargaining, and a savior, as refutations of ransom and redemption. Jesus’ declaration in (5:116–118) that he merely conveyed God’s command and witnessed his people, leaving their punishment or forgiveness to God, also excludes his possessing authority to ransom them.

Intercession is not a transfer of authority, cancellation of the law, or negation of reward and punishment. It is the request of one near to the Master that He manage the sinner’s affair with mercy. The intercessor acknowledges the Master’s right to punish and asks Him to exercise His equally real right of forgiveness. Atonement, by contrast, is said to transfer the Master’s claim from the sinner to a ransom and to remove the sinner from the Master’s power. Jesus is therefore an intercessor, not a redeemer: his knowledge, witnessing, and inclusion among those who bear witness to the truth support this status, but only under God’s authority.

Al-Mizan says that these doctrines did not originate with Jesus. Christians, it argues, followed their leaders blindly, and those leaders brought ancient idolatrous myths into Christianity. The phrase that Jews and Christians imitate those who disbelieved before is taken to refer not to pre-Islamic Arabs, who were themselves not the original source of idolatry, but to earlier idolaters of India, China, Rome, Greece, North Africa, and related civilizations. The commentary finds resemblance between their myths and later beliefs concerning divine sonship, fatherhood, trinity, incarnation, crucifixion, and atonement. It similarly understands the warning against following people who went astray before and led many astray as referring to influential prior idolatrous civilizations rather than to Arab idolaters or merely to Jewish and Christian religious leaders.

The commentary distinguishes the Qur’anic People of the Book, namely Jews and Christians, from Zoroastrians, whose Avastha is not mentioned in the Qur’an. It says that the Qur’an mentions the Torah of Moses and the Psalms of David, and teaches that Jesus received one revealed Book, the Injīl, rather than the multiple Christian writings. It nevertheless holds that portions of the genuine Torah and Injīl remain in Jewish and Christian scriptures, citing the Torah’s containing God’s judgment and Christians’ having forgotten part of what they were admonished with.

Its historical discussion maintains that the present Torah lost its continuous connection with Moses after Nebuchadnezzar’s conquest, destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple, and loss of the Torah and Ark. It presents Ezra, after the Babylonian captivity, as compiling and editing the books attributed to Moses, and argues that this leaves unanswered questions about Ezra’s identity, learning, trustworthiness, sources, and means of correcting errors. It notes that some Western scholars consequently denied Moses’ historical existence, while rejecting any parallel denial of Jesus because the Qur’an plainly confirms him.

The commentary says Jewish literature gives no clear account of Jesus’ birth, mission, miracles, or death, while the Qur’an attributes to Jews the calumny against Mary and the claim to have killed the Messiah, not a certain claim of crucifixion. It describes them as confused and divided over the matter. Christian accounts, it says, depend on the four Gospels and associated Acts and Epistles. It questions the textual basis of Matthew because it was written after Jesus, was reportedly first written in Hebrew, and survives only in an unverified translation whose translator is unknown. It describes Mark as Peter’s disciple rather than one of the twelve, and reports that some held he wrote on Peter’s order and presented Jesus as God’s messenger. Luke is described as neither an apostle nor an eyewitness, but as one who learned Christianity from Paul; the commentary treats his prologue as indicating a human composition rather than revelation. It portrays Paul as the principal founder of later Christianity, teaching salvation through belief without corresponding action, allowing matters forbidden in the Torah, and setting aside circumcision and much of Mosaic law, whereas Jesus came to verify and restore the Torah, with only limited changes.

Regarding John, the commentary reports conflicting claims over date and authorship. Some ascribe it to John son of Zebedee and say Asian bishops urged him to write especially about Christ’s divinity in response to those who considered Christ a created man. Others attribute it to an Alexandrian student or another unknown writer who used John’s name, and others say the final chapter was later added. It concludes that the Christian narratives ultimately depend upon uncertain human reports, especially an allegedly lost original of Matthew, and asks whether that original taught Christ’s messengership or divinity.

The commentary further reports that some European writers, seeing these weaknesses and alleged parallels with Krishna, called Jesus mythical; others posited two Christs. It rejects such claims concerning Jesus because of the Qur’an, while using them to criticize the historical basis of Christian doctrine. It also reports that more than a hundred Gospels were written in the first centuries before the Church canonized four, and that the Gospel of Barnabas, though excluded, presents a story generally corresponding to the Qur’anic account. It cites a narrative reproduced by Hendrick Willem Van Loon concerning a Roman inquiry into Jesus, in which Jesus appears as a prophet who taught love, brotherhood, and one God, rather than as a divine being who descended to atone for sins. The commentary takes this as evidence that early Christianity in Israel concerned a prophetic mission, and that later disputes arose over Christ’s godhood, salvation by belief alone, and the relation of the Gospel to Mosaic law.

It argues that Christianity’s earliest missionary fields—such as Rome, India, and Africa—contained idolaters and traditions of incarnation, divine triads, a descending deity, suffering, crucifixion, and redemption. Citing reports about Indian, Chinese, Egyptian, Persian, Greek, Roman, and other ancient religions, it claims that Christian leaders reshaped Christianity in patterns familiar to idolaters. It connects this process with Paul’s and others’ contempt for philosophy and rational inquiry. Their doctrines, it says, were rejected by schools of logic as unintelligible; appeals to revelation, visions, and being filled with the Holy Ghost then served to evade rational criticism.

The commentary attributes Christianity’s spread, especially under Roman conditions, partly to oppression, economic inequality, and the promise of brotherhood, love, equality, and a happy heavenly life. It says rulers initially tolerated the movement because this teaching served their interests, but that its increased strength led Christians to oppose pagan leaders and imperial demands, producing persecution until Constantine recognized Christianity and churches spread through the empire. It then sketches the increasing power of the Roman Church, its division from the Eastern Church, the later claims of Russian rulers to Orthodox headship, and the emergence of Catholics, Orthodox, and Protestants. Church councils are portrayed as mechanisms for enforcing approved doctrine against dissenting groups through condemnation, exile, or death; the Nicene creed is presented as affirming the Father, the Son as true God and of one substance with the Father, the Holy Spirit, incarnation, crucifixion, resurrection, and the Church.

The final purpose of this history is to show, in the commentary’s view, how foreign and idolatrous ideas entered Christian belief and practice, how papal temporal and spiritual power reached a height in the Middle Ages, and how European Christians propagated false images of Islam during the Crusades, including claims that Muslims worshipped Muḥammad and other imagined gods. It sees a long progression from excessive reverence for Christ, to trinity, crucifixion and atonement, and then the notion that faith alone suffices and obedience to law is unnecessary. Religious rites initially remained, but Protestantism, political change, secular law, unrestricted freedom, materialism, socialism, and communism are presented as successive stages in the weakening and abandonment of belief, virtue, and religious action. Modern religious revivals are judged to be political instruments or to seek Divine approval for prevailing cultural values rather than submission to God. The commentary concludes that Christianity began with the revival of belief, moral character, and shariah, but ended, through what it regards as Paul’s first deviation and its consequences, in a civilization of materialistic animality that threatens mankind; it is therefore nearer the truth, in its judgment, to call modern civilization Paulian rather than Christian.
verses.81:
Al-Mizan explains mīthāq al-nabīyyīn, literally the “covenant of the prophets,” as one covenant seen from two aspects: it was made with the prophets and for them, and, through them, with their peoples. In its context, this covenant makes it impossible for prophets, after receiving Book, Wisdom, and prophethood, to summon people to worship anyone besides God; they were bound to believe in and aid God’s other prophets, who call to the One God.

The covenant is that, when God has given Book and Wisdom and then a Messenger comes confirming what is with them, they must believe and aid him. Al-Mizan considers the conditional reading of lamā more appropriate, although the relative reading yields substantially the same sense; the alternative recital limā carries less weight. Though the address is outwardly to the prophets, the command includes their ummahs: “accept My compact” means that the prophets make God’s compact with their peoples, who are equally obliged to believe in and help the coming Messenger.

The “then” indicates temporal succession, requiring an earlier prophet to believe in and help one who comes later. That later prophets must also believe in and help earlier ones is inferable from the subsequent collective declaration of faith, but is not stated by the wording itself. While both pronouns in “believe in him” and “aid him” could refer to the coming Messenger, Al-Mizan finds it apparent that the first concerns the bestowed Book and Wisdom and the second the confirming Messenger.

God’s question seeks confirmation. The view that the compact concerns the prophets alone is challenged by “Then bear witness,” since witnessing is for or against others, and by the later use of “We,” which apparently speaks for the Messenger and his ummah. Thus the prophets bear witness concerning their peoples, while God bears witness over both. Interpretations that make the prophets witnesses for one another, or make the angels the witnesses, may be possible in themselves, but cannot be drawn from the verse without an association; its context points otherwise.

Because every messenger is a prophet but not every prophet is a messenger, the covenant is made with the rank of prophethood for the rank of messengership, not conversely. It is therefore insufficient to describe it merely as a pledge that all prophets would affirm one another. Rather, prophets and their peoples pledged that, when a confirming messenger came, they would believe what he brought and help him: a later prophet supports an earlier or contemporary messenger by affirming his truth, while an earlier prophet foretells the later messenger and commands his ummah to believe, affirm, and help him. The covenant thereby affirms the Oneness of Divine Religion. The interpretation that it specifically requires prophets to affirm Muḥammad and announce his advent is correct in itself and may be inferred from the context, but cannot be established from the verse’s wording alone.
verses.82: Al-Mizan says that the verse emphatically declares those who turn away after this covenant to be transgressors.
verses.83:
Al-Mizan takes the question as a reproach to the People of the Book: God’s religion is one, and the covenant required earlier prophets and their peoples to announce, believe in, and aid the Messenger who followed. Their denial of his truth therefore amounts to seeking a religion other than Islam, the sole Divine Religion. Islam must be followed because it accords with nature; since rational beings in the heavens and earth submit to God in creation, they should submit to Him in legislation as well.

The universal submission expressed by aslama is already accomplished and concerns creative affairs, in which none can resist God’s decree. It does not mean Islam as religious belief and worship; “willingly or unwillingly” proves this. The phrase thus supplies an implicit proof: if people accept God’s religion, they submit willingly; if they dislike His decrees and seek another way, His decree is still enforced. The alternatives distinguish willing acceptance of what people like from resentment of decrees they dislike, such as death, poverty, and sickness.

Their return to God is a further reason to seek Islam. They must return to their true Lord and cannot hide from Him or flee to the things on which disbelief and polytheism make them rely.
verses.84:
Al-Mizan explains that God commands the Prophet to uphold the covenant by declaring faith for himself and the believers of his ummah in God and in all revelation given to the prophets. This collective declaration supports the conclusion that the covenant included both prophets and their peoples.

Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and those named with them are prophets from Abraham’s progeny. “The tribes” apparently denotes prophets descended from Jacob among the Children of Israel, while “the prophets from their Lord” makes the declaration comprehensive, including Adam, Noah, and all other prophets. The final statement therefore affirms that no distinction is made among any of them and that submission belongs to God alone.
verses.85: Al-Mizan says that the verse nullifies every religion outside the covenant’s scope and further emphasizes the obligation to fulfill its terms.
verses.86:
Al-Mizan explains the question as declaring it impossible for such people to receive guidance while they persist in injustice: God does not guide them because they are unjust. Repentance and return to God would, however, remove this bar.

Their witness that the Messenger is true means that the truth had been made clear and the proof completed against them. If the reference is to the People of the Book, they had recognized that the foretold signs of the awaited prophet fitted the Messenger; if it concerns apostates from Islam, their affirmation was an informed recognition of the Prophet’s truth, not a merely ritual or tribal profession. Their subsequent disbelief therefore arose from hatred of truth, arrogant contention with believers, and unjust transgression, which prevents deliverance.

The commentary also reports two syntactic possibilities: “And they have borne witness” may be conjoined to īmānihim, meaning that they disbelieved after belief and after bearing witness; or its “And” may be circumstantial, meaning that they disbelieved while bearing witness. Verses (3:87–88) then declare for them the curse of Allah, the angels, and all people, abiding without relief or respite; the commentary refers to its earlier exposition of how this curse returns upon such people.

verses.89: Al-Mizan explains aṣlaḥū as indicating the sincerity of repentance: they repent truly, so that disbelief’s impurity is removed and the soul is purified through true belief. It does not mean performing good deeds, although such deeds necessarily follow sincere repentance and are inseparable from it. “Then surely Allah is Forgiving, Merciful” implies its unstated result: He forgives them and has mercy on them because He is Forgiving, Merciful.
verses.90:
Al-Mizan reads the two verses as explaining why one who disbelieves after believing is not guided. Once truth has become manifest and proof has been completed, one who does not sincerely return to God falls into one of two classes. The first is the apostate who increases in unbelief and transgression without intending to amend. God neither guides him nor accepts his insincere repentance, because he does not turn to God sincerely; he is wholly lost, with no hope of return to the right path. The second is one who dies an unbeliever, averse to truth and without repentance. He will not be guided to the Garden in the hereafter, because he never sought to return to his Lord; repentance has no substitute there. Thus neither an earth-full of gold offered as ransom nor any helper or intercessor can benefit him.

The wording “these are they that have gone astray” intensifies their permanent remoteness from God’s mercy. Its nominal construction, predicate al-ḍāllūn, and the distant demonstrative ulāʾika indicate enduring straying; the separate pronoun “they” and the definite article add further emphasis. Together they show hardened wrongdoers for whom guidance is no longer hoped.

“And they shall have no helpers” means that they cannot benefit from intercession on the Day of Resurrection. The plural “helpers,” like the plural “intercessors” in 26:101 (So we have no intercessors), indicates that intercessors exist, but unbelievers cannot avail themselves of them. Ransom and helpers are substitutes when the original is unavailable; having lost repentance in this life, they find no substitute for it in the hereafter.

Finally, dying as unbelievers means dying without repentance, so this does not conflict with (4:18). There, “when death comes” means when death approaches, the person sees signs of the next world, and worldly ties are severed; at that point the door of repentance is closed.

verses.92:
Al-Mizan explains al-birr as comprehensive good-doing: inward acts such as true belief and pure intention, and outward acts such as worship and spending in God’s way. Its use in (2:177), which gathers together faith and deeds, shows that spending cherished wealth for God is an essential part of righteousness, not righteousness itself. It also rules out interpreting al-birr as God’s bounty or favour, or as the Garden.

The special stress on spending what one loves reflects the human attachment to accumulated wealth, which a person feels to be part of himself; unlike many other good deeds, such spending seems to involve a real loss. The assurance that Allah knows whatever is spent therefore comforts and encourages spenders: their beloved property has neither been lost nor escaped the notice of the One who commanded the expenditure.
verses.93:
Al-Mizan identifies Israel as the Prophet Jacob, whose name was acquired through striving hard in God’s way. It rejects the People of the Book’s claim, reflected in the Torah’s account of Jacob wrestling with and overcoming God, because both the Qur’an and reason make such a thing impossible.

Grammatically, “except that which Israel had forbidden to himself” is an exception from “all food,” while “before the Torah was revealed” qualifies “was lawful.” Thus no food had been divinely prohibited to the Children of Israel before the Torah, apart from what Jacob had personally forbidden himself. “Bring then the Torah and read it” challenges the Jews to let the Torah decide who is truthful.

The commentary holds that the verse answers a Jewish objection to abrogation. The Jews denied both that all foods had originally been lawful and that lawful things were later forbidden to them because of their iniquity, since they held that a Divine Law could never change. By this denial they sought to cast doubt among Muslims on the Prophet’s revelation-based claim that his religion was Abraham’s upright, natural religion. Al-Mizan infers that they apparently spread these objections in contact with believers rather than addressing the Prophet directly, because the Qur’an here answers without first quoting their words; the later verses about the People of the Book misleading believers support this inference.

God directs the Prophet to demand that they produce and read the Torah. Its testimony that foods were lawful before the Torah refutes their denial of abrogation; refusal to accept this proof exposes them as fabricators against God and establishes the truth of the Prophet’s mission, to which the religion of Abraham calls them.

Al-Mizan rejects two related explanations that make “Israel” mean the whole Children of Israel: one says their sins caused God to prohibit foods, and the other says they legislated prohibitions for themselves without revelation. These readings wrongly attach “before the Torah was revealed” to “Israel had forbidden” instead of to “all food was lawful,” and thereby distort the verse’s course. Although Arab tribal names can sometimes stand for their descendants, neither Qur’anic usage nor contemporary Arabic usage supports using “Israel” for the Children of Israel. The verse itself first says “the Children of Israel” and then “Israel,” and the singular masculine phrase “to himself” decisively indicates Jacob, not a tribe or people.
verses.94:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse apparently is God’s address to the Prophet, meant to strengthen him by indirectly declaring the Jews—who fabricate lies against God—to be the unjust. It may alternatively continue the Prophet’s reply to them, though the second-person singular in dhālika makes this less fitting. Even on that reading, its general wording is a veiled rebuke that allows the defeated adversary to yield without being expressly named.

“This” in “after this” refers to the explanation and proof presented to the Jews. A person who lies against God is not called unjust until proof has been plainly set before him, as some scholars have said; once it has been so established, the verse’s exclusive formulation means that such fabricators can be nothing but unjust.
verses.95: Al-Mizan explains that, since the Prophet’s declaration is true, the Jews should follow his religion and acknowledge that foods such as camel meat are good things God made lawful, though He later prohibited them to the Jews as punishment for their injustice and transgression. The command to follow Abraham’s religion is an indirect summons to follow the Prophet: the Jews accepted Abraham’s religion as true, and the wording presents the religion offered to them as upright and natural, for human nature does not forbid the good sustenance God has provided, including meat.
verses.96:
Al-Mizan explains that the House at Bakkah, the Kaʿbah, was “appointed for men” by being dedicated to the worship of God. It assists worshippers in praying to Him through journeying to it, facing it, and the various acts performed there. Its designation as Bakkah, meaning a gathering, alludes to the continual assemblage of people for circumambulation, prayer, and other rites. The wording does not mean that it was the first house ever built on earth, nor the first house appointed for mankind’s general benefit.

Bakkah properly denotes the land on which the Kaʿbah stands, so called because of the crowds gathered there. Other explanations identify it with Mecca, the Meccan Sanctuary, the Sacred Mosque, or the circumambulation area.

“Blessed” means endowed with abundant good. Although such good embraces both worlds, its contrast here with “a guidance for the worlds” indicates worldly blessing: especially Mecca’s provision and people’s deep yearning to make pilgrimage and honor the House. This manifests Abraham’s prayer: O our Lord! surely I have settled a part of my offspring in a valley, uncultivable, near Thy Sacred House, our Lord! that they may establish prayers; therefore make the hearts of some people yearn towards them and provide them with fruits; haply they may be grateful (14:37).

The Kaʿbah guides people to happiness in the hereafter, nobility, and Divine Nearness because God designated it for worship and prescribed prayers, rites, and acts of worship there. The Qur’an shows that, after Abraham completed its construction, pilgrimage was first prescribed: Abraham and Ishmael were commanded to purify the House for those who circumambulate, remain in devotion, bow, and prostrate; Abraham was also commanded to proclaim the Ḥajj, which people would answer from near and far. The use of “pilgrimages” for years in Shuʿayb’s words to Moses shows that pilgrimage was an established annual institution. Abraham’s invocation likewise indicates that the House continually functioned as a centre of worship and symbol of guidance.

Even in the days of ignorance, the Arabs revered the House and performed its pilgrimage as part of Abraham’s shariah; other nations also respected it. Such reverence itself guides by fixing minds upon the remembrance of God. After Islam, its guidance is evident in its worldwide renown and in Muslims’ continual orientation toward it in prayer, worship, slaughter, and other religious matters.

Thus the House guides through every stage, from mere attentiveness of mind to complete surrender to God, a stage attained only by God’s purified servants who are free from sin and error. It guides to the happiness of both this world and the next, unconditionally and without restriction to any particular people. It also unifies the Muslim ummah in purpose and opens worldly avenues of benefit and profit, while showing others the advantages of uniting separate forces.
verses.97:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse’s “clear signs” are the Standing Place of Abraham, the House’s sanctuary and security for those who enter it, and the obligation of pilgrimage upon those able to make the journey. The latter three clauses are not grammatically an explicative apposition or substitute for “clear signs,” because this would require changing independent sentences into nouns or otherwise reconstructing them contrary to the context. Rather, they are independent sentences, declarative or imperative in force, which collectively explain the House’s clear signs.

“The standing place of Abraham” has an omitted predicate: there is in it the standing place of Abraham. It refers to the stone bearing the imprint of Abraham’s feet, though the phrase can also suggest the place in, or the House itself, where Abraham stood or stayed in Divine Worship. An alternative analysis takes the implied expression to be: the signs are the Standing Place of Abraham, security, and pilgrimage; “security” and “pilgrimage” are omitted because the following sentences indicate them. On this reading, the following declarative forms convey an imperative sense.

The commentary identifies this as a Qur’anic style in which a statement retains its own theme while simultaneously indicating another meaning; one expression thus serves two purposes without losing either. If explicative apposition must be used, it is better applied only to “the Standing Place of Abraham,” while the next two independent sentences point to omitted appositions: the security of the visitor and the pilgrimage of one able to undertake it.

Each of these is a clear sign leading to God and reminding people of His majesty: Abraham’s standing place, the sanctuary’s security, and the enduring worship and rites performed by millions year after year. A sign need not be a supernatural or miraculous phenomenon. Qur’anic usage includes abrogated laws among God’s signs and calls a monument a sign. Therefore, the view that only the Standing Place of Abraham is a clear sign, excluding security and pilgrimage, is untenable. So too is the claim that the signs are merely special, miraculous characteristics of the Kaʿbah, since there is no evidence that “signs” has this restricted meaning.

“Whoever enters it shall be secure” refers to a legislative law, not an inherent creative property of the sanctuary. Apparently declarative, it describes a long-established law of sanctuary traceable to Abraham and recognized even by the pre-Islamic Arabs. The claim that violence and turmoil cannot occur there is refuted by the battles and violence that have occurred in the area. Nor does 29:67 establish inherent security; it points to the security resulting from people’s respect for the House’s sanctity under Abraham’s shariah, and thus ultimately from Divine Legislation. Abraham’s prayers, My Lord! make this city secure (14:35) and My Lord! make it a secure town (2:126), were answered by God’s legislating this protection and instilling acceptance of it in people’s hearts across generations.

Ḥajj literally means intending or aiming, then came to mean proceeding to the House in the manner prescribed by the shariah; sabīlan specifies the ability to afford the journey. The verse approvingly describes ḥajj as an Abrahamic law, as indicated by God’s command to Abraham to proclaim it. Like the declaration of sanctuary, the declaration that pilgrimage is incumbent is best understood as declaratively affirming a previously ordained law, though it is possible to read both as imperatives reconfirming the two Abrahamic laws; the context clearly favors the former.

Finally, disbelief here is disbelief in a religious law, such as that resulting from neglecting prayer or zakāt; in this context, it means neglect of the weighty obligation of ḥajj. The wording uses the effect for its cause: one who neglects ḥajj becomes a disbeliever. “Allah is Self-sufficient” uses the cause in place of the effect: such disbelief cannot harm God, who is independent of all worlds.
verses.98: Al-Mizan explains that the communications denied by the People of the Book concern the lawfulness of food before the Torah and the Kaʿbah’s being Islam’s qiblah; Allah witnesses what they do.
verses.99: Al-Mizan explains that al-Ṣadd means hindering or diverting believers from God’s way, while seeking it iwajan means wanting that way to become crooked rather than straight. The Jews knew that food had been lawful before the Torah and that the promised prophet would change the qiblah to the Kaʿbah. Thus they themselves witness the truth of the Prophet’s claim while denying it, whereas Allah witnesses their denial and disbelief and is not heedless of what they do. The shift from Allah’s witnessing to their witnessing highlights that Allah is witness over everyone and everything.
verses.100:
Al-Mizan identifies the party among those given the Book as the Jews, or a Jewish group, whose obedience would turn believers back into unbelief after faith. Believers can protect themselves by holding to the revealed communications and the Messenger: they should hear and reflect upon the verses, seek the Messenger’s clarification if reflection causes difficulty, or consult him directly, since he is present and accessible. In this way they can discover the reality and remove the doubts the Jews try to create.

Holding fast to the Messenger and the Divine Communications is holding fast to Allah. The statement that whoever holds fast to Allah is guided functions as the major premise establishing this conclusion. Guidance to the straight path is firmly rooted true belief: a path that neither deviates nor fails to reach its destination, and keeps its travellers from straying. The passive past tense rendered “is guided” implies that they have been guided without realizing who guided them. The Book of God together with the Messenger’s verbal and practical guidance is sufficient for every truth and reality in which a person might go astray.
