verses.102:
Al-Mizan explains al-taqwā, when related to God, as guarding oneself against His punishment by acting according to His pleasure: obeying His commands, avoiding His prohibitions, showing gratitude for His favors, and being patient in adversity. Gratitude and patience are both aspects of putting things in their proper place. Thus fear of God is obedience and submission in all that He gives or withholds.

The verse demands al-taqwā in its full right: pure servitude untouched by wrongdoing, heedlessness, disobedience, ingratitude, or forgetfulness. This is true Islam at its highest degree. “And do not die unless you are Muslims” therefore commands believers to remain in this condition of ideal piety until death.

This does not conflict with “Therefore fear Allah as much as you can (64:16).” The latter directs each person to advance toward piety according to his strength, understanding, and will; people differ in their capacities and in the spiritual stations they can recognize and attain. It is the path toward the former verse’s ultimate goal, ideal piety, just as all are invited to the Straight Path although only true believers and pure monotheists reach it. Divine help is bestowed on those deserving it.

Although death itself lies beyond human control and may be the subject of a creative command, it can be joined to a voluntary condition. The prohibition is therefore legislative: believers must hold fast to Islam in every circumstance and at every time, so that death reaches them while they are Muslims.
verses.103:
Al-Mizan explains that holding fast to God means holding fast to His communications and His Messenger: the Book of God and the Prophet’s sunnah. Since the Book itself commands obedience to the Messenger, holding fast to the Messenger is also holding fast to the Book. Here the expression “the cord of Allah” specifically presents the revealed Book as the bond joining the creature to his Lord and heaven to earth; it may also denote the Qur’an together with the Prophet, because the result is the same.

Where the preceding command concerned the individual’s ideal piety and dying in Islam, this verse concerns the Muslim society. “All together” and “be not divided” require that society collectively to hold fast to the Book and the sunnah.

The command to remember God’s favor in turning enemies into brethren exemplifies the Qur’anic method of education: it explains the realities, causes, and paths of human happiness rather than requiring blind following. This does not remove the duty of unconditional submission to God and obedience to His Messenger. God’s lordship and complete ownership are the fundamental proof requiring submission to Him, and the Messenger’s messengership proves that what he conveys is from God. Thus believers should accept an established religious reality when they understand its reason; if they do not, they should seek understanding through research and reflection rather than reject or object to it. Requiring a further proof from God or His Messenger after these basic proofs would be folly. The Islamic and prophetic way calls to knowledge, not blind following.

Unity is called a divine favor because the believers had experienced both the misery of enmity and the sweetness of love and brotherhood. The verse offers two proofs for unity: their experienced former enmity, and the rational explanation that they stood at the brink of a pit of fire. Brotherhood denotes the love and unity produced by this favor; it may also refer to the legislated brotherhood of believers, with its important reciprocal rights and duties.

The “fire” may be the Fire of the hereafter: while unbelievers, they were near to falling into Hell at death, and true faith saved them. Or it may be the fire of their former social condition—wars and conflicts. A society of divided hearts and divergent minds cannot move under one leader or toward one end; each faction pulls toward its own desires, producing continual dissension, conflict, war, decline, and possible extinction. The immediate audience had lived before Islam amid insecurity, warfare, and the absence of public order protecting property, honor, and life. Their own experience of unity under God’s cord made the reminder especially compelling.

The warning is consequently grounded in lived observation, and the following warning about earlier divided peoples likewise calls believers to learn from nations ruined by disunity and internal strife. God makes these signs clear so that they may follow the right way.
verses.104:
Al-Mizan holds that knowledge and action sustain one another: knowledge is the strongest motive for action, while action is the greatest teacher of knowledge. Knowledge that is not repeatedly recalled and practiced is soon forgotten, and the quality and effectiveness of action depend on the quality of knowledge. A sound society must therefore preserve its useful knowledge and virtuous culture, restore those who deviate to the right path, and protect them from sin and error. This is the social educational duty of inviting to good, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong.

The terms al-maʿrūf and al-munkar literally mean what is “known” and “unknown.” In the ideal society founded on holding fast together to God’s cord, good and right are what its members recognize, while evil and wrong are what they do not recognize. Without this point, the terms could only be understood as known and unknown in religion rather than in the society’s actual life.

Some interpret “from among you” as requiring only a section of the Muslim ummah to perform this duty; others take it as explanatory and therefore address the whole ummah. Al-Mizan considers the dispute practically irrelevant: this duty cannot remain obligatory upon everyone once its purpose has been achieved by some. Initially the responsibility rests on all, but when a selected group performs it, they receive its reward and the rest are exempt. The closing promise of success belongs to those who carry it out. Apparently, however, “from among” denotes a portion, as is ordinarily understood unless there is reason to depart from that sense.
verses.105:
Al-Mizan says that “after clear evidences had come to them” probably qualifies “disagreed” alone. Division then means physical separation and dissociation, while disagreement means divergence in belief. Division is mentioned first because it leads to ideological difference: continued contact among a community’s members harmonizes and unifies their ideas, whereas separation ends their mutual influence and permits each group to develop independent views, theories, and beliefs. The verse warns Muslims against beginning the course of ruin by withdrawing from one another and ending in divergent doctrines.

The commentary notes that the Qur’an traces such disagreement to revolt and envy. Differences in ideas are unavoidable because people’s knowledge and understanding differ, but society must remove them and return deviators to unity; neglecting this duty is itself a revolt leading to perdition.

Al-Mizan maintains that the Qur’an’s emphatic warnings against Muslim disunity also foretell that the ummah would fall into it, even more than earlier peoples. The Prophet likewise foretold that divisions and sects would arise in his ummah as they had among Jews and Christians. History, the commentary says, confirms this: after the Prophet’s death, people scattered into sects accusing one another of apostasy, and attempts to unite two sects produced a third.

It further concludes from Islamic history and literature that hypocrites were the fountainhead of these differences. Though the Qur’an forcefully exposed their danger during the Messenger’s lifetime, they were subsequently treated in Muslim literature as though they had disappeared after his death. Sectarian division then prevailed, tyrannical governments subjugated the community, and its felicity became the misery of error and straying.
verses.106: Al-Mizan explains that, because the discussion concerns ungratefulness—a source of shame like treachery and breach of trust—the corresponding punishment is blackness of face, metaphorically signifying disgrace, abashment, and shame. The question, “Did you disbelieve after your believing?” makes this clear. Conversely, those grateful for the divine favor receive brightness of face, denoting contentment and delight, and abide in Allah’s mercy.
verses.107: Al-Mizan explains that, because the discussion concerns ungratefulness—a source of shame like treachery and breach of trust—the corresponding punishment is blackness of face, metaphorically signifying disgrace, abashment, and shame. The question, “Did you disbelieve after your believing?” makes this clear. Conversely, those grateful for the divine favor receive brightness of face, denoting contentment and delight, and abide in Allah’s mercy.
verses.108:
Al-Mizan explains that “with truth” may qualify the act of recitation, the communications themselves, or an omitted expression. In every case, the communications describing God’s treatment of the ungrateful and grateful are grounded in truth, free of falsehood and injustice.

The negation of “any injustice” is comprehensive, as is “the creatures”: God does not desire injustice of any kind for any creature or group of creatures. The commentary adds that human difference and conflict are so evil that their consequences harm all mankind.
verses.109:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse establishes God’s freedom from injustice through two complementary proofs. First, everything in the heavens and earth belongs to Him in every respect, so nothing lies outside His ownership such that His managing it could be usurpation or transgression. An exegete’s argument from God’s self-sufficiency is rejected as not conforming to the verse’s apparent meaning, which rests on divine ownership rather than self-sufficiency.

Second, every thing and affair returns to God. If another possessed independent authority over anything, God’s removing it from that authority and disposing of it as He willed could be called injustice; but all things return to Him. Thus one proof rests on the fact that everything belongs to God, and the other on the fact that no affair belongs to anyone else.
verses.110:
Al-Mizan explains ukhrijat, “raised up,” as carrying the sense of being brought forth or introduced, and understands “men” as humanity generally. Ummah may denote a group or an individual united by a common aim. Some exegetes take kuntum, “you were,” without temporal force, meaning that Muslims are the best community brought forth for mankind because they are united, believe in God, and enjoin right and forbid wrong. On that view, the whole ummah receives this honor because some of its members possess true belief and perform these duties.

The commentary rejects that reading: kuntum is plainly past tense and refers to the believers’ condition in Islam’s early days, especially the foremost Emigrants and Helpers. Their belief was their affirmative response to the command to hold fast to God’s cord without division, the opposite of the disbelief mentioned in “Did you disbelieve after your believing?” The People of the Book’s belief in this verse has the same import.

Thus the Muslims were, when first brought forth for people, the best group ever formed because they enjoined good, forbade evil, and, through holding fast to God’s cord, were united as one body and soul. If the People of the Book had likewise believed, it would have been better for them; instead, some are believers while most are transgressors, divided and disunited.
verses.111: Al-Mizan explains that al-Adhā, or “slight distress,” is harm suffered in one’s soul, body, or relations, whether in this world or the next.
verses.112:
Al-Mizan explains al-dhillah as a condition of abasement and degradation: al-dhull is humiliation imposed by another, while al-dhill results from one’s own obstinacy; its opposite, al-ʿizz, denotes honour, strength, and pride. Thuqifū means “are found,” and al-ḥabl, literally a rope that protects one who holds it, extends to a covenant, guarantee, amnesty, or other protection.

Apparently, abasement is either stamped upon them, like a design on a coin, or encompasses them like a tent. The repeated “protection” has distinct senses: God’s protection is His creative or legislative decree and command, whereas human protection is people’s decision and action. The more obvious meaning is legislative: wherever believers find and subjugate them, God’s law affirms their abasement, one effect of which is jizyah. Thus they are abased under Islamic shariah unless protected by an Islamic State or otherwise by people.

An exegete instead takes the clause as a factual account of divinely decreed abasement already suffered by the Jews, who at Islam’s advent paid jizyah to Persian fire-worshippers or were subject to Christians. Al-Mizan allows that this may be correct, and that the ending apparently supports it by linking abasement to disbelief in God’s signs, unjust killing of prophets, and continuing transgression. Yet this interpretation would restrict the verse to the Jews, while the verse apparently gives no indication of such exclusiveness.

Bāʾū means that they settled in or returned with God’s wrath. Al-maskanah, rendered “humiliation,” literally signifies extreme poverty from which one apparently finds no escape; thus the end conforms to the beginning. Their disobedience came after an already habitual and continuous exceeding of limits.
verses.113:
Al-Mizan holds that the People of the Book are neither alike in conduct nor subject to identical rules: among them is an upright party. Qāʾimah can mean firm in obedience, just, or proceeding on the straight path, but the reference to the Book and their deeds makes its intended sense firmness in belief and obedience. They recite God’s communications at times during the night, prostrate, believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin right, forbid wrong, and vie in hastening to every kind of good deed, including worship, spending in God’s way, justice, and care for the needy.

The commentary distinguishes al-Surʿah, praiseworthy promptness in something where promptness is allowed, from al-ajalah, blameworthy haste where one should not proceed; the former characterizes movement, the latter the mover. These traits—belief, enjoining good, forbidding evil, and hastening to good—make them among the good: people of the straight path and companions of the prophets, the truthful, and the martyrs. It has been said that the verses refer to ʿAbdullāh b. Salām and his companions. Their good will not be denied or lost: God will reward it fully, and He knows the pious.

The commentary apparently takes “those who disbelieve” in (3:116) to mean the other groups of the People of the Book who did not answer the Prophet’s call, conspired against Islam, and strove to extinguish the truth. Their wealth and children cannot avail them against Allah, and they will abide in the Fire. The view that the verse concerns idol-worshippers and introduces the Battle of Uḥud ignores the subsequent description of Jews dealing with Muslims—“and you believe in the Book (in) the whole of it” and “when they meet you they say: We believe”—and therefore wrongly treats the context as having changed. Combining the two views by assigning this verse to idolaters and the next to Jews is likewise a mistake.

verses.117: Al-Mizan explains that al-Ṣirr is intense cold. By qualifying their spending as being “in this life of the world,” the verse shows that they are wholly cut off from the hereafter and that all their spending belongs to worldly aims. Their expenditures to improve their position and attain evil ends yield only misery, destroying what they desire and imagine will make them happy. They are like an intensely cold wind that destroys the crop of people who have wronged themselves: God does not wrong them; their own evil deeds can produce only evil results.
verses.118:
Al-Mizan explains that al-biṭānah, literally a garment’s inner lining and opposed to al-ẓihārah, denotes an intimate friend because such a person knows one’s inward thoughts and secrets. Believers are forbidden to take intimates from others than their own people because such people leave no effort undone in causing khabālan—harm and mischief that, like insanity, destroys understanding—and love the believers’ grievous distress.

Their vehement hatred is already evident in their speech and slips of the tongue. The verse does not specify what their breasts conceal; this vagueness itself emphasizes that their hidden hatred is too extensive and varied to describe, and is greater still.
verses.119:
Al-Mizan explains that ūlāʾi is a demonstrative pronoun and hā an exclamatory particle, with “you” inserted between them, yielding the sense of “you these.” The definite article in “the Book” denotes all revealed Books: believers accept both their own Book and those of the others, whereas the others do not believe in the believers’ Book.

Their claim, when meeting believers, that “We believe” demonstrates hypocrisy. When alone, they bite their fingertips—a proverbial expression for forceful rage or sorrow—out of rage against the believers. “Say: Die in your rage” is a curse expressed as a command: “O God! cause them to die in their rage,” for Allah knows what lies in their breasts, that is, their hearts or souls.
verses.120: Al-Mizan explains that al-Masāʾah, grief, is the opposite of al-Surūr, happiness. The believers can protect themselves from their opponents’ schemes only through patience and piety; Allah comprehends what those opponents do.
verses.121:
Al-Mizan explains the verse as an injunction to remember when the Prophet went out early from his ahl to assign the believers their positions for battle. Ghadawta means going out early in the morning, at-tabwʾah preparing or assigning a place, and maāʿid means seats or encampments. Ahl denotes human beings exclusively connected with someone—by household, genealogy, religion, locality, or craft—and can be singular or plural and masculine or feminine. Here it denotes a group exclusively related to the Messenger, not a single wife or mother. Thus there is no need to posit an omitted word, such as “house,” as one exegete did.

The shift from the surrounding plural address to the singular address of the Prophet is significant. These battle verses carry an undercurrent of reproach for the Muslims’ cowardice and lack of resolve; when the matter concerns the Prophet alone, the address turns away from them to him. By contrast, the plural is retained where direct rebuke of the believers is more effective, while the verse about God’s favor in raising a Messenger among them is phrased so as to make that favor more impressive.

The expression that the Prophet went forth from his family indicates that the battlefield was near his house and clearly identifies the event as Uḥud, not Badr or the Confederates. Allah being Hearing and Knowing means that He heard what was said there and knew what was concealed in their hearts. It indicates that some Muslims uttered undesirable things and hid others; apparently, the following reference to two groups intending cowardice is connected to these attributes.
verses.122:
Al-Mizan explains al-hamm as a determination or intention held in the heart, and al-fashl as weakness joined with cowardice. The two parties truly determined to show cowardice, although Allah was their guardian. That guardianship, together with the command that believers trust in Allah, is an admonition and reproof: one who knows Allah to be his guardian and entrusts affairs to Him should not succumb to weakness, for whoever trusts Allah finds Him sufficient.

The commentary rejects the claim that their intention was only a passing thought, on the ground that such a thought is neither what Arabic calls a determination nor something that would have been apparent to others. The verse indicates an intention that affected their conduct, and its reminder of divine guardianship and reliance upon Allah fits a firm resolve, not a fleeting notion. “Allah was the guardian of them both” is therefore not praise in this context.

A tradition attributed to Jābir b. ʿAbdillāh al-Anṣārī says that the verse was revealed concerning his group and that he would not wish it unrevealed because Allah called Himself their guardian. Even if authentic, Al-Mizan holds that Jābir meant that Allah accepted and confirmed their faith, since Allah is guardian of believers, not that the clause praised their intended cowardice amid evident censure.
verses.123:
Al-Mizan holds that the reminder of Allah’s help at Badr either serves as supporting evidence that completes the preceding reproach—so that they should not have intended cowardice while Allah had helped them in weakness—or stands independently as a reminder of the extraordinary aid sent through angels at Badr.

The description of them as weak means that human beings, considered in themselves, possess only neediness and weakness; all strength comes through Allah’s help. It therefore does not conflict with the believers’ might, for their might derives from Allah’s might and from His assistance. They were also relatively weak at Badr compared with the polytheists’ strength, power, and zeal. Relative weakness may properly be attributed even to people otherwise described as mighty.
verses.124:
Al-Mizan explains al-Imdād as continuously supplying al-madad, help. Balā means affirmation, while al-fawr, originally the boiling of a pot, came to mean haste; thus min fawrihim hādha means that the enemy comes upon them at once, in a headlong manner.

The promise of angelic assistance concerns Badr and is conditional: the believers must remain patient and guard against evil, and the enemy must attack immediately. The commentary rejects interpretations that make it a promise for an attack after Badr or a general promise for later battles such as Uḥud, Ḥunayn, and the Confederates. Nothing here indicates angels at Uḥud; although the Qur’an elsewhere mentions unseen hosts at the Confederates and Ḥunayn, this wording does not establish a general promise.

There is no contradiction between the three thousand angels mentioned here and the thousand in al-Anfāl: “… so He answered you: ‘‘I will assist you with a thousand of angels following (after others)’’ [8:9]. “Following” indicates that this thousand followed others, namely the remaining two thousand completing the number stated here.

verses.126:
Al-Mizan takes “it” to mean the promised help. While ʿind originally denotes nearness and presence in place and later extends to temporal, general, and spiritual nearness, min ʿind allāh here denotes the station of Lordship from which every affair and command proceeds and without which no cause can suffice independently.

The angels are only apparent causes, providing good news and reassurance to the believers’ hearts; they have no real share in the promised help. Help in reality is only from Allah, to whom everything ultimately returns: the Mighty, who cannot be overcome, and the Wise, who is unaware of nothing.
verses.127:
Al-Mizan connects “That He may cut off a portion” to Allah’s assistance at Badr. Cutting off a portion metaphorically means reducing and weakening the unbelievers through killing and capture, as at Badr, where seventy idol worshippers were killed and seventy taken prisoner; al-kabt means to abase and exasperate.

“You have no concern in the affair” is parenthetic and confirms that the power to diminish or abase the enemy belongs wholly to Allah, not to the Prophet. The believers therefore should neither praise and acclaim him when they prevail nor blame and remonstrate with him when events go against them, nor become weak and grief-stricken as they did at Uḥud.

Whether Allah turns to them mercifully or chastises them continues the preceding purpose: the divine arrangement at Badr could cut off and abase the polytheists, disappoint them, turn to them mercifully, or punish them. The statement that whatever is in the heavens and earth belongs to Allah explains why repentance, forgiveness, and chastisement rest exclusively with Him: He owns all things and forgives or chastises whom He pleases. Yet His forgiveness and mercy surpass His chastisement and anger, for He is Forgiving, Merciful. The commentary sets aside alternative exegetical connections because they oppose the apparent meaning and context.

verses.130: Al-Mizan explains that “devouring” interest means taking it, while “making it double and redouble” identifies interest’s essential effect: it multiplies the creditor’s wealth by draining the debtor’s resources and adding them to the creditor’s capital. The warning to fear the Fire prepared for unbelievers indicates that the taker of interest is an unbeliever, as explained in connection with: And Allah does not love any ungrateful sinner [2:276].

verses.133:
Al-Mizan states that al-Musāraʿah, rushing or hastening, is praiseworthy in good deeds and blameworthy in evil ones. Forgiveness is generally joined in the Qur’an to the Garden because the Garden is a realm of purity into which the pollution of sins and vices cannot enter until forgiveness removes it.

Forgiveness here corresponds to the later description of those who commit indecency or wrong themselves and seek pardon, while the Garden corresponds to those who spend benevolently in ease and straitness. Its “extensiveness” denotes the utmost spaciousness, beyond human imagination. That it is prepared for the pious introduces the qualities needed by believers after Uḥud: qualities that would give them unity, harmony, and solidarity in future similar trials, after their weakness and disobedience.
verses.134:
Al-Mizan explains that spending is required both in ease and difficulty. Restraining anger translates al-Kaẓm, originally tying the mouth of a filled waterskin and then used for suppressing emotions. al-Ghayẓ is the stirring of vengeful feeling in response to unpleasant things, unlike al-ghaḍab, which is the intention to retaliate or punish.

Those who spend, restrain anger, and forgive people are thereby described as doers of good to others. Yet these acts have no value before God unless done for Him. Doing good in its fuller sense requires firm, steadfast faith in God, striving against one’s desires through sincere worship, benevolent spending in His way, and upright conduct in society. Thus it means performing all actions properly while remaining steadfast in divine faith.
verses.135:
Al-Mizan explains al-Fāḥishah as an indecent or shameful act, generally fornication. Since al-ẓulm is placed alongside it, it denotes other sins, great or small; alternatively, if indecency means major sins, injustice denotes minor ones. Seeking forgiveness must arise from remembering God, not from a habitual verbal formula, and the question, “who forgives the faults but Allah?”, urges the sinner to return and take refuge in Him.

Not knowingly persisting in sin is an essential condition of forgiveness. Persistence, whether in a major or minor sin, corrupts the soul, renders remembrance ineffective, and displays disregard for God’s command, contempt for religion’s sanctity, and arrogance before God; then neither servitude nor remembrance remains of use. “Knowingly” confirms that injustice includes minor sins, while “what they have done” includes both the indecency and the injustice, though minor sin belongs to the latter rather than to indecency.

Their reward is forgiveness and gardens beneath which rivers flow, the very things to which believers are commanded to hasten. The passage thus enjoins haste toward benevolent spending, restraint of anger, forgiveness of people, and seeking pardon for one’s faults.

verses.137:
Al-Mizan explains al-Sunan as the ways or traditions followed by societies. Believers are told to travel the earth and learn from the remains of ancient peoples: pharaohs, nimrods, kings, and emperors, whose palaces, treasures, thrones, and armies ultimately did not benefit them. Their remains are lessons for those who reflect, though mere attractions for the heedless.

The Qur’an, the commentary adds, is not concerned with preserving monuments or statues merely to discover and admire former grandeur; this is idolatry in a new disguise.
verses.138: Al-Mizan explains that the verse classifies people by the degree of its effect: for some it is only a clear, faithfully conveyed statement, while for others it becomes guidance and admonition.
verses.139:
Al-Mizan explains that al-wahn here is weakness of resolve: neglect in establishing religion and lack of courage before its enemies. Grief is the distress felt at losing what one loves or regards as one’s own. The believers at Uḥud had actually fallen into both conditions because of their wounds, the martyrdom of seventy brave men, their humiliation on their own ground, and the apparent advantage gained by the polytheists. The verse therefore forbids their present infirmity and grief, rather than merely warning them against future conduct.

The promise that they will have the upper hand is unrestricted in itself but conditioned by their being believers. True belief entails piety and patience, the foundations of victory; hence the unbelievers’ comparable losses mean that they had gained no real advantage over the believers. Although addressed as believers, the masses had not adhered to faith’s requirements, especially patience and piety, or faith would have produced its proper effect.

Such an address distinguishes grades within every believing community: it strengthens true believers, admonishes and revives the weak in faith, and censures hearts diseased by hypocrisy.
verses.140:
Al-Mizan takes the wound as a metaphor for the calamity suffered by the Muslim community at Uḥud as one body: its martyrs and wounded, as well as the loss of victory. This verse, like the promise that believers shall have the upper hand, supplies the reason for forbidding weakness and grief. The earlier promise corrects the misconception that the polytheists had truly prevailed: believers possess the essential condition of victory if they are genuinely believers. This verse instead describes the condition shared by both parties and the Divine practice behind it.

“Days” means periods of predominance, rule, or power, not merely the interval from sunrise to sunset; their rotation is the succession of such fortunes among peoples. God invariably circulates them rather than confining them to one group, according to common benefits of which human beings grasp only part. The conjunction in “and that Allah may know” is joined to an omitted clause, indicating further purposes beyond human comprehension; the benefits stated across these verses include making believers manifest, taking witnesses from among them, purging believers, and eradicating unbelievers.

God’s “knowing” believers does not mean acquiring knowledge as humans do. Since things are known to Him through their existence, His willing to know them means willing to bring about what manifests them. As believers already exist, the point is to expose their hidden belief through events governed by cause and effect.

Al-shuhadāʾ means witnesses of deeds, not battlefield martyrs; the Qur’an does not use the word in the latter sense, which is later usage. The verb “take” also suits the appointment of witnesses, rather than those killed in God’s way. By saying witnesses “from among you,” the verse indicates that only a few of the ummah will truly bear witness for it, although witnessing may be metaphorically ascribed to the whole community. The ending, “and Allah loves not the unjust,” may support this interpretation.
verses.141:
Al-Mizan explains al-tamḥīṣ as cleansing something of extraneous pollution, and al-maḥq as gradual depletion and effacement. The rotation of fortunes has this purgative purpose, distinct from merely distinguishing believers from unbelievers. Through it God gradually removes disbelief, hypocrisy, and immorality from a believer until faith is pure; correspondingly, He gradually removes the elements of disbelief, polytheism, and deceit from the unbeliever until they are destroyed.

This is one reason power is not permanently confined to one party. All affairs belong exclusively to God, who does what is most suitable and beneficial for His creatures; He has also denied the Prophet authority over this affair. The circulation of days thus tests and separates people, purifies believers, and progressively obliterates unbelievers.

The commentary holds that most believers had mistakenly thought adherence to the true religion alone guaranteed victory wherever they fought, regardless of their condition. Their unexpected angelic-assisted victory at Badr reinforced this idea. Yet this misunderstanding would abolish trial and purification, and thereby the rationale of command and prohibition, reward and punishment, undermining religion itself. Divine religion accords with nature and does not suspend the established causes through which victory and defeat occur. The verses consequently begin to admonish them and set out the real position.
verses.142:
Al-Mizan explains that the expectation of entering the Garden without trial followed from the believers’ mistaken belief that, because they were upon truth, they must always prevail and could never be defeated. Were this so, mere entry into the believing community would secure worldly victory and booty as well as forgiveness and the Garden, without distinguishing the outward appearance of faith from its reality, higher ranks from lower ones, the fighter from the patiently steadfast fighter, or one who fulfils a good intention from one who retreats when its moment arrives. The question about entering the Garden therefore puts the effect in place of its cause: they imagined themselves exempt from the trial that separates worthy from unworthy and distinguishes ranks of believers.

Their earlier desire for death is then turned into a reproach. When death appeared at the battlefield, they saw it but did not advance to meet what they had professed to desire; instead, they showed cowardice and fled. The verse contains an implied clause: they saw death, yet did not go forward to attain it. Alternatively, “looking” itself metaphorically conveys merely observing death without grappling with it. Either reading censures the claim that verbal desire can secure the Garden without testing and purification.

Al-Mizan then sets out the reality of test. The Qur’an assigns all guidance exclusively to God, including a universal creative guidance by which every thing, rational or otherwise, is led from its creation toward the perfection and goal proper to it. This is distinct both from the special guidance opposed to misguidance, which may be withheld from the unjust and transgressors, and from the voluntary guidance that simply shows the way to believers and unbelievers alike. Universal guidance is inseparable from the divine measure that prepares causes and directs each thing toward its created end; it includes societies as well as individuals. God has made such guidance incumbent on Himself: Surely on Us is the guidance, and most surely Ours is the hereafter and the former [92:12–13].

Human perfection requires voluntary acts arising from belief and practical awareness. Therefore God has provided orders and prohibitions, the shariah, as well as collective and individual events. In their interaction, these bring human capacities into actuality and disclose whether a person becomes happy or unhappy; in this respect they are tests. One who persists in ignoring the divine call has the word of punishment established against him. The same commands and events that actualize his potential increase his misery, even if he considers his condition a success. His apparent happiness is a Divine plan that draws him deeper into error, so that the very thing he took for felicity becomes his failure. When such temptation and the events leading to sin are ascribed to Satan, they are called his misguidance, call, whispering, misleading inspiration, embellishment, tools, and traps.

For the believer whose faith is firmly rooted, obedience and the events that lead to it are divine help, guardianship, and special guidance; when attributed to angels, they are angelic help and strengthening. Universal guidance begins at creation and continues until the end of a thing’s return to God. Divine measures continuously impel things from behind through successive states, while their decisive, unalterable appointed terms draw them from before. Thus everything is encompassed by a pushing force, an attracting force, and a force accompanying and bringing it up, besides such protecting and attending forces as angels and satans.

A human test may seek knowledge that the examiner lacks, or may disclose to others an ability already known. The Divine test belongs to the latter kind, for God does not lack knowledge of the unseen. By obliging rational beings to follow the shariah and placing them amid events, God trains them toward good result and felicity and makes their true reality manifest to all, so that their proper destination—reward or chastisement—is evident. Legislation, ease and hardship, possessions, relations, life, death, and every circumstance connected with a person are consequently Divine tests. They encompass every person, believer or unbeliever, good or evil, prophet or otherwise; none is exempt.

Test is therefore an established and unabolishable Divine system, founded on universal creative guidance, divine measure, and the appointed term. To abolish it would undermine creation, which is created with truth rather than in vain and moves to real destinations through true measures, terms, and guidance. Responsible beings must consequently encounter events that actualize their latent perfection or defect, happiness or misery.

This also clarifies purge and eradication. Trial separates a believer’s hidden virtues from vices and, in collective hardship, believers from hypocrites with diseased hearts; this is purification and distinction. Repeated testing of an unbeliever or hypocrite gradually exposes concealed evil; as each vice appears, it effaces an apparent virtue. This is the gradual eradication of shallow virtues described in 3:140–141. Unbelievers also face eradication in the world’s movement toward the good of humanity, when religion will be purely for God and the earth inherited by His righteous servants.

verses.144:
Al-Mizan distinguishes death, the end of bodily life, from killing, death caused externally. Used separately, “death” can include killing; used together with it, it means natural death. “Turning back upon one’s heels” means returning, and in this verse it means apostasy—returning to prior disbelief—not simply flight from battle. Flight has no necessary connection to the Prophet’s death or killing, whereas apostasy does; moreover, the Qur’an speaks less severely of retreat at other battles, including Ḥunayn.

The verse censures those whose faith depended on Muḥammad’s continued life. He is a messenger like those before him, charged only to convey his Lord’s message; all affairs and the religion belong to God, who preserves it. Thus his death or killing cannot justify abandoning guidance for former disbelief. The context strongly indicates that, amid the fierce fighting at Uḥud, Muslims believed the Prophet had been killed and fled. As a report, Ibn Hishām’s al-Sīrah relates that Anas b. al-Naḍr found ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, Ṭalḥah b. ʿUbaydillāh, and others who had given themselves up because they thought the Messenger had been killed; he urged them to die for what the Messenger had died for, then fought until he was martyred.

This retreat showed that some sought worldly reward through belief and expected it to last only with the Prophet’s life. “And Allah will reward the grateful” is an exception: a few neither turned back nor retreated. Gratitude is displaying a bounty by remembering its giver in heart and speech and using it as the giver intends. Since everything is God’s bounty, absolute gratitude means never remembering anything without remembering God and never using anything except in His obedience. It requires complete sincerity to God and purity in knowledge and action.

The word “the grateful” is an adjective, indicating a permanent, inseparable quality rather than a passing act. Such people are purified, sincere servants beyond Satan’s hope and designs: Satan seeks to make people forget their Lord and disobey Him, but has no hold over the purified and grateful. This understanding is supported by the later verse about those who turned back at Uḥud, where Satan caused them to slip because of some deeds they had done, rather than by the reported cry that Muḥammad had been killed; Al-Mizan rejects the latter explanation as a trivializing reading.

The grateful at Uḥud remained steadfast without weakness, loss of courage, or abandonment of God’s cause, and this gratitude was their settled characteristic. The Qur’an praises “the grateful” only in this verse and the following one, yet leaves their reward unspecified, which indicates its greatness and value.
verses.145:
Al-Mizan reads the verse as an adverse allusion to believers who said that their slain brethren would not have died or been killed had they remained with them, and to those who said, “Had we any hand in the affair, we would not have been slain here” [3:154]. These were believers, not the hypocrites who had already left the Messenger and did not fight. Their words implied that death did not depend on God’s permission and fixed decree; this would negate God’s Kingdom and the precision of His ordering.

Those who spoke this way had accepted Islam seeking worldly benefit, imagining affairs to lie in the hands of the Messenger and believers. Those who avoided such thoughts sought the hereafter. God says of each seeker that He will give him “of it,” rather than simply give him the desired reward: a person may not supply all the causes required for everything he desires, and so receives only what those causes yield. This accords with: Whoever desires this present life, We hasten to him therein what We please for whomsoever We desire, then We assign to him the hell; he shall enter it despised, driven away. And whoever desires the hereafter and strives for it as he ought to strive and he is a believer; (as for) these their striving shall surely be thanked [17:18–19].

“The grateful” are specially excepted from both seekers of worldly and otherworldly reward, because they act solely for God’s sake, looking neither to this world nor to the hereafter.
verses.146:
Al-Mizan explains that “how many” indicates a great number. Al-ribbiyyūn may mean Godly persons exclusively attached to God, like al-rabbānī, though it is also said to be the plural of rabā, “thousand”; al-istikānah means submission or abasement.

The verses offer counsel, admonition, and encouragement through the example of the Godly men who fought alongside many prophets. Despite what befell them in God’s way, they neither lost heart, weakened, nor abased themselves. Their response was to ask their Lord to forgive their faults and excess in their affair, make their feet firm, and help them against the unbelieving people. Believers are to make their conduct and prayer a model, so as not to repeat the blameworthy words and deeds of Uḥud.

If they follow this example, God will combine for them the reward of this world and the excellent reward of the hereafter, as He did for those men, and love them for their good-doing. Calling the otherworldly reward “excellent” marks its sublimity and high rank over worldly reward.

verses.151: Al-Mizan describes this as a promise that God will aid the believers by casting terror into the unbelievers’ hearts. The Messenger of God reportedly counted this “scare” among the special bounties reserved for him, and traditions to that effect are transmitted by both sects. The unbelievers deserve this terror because their alleged partners of God have no divine authority or proof. Polytheism includes even denying the Creator by attributing creation and its management to entities such as time or matter.
verses.152:
Al-Mizan explains that Allah fulfilled His conditional promise of help at Uḥud: while the believers remained vigilant and patient, He gave them their initial victory and enabled them to slay the enemy. Traditions and history report that most archers then abandoned the mountain-pass to join in gathering booty. Khālid b. Walīd’s group killed ʿAbdullāh b. Jubayr and the few archers who remained, attacked the Muslims from behind, and, joined by the returning polytheists, inflicted defeat and killed seventy companions.

The archers’ conduct is apparently meant by their becoming weak-willed, disputing, and disobeying after being shown what they loved. Here al-fashal means lack of resolve, not cowardice: they left through avarice for war-booty, not fear. Their dispute also proves that some remained determined to obey, which explains the division between those desiring this world and those desiring the hereafter. If al-fashal were instead taken as cowardice, it would apply to the whole army, and “then He turned you away” would mark an ordinal rather than temporal sequence.

God stopped them from engaging the idol-worshippers after their disunity, weakness, and disobedience in order to test their faith and patience. Such a test distinguishes believers from hypocrites and steadfast conviction from fickleness. Yet He pardoned them by His grace.
verses.153:
Al-Mizan notes that al-Iṣʿād normally means going far over the ground, unlike al-ṣuʿūd, ascending, although it is sometimes used in that latter sense. The verse’s “when” may be connected to an implied “remember,” to “He turned you away” in the preceding verse, or to “He might try you.” The Messenger called from the fugitives’ rear, showing that they had fled from around him en masse and would not turn toward him, leaving him almost alone among the enemies. A few, however, did not retreat; the wording also shows that the rumour of the Prophet’s martyrdom spread only after the others had fled.

The commentary gives two related readings in which God’s giving “another sorrow” follows His pardon and is a grace that diverts them from blameworthy grief. On the first, He exchanged their grief over lost victory and what befell them for remorse and distress over the victory lost through their own weak resolve; bi-ghammin indicates exchange. Alternatively, athābakum may convey change: He exchanged their remorse and distress for a grief that entitled them to reward, reversing the roles of the two sorrows. Under either reading, “what had escaped you” means victory and booty, and “what befell you” their slaughter and injuries; the following security in slumber is closely connected.

A third, contextually supported reading connects the clause directly to their flight: their retreat was the “another sorrow,” caused by the polytheists’ rear attack, itself resulting from their disputation and disobedience. The explanation is then given so that they will not grieve over what escaped them or befell them. Al-Mizan judges the many other proposed grammatical explanations untenable.
verses.154:
Al-Mizan explains that the security of slumber came only upon a party of the believers: those who had fled, then returned to the Messenger, repented, and felt remorse. Divine pardon and gracious security could not cover them while they persisted in fleeing the jihād; their return and repentance therefore preceded this grace. They gathered around the Prophet, probably after he reached the mountain-pass, returning gradually once it became known that he had not been slain.

The other party also consisted of believers, distinguished from the hypocrites discussed later, but they received none of the first group’s honour. Caring only for themselves means that they were preoccupied with saving their lives and obtaining worldly benefit. They embraced Islam on the assumption that it could never be overcome and that God was bound to grant its followers unconditional victory; when circumstances turned against them, they were ready to turn back into disbelief.

Their question, “Do we have any hand in the affair?” thus expressed doubt about religion after defeat. Their unjust, ignorant thought was that victory belonged to them as followers of the true religion. This resembles the polytheists’ division of divine dominion among subordinate lords: one who supposes that religion, its Prophet, or its followers cannot be defeated, or that the Prophet cannot die or be killed, assigns to the Prophet a share in authority over victory and booty. In truth, all authority belongs to God alone; even the Prophet has no independent concern in the affair. Other things are links in the divinely established chain of cause and effect and are governed by the law of testing and trial.

God’s special providence ensures that religion will ultimately prevail and the earth be prepared for His friends, but this does not suspend the universal order for prophethood or divine mission. Believers prevail when the relevant causes are present; where hypocrisy, disobedience, weakness, or nervousness creates a weak link, opponents may prevail, as they did over some prophets. Only when the truth cannot be established without interrupting the normal causal order does God strengthen religion extraordinarily, so that its evidence is not destroyed.

Their concealed claim, “Had we any hand in the affair, we would not have been slain here,” more openly preferred disbelief, treating the deaths as proof that the religion was false. The reply establishes, first, that those ordained to be slain would have gone to their places of death even had the others remained at home; no one can evade or alter the appointed time of death. Second, testing and purging necessarily encompass all, so that martyrs attain their ranks and others are assigned their due places after the beliefs and polytheism concealed in hearts are exposed.

Al-Mizan rejects identifying this second party simply with the hypocrites who withdrew with ʿAbdullāh b. Ubayy before battle, unless “hypocrites” is used loosely for people whose diseased, weak faith had effectively become unbelief. It also rejects the view that they were sound believers merely confessing that authority belonged to God, because that would make the divine replies irrelevant.

Regarding those who turned back when the armies met, Al-Mizan says Satan sought to make them slip because of prior evil traits and deeds: one evil leads to another through desires that seek what resembles them. The preposition bi means “on account of,” not instrument; their previous deeds cannot be identical with the later retreat. The verse therefore does not concern a Satanic cry that the Prophet had been killed, despite reports of such a cry.

The pardon in (3:155) covers all who fled, including both parties, but does not equal the earlier pardon. The first group’s pardon is accompanied by grace, their designation as believers, the change of sorrow, and security in slumber. The later pardon merely states that Allah is Forgiving, Forbearing, indicating that punishment is not hastened but that the sinner is not thereby honoured or necessarily approved. Pardon may thus differ in implication despite bearing the same name.

Al-Mizan further explains that al-ʿafw removes sins, while al-maghfirah, literally covering, follows by concealing what has been removed. Though distinct in analysis, they ordinarily serve the same practical function and may be attributed to humans as well as God. They apply to created as well as legislative affairs, and to this world as well as the next: they remove obstacles and antagonistic factors that impede happiness and nearness to God. Belief and the hereafter are life, while their effects are light; polytheism is death and sins are darkness. An unbeliever has neither life nor light; a forgiven believer has both, whereas a sinful believer remains alive but with diminished light until forgiveness perfects it. Accordingly, when attributed to God, pardon and forgiveness remove impediments in created affairs, obstacles to success in the hereafter in legislative matters, and whatever obstructs happiness in the sphere of felicity and infelicity.

verses.156:
Al-Mizan holds that “those who disbelieve” means unbelievers, not hypocrites as such. Although hypocrites uttered this claim, the claim itself—that those travelling or fighting would not have died or been slain had they remained with their people—arises from disbelief. al-Ḍarb fi al-arḍ means travelling, and al-Ghuzzā is the plural of al-ghāzī, a fighter.

God’s making this thought an intense regret in their hearts means that He punishes them through that regret, expressing the means in place of its end. Their error is ignorance of the fact that life and death belong exclusively to God: “death” here includes both natural death and slaying, and nearness to or distance from one’s people neither gives life nor causes death. God’s seeing what they do explains the prohibition against resembling the unbelievers.

Death is mentioned before slaying because the preceding clause first speaks of travel and then fighting, and because natural death is normal whereas slaying is exceptional. Thus believers must not attribute the death of one away from home, or the killing of one engaged in jihād, to his having left them. Such speech produces the mental agony that is itself divine punishment; believers should fear God, who sees their deeds.
verses.157: Al-Mizan explains that “what they amass” denotes property, wealth, and their worldly accompaniments. Martyrdom is mentioned before ordinary death because being slain in God’s way is closer to divine forgiveness than other deaths; when the following verse speaks simply of being gathered to God, it returns to the normal order of death before slaying, since that special point no longer applies.
verses.158: Al-Mizan explains that “what they amass” denotes property, wealth, and their worldly accompaniments. verses.159:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Faẓz denotes unkindness, ill-nature, and intolerance, while al-infiḍāḍ means dispersal. Though the verse directly addresses the Messenger, its import is that, through God’s mercy, he is lenient with the believers, pardons them, seeks forgiveness for them, consults them in affairs, and, after deciding, trusts in God.

The shift away from addressing the believers is part of the passage’s censure and admonition. Their grief for those slain could lead them to blame the Prophet for bringing them into the danger in which they were killed; therefore God turns from them and addresses him. The context apparently implies that, when they have fallen into a condition resembling that of unbelievers and are intensely grieving, his leniency is solely a mercy from God; otherwise they would have dispersed. And God knows better.

The commands to pardon, seek forgiveness, and consult endorse the Prophet’s established practice, including his consultation before Uḥud, and show that he acts as God commands and with God’s approval. Pardon means not imposing on them the consequences of their disobedience, and seeking forgiveness means asking God to forgive them. These otherwise general commands do not include the shariah’s penal code, for that would abolish the Shariah; their connection with consultation also shows that they concern government and public affairs.

Once a decision is made, trust in God is required. God’s love for those who trust means that He is their Guardian and Helper and will not forsake them. Since no one can overcome those whom God assists, and none can help those whom He forsakes, believers must rely on Him; their faith itself requires this, because no helper or supporter exists apart from Him.

verses.161:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Ghill means defrauding or faithlessness. The statement that such conduct is not attributable to a prophet declares the Prophet’s purity and blamelessness: he is far removed from defrauding either God or people, for defrauding people is also a form of defrauding God. Whoever defrauds will meet his Lord carrying what he defrauded and will be repaid in full for what he earned, without injustice.

Accordingly, accusing the Prophet of defrauding is unjust and untenable. He follows God’s pleasure and never exceeds it, whereas the defrauder incurs God’s severe wrath and has hell as his abode. Those who pursue God’s pleasure and those who bring His wrath upon themselves occupy diverse grades with Him. Since God sees every particle of good and evil they do, people must not be careless about seeking His pleasure and avoiding His wrath.

verses.164: Al-Mizan explains that the verse describes God’s favor upon the believers because of their belief. It calls them “the believers,” rather than “those who believe,” because the adjective expresses an inseparable relationship and more perfectly indicates that their belief is the cause of this favor: God raised among them a Messenger from themselves to recite His signs, purify them, and teach them the Book and wisdom after their manifest error.
verses.165:
Al-Mizan first explains the misfortune according to immediate causality: the believers brought it upon themselves through the archers’ abandonment of their position, the flight from the battlefield, disobedience to the Messenger and Commander, loss of courage, and mutual dispute. They thus destroyed the means of victory. The verse also consoles them by comparing Uḥud, where seventy believers were martyred, with Badr, where seventy unbelievers were killed and seventy captured; their loss was only half of what they had inflicted.

Yet the commentary regards another explanation as supported, indeed proved, by “surely Allah has power over all things.” “It is from your own selves” refers to their own acceptance of ransom for Badr’s captives, despite being told that this would mean a like number of their side being killed the following year; they accepted the condition, expecting any slain among them to be martyrs. The final clause does not properly connect with the explanation based solely on their disobedience at Uḥud.
verses.166:
Al-Mizan holds that the misfortune at Uḥud was “with Allah’s permission” because “It is from your own selves” refers to the believers’ choice to accept ransom for Badr’s prisoners along with its condition. This cannot refer merely to their disobedience at Uḥud, for it would make no sense to describe that disobedience as being by God’s permission. The statement thus explains the preceding verse, leads to God’s distinguishing the believers, exposes and refutes the hypocrites’ words, and prepares for the account of martyrdom.

“Or (at least) defend yourselves” urges those addressed to fight even if they will not fight in Allah’s way: they should at least protect their families and themselves. Their being nearer “to unbelief” than to belief concerns their proximity to open unbelief; they had certainly already fallen into hypocrisy. “They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts” emphatically contrasts their spoken claim with what they conceal in their hearts.
