verses.168: Al-Mizan explains that “brethren” means the martyrs who had family ties with those who held back. Joining this word to their holding back shames them for abandoning their own brothers while the enemy killed them. “Then ward off death from yourselves” refutes their claim that obedience to them would have prevented death; al-Darʾ means to ward off or avert.
verses.169: Al-Mizan notes that the address turns from the Muslims to the Prophet, possibly continuing the preceding command, “Say: ‘Then ward off death.’” Here death means the nullity of consciousness and action. The martyrs’ life is therefore shown by their receiving sustenance, which is action, and rejoicing in God’s grace, which demonstrates feeling and consciousness.
verses.170:
Al-Mizan explains that the martyrs rejoice in the grace they continually receive from God and in good tidings about the righteous believers whom they left alive in the world: those believers will have neither fear nor grief. Thus those killed in God’s way continue to receive news of good believers still in this world.

The glad tidings concern the recompense of believers’ deeds, which the martyrs behold in their present abode. Their knowledge comes through observation rather than argument. The verse consequently proves that human existence continues after death until the Day of Resurrection, in the life of al-Barzakh.
verses.171:
Al-Mizan explains that this rejoicing includes joy for others as well as for the martyrs themselves, since “Allah will not waste the reward of the believers” is unrestricted and embraces all believers. Perhaps this explains the repetition of rejoicing and grace. “Favor,” “grace,” and sustenance are left indefinite, as are fear and grief when negated, conveying comprehensiveness.

The verses describe the believers’ reward: sustenance near God, which is His favor and grace, manifested in their having neither fear nor grief. Fear is expectation of something that may destroy an existing happiness, whereas grief follows when the loss has occurred. Complete removal of fear requires that no enjoyed bounty can deteriorate or perish; complete removal of grief requires that one has never lacked or lost such bounty. It therefore means receiving every possible bounty permanently: everlasting life in everlasting happiness.

This absence of fear and grief is identical with sustenance from God, for what is with Him is enduring and free from affliction, as indicated by and that which is with Allah is best for the righteous [3:198] and and what is with Allah is enduring [16:96]. It is likewise identical with the affirmation of favor and grace. Since “favor” in the Qur’an means divine guardianship, God is their Guardian, managing their affairs and granting them exclusive grace.

The commentary rejects the view that grace is a bounty beyond one’s desert while favor corresponds to one’s deeds. The word “reward” shows that believers are eligible for both favor and grace; sustenance from their Lord, rejoicing in what Allah has given, favor and grace, and God’s not wasting believers’ reward all express one reality.
verses.172:
Al-Mizan connects verses (3:172)–175 with Uḥud, especially through the phrase concerning those wounded after the battle. al-Istijābah and al-ijābah reportedly both mean receiving a positive response to a request.

The mention of both Allah and the Messenger in (3:172) is apparently deliberate. At Uḥud, the Muslims had disobeyed Allah by fleeing although commanded to fight and forbidden to flee; they had also disobeyed the Prophet when the archers left their assigned post and when others failed to answer his call from behind them. Their later response is therefore described as a response to both Allah and the Messenger, in contrast to that earlier disobedience.

The promise of a great reward is not for every person who outwardly responded, but for those among them who did good and guarded against evil. An external response need not arise from genuine goodness and piety, whereas these inward qualities are what make one deserving of the great reward. Thus, not all who went out were sincere in this matter. The view that min in minhum is merely explanatory, rather than indicating a part of the responders, does not fit the context. Likewise, the later praise of those addressed as a group in fact concerns a selected band within it.

In (3:173-174), the first al-nās refers to those who had abandoned the believers at Uḥud and then sought to deter them, while the second refers to the polytheist enemy gathering to attack again. The former were agents within the Muslim camp working against the believers, and the wording indicates that they were a group, not a single individual. This supports the report that the verses concern the Prophet's post-Uḥud pursuit of the polytheists rather than Lesser Badr, although reports concerning both events are transmitted. The enemy had assembled for a renewed attack, God knows best.

Warnings from those not trusted can strengthen a person's resolve, particularly when he believes himself bound by duty and convinced that he is right. Accordingly, attempts to blame the believers for divine commands or to obstruct them increased their faith, courage, and determination. Their faith may also have been increased by seeing fulfilled the prior revelation that they would suffer hardship in God's cause before their affairs were settled by His permission; His promised help, in this case, presupposed fighting and war.

Their saying that Allah was sufficient for them and the best Protector expresses complete reliance on God. Ḥasbunā denotes sufficiency measured against need, and al-Wakīl is one who manages another's affairs. Their trust did not rest on external causes, even though God has established such causes in the world; it accords with the meaning of 65:3, that whoever trusts in Allah finds Him sufficient and that Allah attains His purpose. Since they followed God's pleasure, they returned with His favor and grace unharmed, and He praised them as following His pleasure and as recipients of His mighty grace.

Al-Mizan explains that success in the material world requires material and psychological causes. Once the material means are supplied, failure may arise from psychological defects such as weak will, fear, grief, recklessness, greed, foolishness, or distrust. Reliance on God joins a person to the unconquerable cause above all causes, strengthening the will so that such adverse states cannot overcome it and thus leading to success and triumph. Trust also has an aspect connected with supernatural, miraculous phenomena, as indicated by 65:3.

In (3:175), dhālikum apparently refers to those who brought the alarming news. The Qur'an here calls human beings Satan, as it also speaks of whisperers among jinn and men in [114:4–6]. The command not to fear them confirms that these speakers themselves are the Satans who sought to frighten the believers.

Al-Mizan cautions that the innumerable reports on Uḥud are highly contradictory, especially reports assigning occasions of revelation to its nearly sixty verses. Sectarian inclinations may have made such reports serve partisan interests, and the reader should consult the larger collections critically. Abu al-Ḍuḥā, as reported by Ibn Abī Ḥāim in al-Durr al-manthūr, says that seventy men were martyred and takes al-shuhadāʾ in 3:140 to mean martyrs; although most exegetes followed this meaning, Al-Mizan holds that the Book provides no apparent proof for it and that the word means witnesses of deeds.

A report from al-Ṣādiq in al-Tafsīr, al-ʿAyyāshī, distinguishes God's knowledge before creation from factual knowledge identical with the action itself: 3:142 does not deny His pre-creative knowledge of those who would strive. Al-Ṣādiq is also reported in al-Tafsīr, al-Qummī to explain that believers, having heard of the honor granted to Badr's martyrs, desired a battle in which they might be martyred; God showed them Uḥud, but only those He willed remained firm. Similar meanings are reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Ḥasan, and al-Suddī.

An Imām is reported to say that, when the wounded Prophet was thought killed at Uḥud, people urged safety; upon their return to Medina, 3:144 was revealed, asking whether they would turn back upon their heels if Muḥammad died or was killed. Al-Rabīʿ, reported by Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim, similarly relates that some doubted the Prophet's prophethood after the rumor, whereas leading Companions and a wounded Helper insisted that they should fight for their religion even if he had been killed. Al-Suddī reports that some fugitives sought protection through ʿAbdullāh b. Ubayy and proposed returning to polytheism, while Anas b. al-Naḍr declared that the Lord of Muḥammad had not been killed, fought, and was martyred. This theme is reported through many chains.

Al-Bāqir is reported in al-Kāfī to say that ʿAlī suffered sixty wounds at Uḥud. When the Prophet touched them, they healed; ʿAlī praised God that he had neither fled nor turned back, and the Prophet affirmed his bravery and freedom from blame. Al-Mizan explains that the Qur'anic gratitude for him concerns his steadfastness, not merely his spoken praise. Al-Ṣādiq's recitation of a verse as speaking of myriads of godly men is explained as thousands upon thousands, who were martyred; this recitation and meaning are also reported from Ibn Masʿūd and others, while Ibn ʿAbbās reportedly glossed the word as gatherings.

Mujāhid, reported in al-Durr al-manthūr, says that God first gave the believers victory over the polytheists, but then allowed the latter to prevail because the Muslims disobeyed the Prophet. Al-Zubayr reports that God sent a slumber when fear overwhelmed the believers and that Muʿtab b. Qushayr's complaint, that they would not have been slain had they possessed any share in the affair, occasioned the relevant wording about slumber; this is transmitted through numerous chains.

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to name ʿUthmān, Rāfiʿ b. al-Muʿallā, and Ḥārithah b. Zayd in connection with those who turned back when the armies met, with related reports naming others. Al-Mizan holds that these are examples only: the verse covers all Companions who fled and disobeyed the Messenger. It reports that ʿUthmān and those with him reached al-Jalʿab, remained there three days, and then returned, whereupon the Prophet rebuked them for going very far.

Numerous reports state that nearly all the Companions fled and that only two Emigrants and seven Helpers remained with the Prophet, the Helpers being killed defending him. Reports giving eleven, eighteen, or thirty survivors are judged weakest, perhaps because narrators received differing information. The reports of Nasībah al-Māziniyyah's defense of the Prophet indicate that, at a certain point, no one was with him, while those who had not fled were occupied fighting. The traditions unanimously say that ʿAlī did not flee; Abū Dujānah al-Anṣārī, Simāk b. Kharashah, probably also belongs among the steadfast, for he shielded the Prophet with his body and shield until seriously wounded. Other Companions returned after recognizing that the Prophet had not been killed, and it was upon these returnees that God sent slumber. God nevertheless pardoned them; some exegetes interpret that pardon as His turning the polytheists away so that they did not destroy the Muslims completely.

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported through Ibn ʿAdiyy and al-Bayhaqī to transmit that the Prophet said God and His Messenger had no need of consultation, but God made it a mercy for the ummah: one who consults is not deprived of guidance, while one who abandons it does not avoid error. Anas reports through al-Ṭabarānī that one who seeks God's good does not go wrong and one who consults does not regret. Nahj al-balāghah says that self-reliance in opinion brings destruction, while seeking advice shares in others' wisdom, and that consultation itself is guidance whereas independent opinion incurs danger. A report in al-Tafsīr al-Ṣāfī calls consultation the strongest support and pride the most desolate solitude. Al-Mizan limits consultation to matters in which one may choose according to what appears preferable; definite divine laws are not subject to consultation, for no one may alter them as though events and new fashions could abrogate God's words.

Al-Ṣādiq reports in al-Majālis that people accused the Prophet at Badr of taking a red velvet from the booty, until God disclosed its location and cleared His Prophet of fraud, revealing that a prophet cannot defraud. Al-Qummī's version says that a man identified the person who had buried it and that it was found on the Prophet's order. Similar reports occur through many chains; if they call this the occasion of revelation, they perhaps mean that the verse points to the event, since its context indicates revelation after Uḥud. Al-Bāqir's report that a defrauder will see the thing defrauded in the Fire and be ordered to enter and retrieve it is a fine inference from the verse that the defrauder shall bring what he defrauded.

Al-Ṣādiq reports concerning diverse grades with God that those following God's pleasure are the Imāms, who are grades for believers; through love and devotion to the Ahl al-bayt, God increases believers' deeds and raises their grades. Those under divine wrath are those who reject the right of ʿAlī and the Imāms of the Ahl al-bayt. Al-Mizan calls this an application by the Qur'an's flow to its most prominent instance. Al-Riḍā reportedly says that a grade is the distance between heaven and earth. Al-Ṣādiq explains the misfortune after inflicting twice as much by saying that at Badr Muslims killed seventy and captured seventy, whereas at Uḥud they suffered seventy deaths.

ʿAlī is reported through several authorities to say that Gabriel offered the Muslims a choice after Badr: execute the captives or accept ransom on condition that an equal number of Muslims would later be killed. They chose ransom, accepting the prospect of equal martyrdom, and seventy were martyred at Uḥud, equal to Badr's captives. Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Qummī also transmit this from ʿAlī.

Al-Bāqir reportedly says that the verse, And reckon not those who are killed in God’s way as dead, was revealed concerning Badr's and Uḥud's martyrs together. Al-Mizan maintains that the verses are general, embracing everyone truly martyred in God's way or counted a martyr. Another claim assigns them to the victims of Biʾr Maʿūnah, where the Prophet's envoys to ʿĀmir b. al-Ṭufayl's people, after Abū Milḥān al-Anṣārī was killed, were attacked and slain.

Al-Ṣādiq applies the verse, by the Qur'an's flow, to the Shīʿahs: upon entering the Garden and receiving God's honor, they attain the certainty that they were upon truth and God's religion, and rejoice for believing brethren left behind. This does not mean they formerly doubted; they perceive by the eye of certainty what they had known in this world by knowledge of certainty.

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported through numerous authorities to transmit a Prophetic account in which Uḥud's martyrs' souls are placed in green birds that eat from the Garden's fruits and lodge in golden candelabra under the Throne. Delighted with their sustenance and resting place, they wished their brethren knew their condition so that they would not abandon jihād or shrink from fighting, and God promised to convey it through the verses concerning those slain in His way. Parallel reports vary between souls being in, like, or in the forms of green birds. Yet reports reaching the Imāms of the Ahl al-bayt deny that this was said by the Prophet, or interpret it otherwise; in light of established principles, Al-Mizan says it must be interpreted away or rejected. In any case, the reports concern the Garden of al-Barzakh, not the Garden of the hereafter. Mujāhid's report says the martyrs receive fruit and scent from the Garden but are not in it, and al-Suddī's account has them feed in the Garden by day and lodge in candelabra by night. Such descriptions may fit the Garden of this world, but not the hereafter.

Regarding (3:172)–174, ʿAbdullāh b. Abī Bakr b. Muḥammad b. ʿAmr b. Ḥazm reports that the Prophet pursued the retreating force to Ḥamrāʾ al-Asad after Abū Sufyān had resolved to return and annihilate the remaining Muslims. When news that the Prophet had come out deterred Abū Sufyān, he instructed passing ʿAbdu al-Qays riders to tell the Prophet that Quraysh would reattack. The Prophet and believers replied that God was sufficient and the best Protector, and the verses were revealed. Al-Qummī reports that only men wounded at Uḥud went with the Prophet; other reports say only those who had been with him at Uḥud, which has practically the same import.

Ibn Shahāb reports through Mūsá b. ʿAqabah and al-Bayhaqī that, at a later appointed meeting at Badr, Satan's human friends frightened the Muslims with news of a vast enemy army. The Muslims nevertheless went out with trade goods, intending either to meet Abū Sufyān or trade at Badr's fair. Abū Sufyān did not come and, after learning that the Muslims awaited him, returned to Mecca; the Prophet returned to Medina with God's favor and grace. The report calls it the expedition of the army of al-sawīq. Al-Ṭabrisī, reporting from al-Bāqir, likewise identifies the verses with Lesser Badr and says Abū Sufyān's force was mockingly called the army of al-sawīq because it had taken sawīq provisions and turned back through fear.

A report from Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿIkrimah says the polytheists regretted leaving Uḥud without killing Muḥammad or taking captives and proposed returning. The Prophet gathered the Muslims and reached Ḥamrāʾ al-Asad, or perhaps the Well of Abū ʿUtbah. The polytheists deferred their return for a year, and an appointed meeting at Badr followed: cowards returned, while the brave took weapons and trade goods, found no enemy, traded, and returned with God's favor and grace.

Al-Mizan includes these comprehensive reports to show that many alleged occasions of revelation rest on personal judgment: historians match verses to events and then call those events their causes of revelation. This often fragments a coherent verse or passage into separate causes, even where that damages its structure or contradicts its context. Sectarian partisanship, political conditions, and ruling powers have also obscured or concealed realities; a serious scholar must keep these influences in view. Finally, Al-Mizan records, from Ibn Hishām's al-Sīrah, the names of the seventy Muslims martyred at Uḥud, including four Emigrants and the remaining Helpers and allies.
verses.173:
Al-Mizan explains that the two occurrences of al-nās in 3:173 refer to different groups. The latter, rendered men, is the enemy gathering an army to attack the believers again; the former, rendered people, denotes those who had abandoned the believers at Uḥud and now tried to restrain them from fighting. They were agents within the Muslim camp working insidiously for the polytheists, and the verse plainly indicates a group rather than one person. This supports the report that the verses concern the Prophet's pursuit of the polytheists after Uḥud, rather than Lesser Badr, although both accounts occur in the transmitted reports.

The warning meant that the enemy had assembled for a renewed attack, God knows best. Yet instead of producing fear, it increased the believers' faith. When someone not trusted attempts to prevent a person from an intended action, the resistance itself can intensify resolve; this is stronger still where the person believes he is right and obligated by duty. Thus, reproach or obstruction directed at believers concerning divine commands strengthens their belief, courage, and determination.

Their faith may also have increased because events confirmed prior revelation that they would undergo suffering, injury, and loss in God's cause before their affairs were settled by His permission. Since God had promised help, and the help in question naturally entailed war and fighting, the threatened danger was itself consistent with what they had been told.

Their statement that Allah was sufficient for them and the best Protector expresses total dependence on God. Ḥasbunā denotes sufficiency in relation to need, while al-Wakīl means one who manages affairs on another's behalf. Through faith, they relied on God without being concerned with the external causes God has established in the world. The expression therefore accords with 65:3: and whoever trusts in Allah, He is sufficient for him; surely Allah attains His purpose. Their reliance is immediately followed by the result: they returned with Allah's favor and grace, unharmed. Because they followed His pleasure, He praised them for doing so and described Himself as the Lord of mighty grace.

Al-Mizan adds that attaining one's aims in the material world depends on material and psychological causes. Even where the necessary material means are present, psychological defects—weakness of will, fear, grief, recklessness, greed, foolishness, or distrust—may prevent success. Reliance on God connects a person with the unconquerable cause above all causes and fortifies his will against these adverse states, bringing success and triumph. Trust in God also has an aspect effectively joined to supernatural, miraculous phenomena, as 65:3 indicates.

Reliance on God connects a person with the unconquerable cause above all causes and fortifies his will against these adverse states, bringing success and triumph. Trust in God also has an aspect effectively joined to supernatural, miraculous phenomena, as 65:3 indicates.
verses.175:
Al-Mizan explains that dhālikum in (3:175) apparently refers to the people who brought the frightening news. The verse is thus one instance in which the Qur'an calls human beings Satan, as in the reference to whisperers among jinn and men in [114:4–6]. The command not to fear them confirms that the people who spoke in this way were themselves Satans seeking to frighten the believers.

Al-Mizan judges the vast body of Uḥud traditions difficult to trust wholesale because of their contradictions, particularly in reports that assign occasions of revelation to nearly sixty verses. Sectarian tendencies may have made such reports serve the interests of their transmitters. Abu al-Ḍuḥā, reported by Ibn Abī Ḥāim in al-Durr al-manthūr, says that seventy were martyred at Uḥud and understands al-shuhadāʾ in 3:140 as martyrs. Although most exegetes followed this reading, Al-Mizan says there is apparently no proof for it in the Book and that al-shuhadāʾ evidently means witnesses of deeds.

Al-Ṣādiq is reported in al-Tafsīr, al-ʿAyyāshī to distinguish God's knowledge before creation from factual knowledge, which is identical with the action. Thus, 3:142, which says God has not yet known those who strive, does not concern His pre-creative knowledge. In al-Tafsīr, al-Qummī, al-Ṣādiq reportedly explains that believers coveted the honor granted to Badr's martyrs and asked God for a battle in which they might be martyred. Uḥud gave them that encounter, but only those God willed remained firm. Similar explanations are reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Ḥasan, and al-Suddī.

An Imām reports that, when the wounded Prophet was believed killed at Uḥud, people urged others to seek safety; after they returned to Medina, 3:144 was revealed, asking whether they would turn back upon their heels if Muḥammad died or was killed. Al-Rabīʿ, reported by Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim, similarly relates that some people said the Prophet had been killed and even claimed a prophet would not have been killed, whereas leading Companions and a wounded Helper insisted that they should keep fighting for their religion. Al-Suddī reports that some fugitives sought protection from Abū Sufyān through ʿAbdullāh b. Ubayy and suggested returning to polytheism, but Anas b. al-Naḍr answered that Muḥammad's Lord had not been killed, fought, and was martyred. This theme is transmitted by numerous chains.

Al-Bāqir is reported in al-Kāfī to say that ʿAlī received sixty wounds at Uḥud. The Prophet's touch healed them, and ʿAlī praised God that he had not fled or turned back. The Prophet declared that one who endured such affliction in God's way had proved brave and was free of blame. Al-Mizan says that God's Qur'anic gratitude for ʿAlī concerned his steadfastness and firmness, not merely his words of praise. Al-Ṣādiq's reported recitation of the verse concerning a prophet with myriads of godly men explains the word as thousands upon thousands, who were martyred. This reading and meaning are also reported from Ibn Masʿūd and others, while Ibn ʿAbbās reportedly glossed it as gatherings.

Mujāhid, reported in al-Durr al-manthūr, says God initially helped the believers until the polytheists were routed, then allowed the polytheists to prevail because the Muslims disobeyed the Prophet. Al-Zubayr reports that when fear overwhelmed the believers, God sent them slumber, and that Muʿtab b. Qushayr's statement that they would not have been slain had they possessed any share in the affair was the occasion of the relevant wording. This account is transmitted through many chains.

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to associate the verse about those who turned back when the armies met with ʿUthmān, Rāfiʿ b. al-Muʿallā, and Ḥārithah b. Zayd; parallel reports add other names. Al-Mizan says the named men are examples, because the verse applies to all Companions who fled and disobeyed the Messenger. It reports that ʿUthmān and those who fled with him reached al-Jalʿab, stayed three days, and then returned to the Prophet, who reproached them for having gone very far.

Numerous traditions state that all the Companions fled except two Emigrants and seven Helpers, who died one after another defending the Prophet. Reports that eleven, eighteen, or thirty remained are judged the weakest, perhaps because of differing information available to narrators. Traditions concerning Nasībah al-Māziniyyah's defense of the Prophet show that, at one point, no one was with him, while the steadfast were engaged in fighting. The traditions unanimously say that ʿAlī did not flee; Abū Dujānah al-Anṣārī, Simāk b. Kharashah, probably also remained steadfast, shielding the Prophet with his own body and shield until gravely wounded. Some others returned once they recognized that the Prophet had not been killed, while others came later. God sent slumber upon these returnees and pardoned all of them. Some exegetes say that this pardon means God diverted the polytheists so they could not exterminate the Muslims.

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported through Ibn ʿAdiyy and al-Bayhaqī to transmit that the Prophet said God and His Messenger had no need of consultation, but that God made it a mercy for the ummah: whoever consults will not be deprived of guidance, and whoever abandons consultation will not escape error. Anas reports through al-Ṭabarānī that one who seeks God's good does not go wrong and one who consults does not regret. Nahj al-balāghah says that independent opinion destroys a person, whereas seeking advice shares in others' wisdom, and that consultation itself is guidance while self-reliance in opinion is dangerous. A Prophetic report in al-Tafsīr al-Ṣāfī calls consultation the strongest support and pride the most desolate solitude. Al-Mizan states that consultation applies where one is free to choose what seems preferable; definite divine laws are not open to consultation, since no one may change them as though present events or new trends could abrogate God's words.

Al-Ṣādiq reports in al-Majālis that people accused the Prophet at Badr of appropriating a red velvet from the spoils, until God disclosed its location and cleared the Prophet of fraud, revealing that a prophet cannot defraud. Al-Qummī's version says that someone identified the person who had buried it and that the Prophet ordered the place dug up. Similar accounts are widely transmitted. Al-Mizan suggests that reports calling this the occasion of revelation may mean only that the verse points to the event, since its context shows revelation after Uḥud. Al-Bāqir's report that a defrauder will see the defrauded thing in the Fire and be ordered to enter and remove it is presented as a fine inference from the verse that the defrauder shall bring what he defrauded.

Al-Ṣādiq reports concerning diverse grades with God that those who follow God's pleasure are the Imāms, who are grades with God for believers. Through love and devotion to the Ahl al-bayt, God increases believers' deeds and raises their grades; those who bring wrath upon themselves are those who reject the right of ʿAlī and of the Imāms from the Ahl al-bayt. Al-Mizan says this is an application through the Qur'an's flow to the most prominent example. Al-Riḍā reportedly defines a grade as the distance between heaven and earth. Al-Ṣādiq explains the verse concerning a misfortune after inflicting twice as much by saying that at Badr Muslims killed seventy polytheists and captured seventy, while at Uḥud they suffered seventy deaths.

ʿAlī is reported through several authorities to say that Gabriel gave the Muslims a choice after Badr: they could execute the captives or take ransom on condition that an equal number of Muslims would later be killed. They chose ransom, accepting that equal martyrdom, and seventy Muslims were martyred at Uḥud, equal to Badr's captives. Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Qummī also report this from ʿAlī.

Al-Bāqir reportedly says that And reckon not those who are killed in God’s way as dead was revealed about the martyrs of Badr and Uḥud together. Al-Mizan nevertheless holds that the verses are general, including all those actually martyred in God's way or counted as martyrs. Another view assigns the verses to the martyrs of Biʾr Maʿūnah, where envoys sent to call ʿĀmir b. al-Ṭufayl's people to Islam were attacked and killed after Abū Milḥān al-Anṣārī had been slain.

Al-Ṣādiq applies the verse, through the Qur'an's flow, to the Shīʿahs: when their souls enter the Garden and receive God's honor, they gain certainty that they were upon truth and God's religion, and they rejoice for believing brethren who remain behind. Al-Mizan explains that this means perception by the eye of certainty after knowledge by certainty in this world, not that they had previously doubted.

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported through several authorities to transmit that the souls of Uḥud's martyrs were placed in green birds that ate from the Garden's fruits and lodged in golden candelabra under the Throne. Having found the goodness of their sustenance and rest, they wished their brethren knew of it, so they would not abandon jihād or shrink from fighting; God promised to convey their message through the verses concerning those killed in His way. Other reports describe the souls as in green birds, in their forms, or like them. Yet reports reaching the Imāms of the Ahl al-bayt deny that the Prophet said this, or interpret it differently. Al-Mizan says that, according to established principles, it must be interpreted away or rejected. In any event, these reports describe the Garden of al-Barzakh, not the Garden of the hereafter. Mujāhid says the martyrs receive fruit and scent from the Garden but are not in it, while al-Suddī says their souls feed in the Garden by day and lodge in the candelabra by night. Such descriptions may fit the Garden of this world, but not the hereafter.

Regarding the verses about responding to Allah and the Messenger, ʿAbdullāh b. Abī Bakr b. Muḥammad b. ʿAmr b. Ḥazm reports that the Prophet pursued the retreating enemy to Ḥamrāʾ al-Asad when Abū Sufyān had resolved to return and annihilate the remaining Muslims. Learning that the Prophet had come out deterred Abū Sufyān; he then instructed passing riders of ʿAbdu al-Qays to tell the Prophet that Quraysh would reattack. The Prophet and the believers replied that God was sufficient and the best Protector, and the verses were revealed. Al-Qummī says the Prophet took only men wounded at Uḥud, while other reports say he took only those who had been with him there; Al-Mizan considers the practical import the same.

Ibn Shahāb reports through Mūsá b. ʿAqabah and al-Bayhaqī that, at the later rendezvous at Badr, Satan's human friends frightened the Muslims with news of a great enemy army. The Muslims nevertheless went out with trade goods, intending either to meet Abū Sufyān or trade at Badr's annual fair. Abū Sufyān failed to come and, after hearing that the Muslims awaited him, returned to Mecca. The Prophet returned to Medina with God's favor and grace. The expedition is called that of the army of al-sawīq. Al-Ṭabrisī, reporting from al-Bāqir, likewise identifies the verses with Lesser Badr and says Abū Sufyān's army was derisively called the army of al-sawīq because it had taken sawīq provisions and turned back through fear.

Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿIkrimah, reports that after Uḥud the polytheists regretted leaving without killing Muḥammad or taking captives and proposed another attack. The Prophet gathered the Muslims and reached Ḥamrāʾ al-Asad, or perhaps the Well of Abū ʿUtbah. A later rendezvous at Badr followed: cowards turned back, while the brave took weapons and trade goods, found no enemy, traded, and returned with God's favor and grace.

Al-Mizan presents these reports to show that many supposed occasions of revelation are based on personal judgments: historical events are matched to verses and then called their causes of revelation. Such practice can fragment a single verse or coherent passage into independent occasions, even where that disturbs its structure or negates its context. Sectarian differences, political environments, and ruling conditions have also hidden realities or covered them in ambiguity; the serious scholar must take these factors into account. The passage closes by recording Ibn Hishām's al-Sīrah list of the seventy Muslims martyred at Uḥud.
verses.176:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse consoles the Prophet: although unbelievers hasten together toward disbelief, strive to extinguish God’s light, and may at times overpower believers, they cannot thwart God or harm Him. The all-encompassing system of trial carries every person toward his appointed end and completes both creative and legislative guidance.

Through health, strength, bounty, and comfort, God gradually draws the unbeliever toward destruction, allowing him to reach the furthest limit of transgression and disobedience. Conversely, trials cleanse the believer’s faith of rust and pollution until he becomes pure for God, while the unbeliever’s polytheistic tendencies are emptied of every trace of belief and he joins the followers of false deities and leaders of unbelief.

Thus the prohibition against grieving is advisory: those rushing into unbelief remain under God’s control, are being driven toward a Hereafter in which they have no share—the final limit of their unbelief—and face painful chastisement. Verse 3:177 then generalizes the point: not only those who hasten into disbelief, but all who exchange faith for unbelief, can do no harm to God. It may explain either the prohibition itself or its stated reason.

verses.178: Al-Mizan says that, after consoling the Prophet about unbelievers who hasten into disbelief, God addresses those unbelievers directly. They should not suppose that their divinely granted respite benefits them: it lets them accumulate sin upon sin and leads to a disgraceful chastisement, with only shame and ignominy in the Hereafter awaiting them. This follows the established divine system in which every creature, by its own choice, brings its potentialities to fruition.
verses.179:
Al-Mizan explains that believers too are necessarily subject to test and trial, through which they reach completion and the purified believer is distinguished from the impure, the evil from the good. Believers cannot avoid the hardships caused by mixing with hypocrites and those with diseased hearts by being told who they are, because knowledge of the unseen belongs exclusively to God. He discloses it only to such messengers as He chooses.

Since neither trial nor the conversion of potentialities into actual attainments can be escaped, believers should believe in God and His messengers in order to belong among the good rather than the evil. Yet belief alone does not preserve the blessedness of life: it must be supported by good deeds, which raise belief to God and preserve its blessings. Accordingly, belief in God and His messengers is the essence of the soul’s goodness and of the happy life, whereas the complete reward depends on piety and good deeds.

The commentary draws three conclusions. First, every soul must arrive at its perfection and destination, whether felicity or infelicity. Second, goodness and evil belong to persons or souls, while depending respectively on belief and disbelief, which arise from human will and choice; this is a Qur’anic reality bearing on the secrets of monotheism. Third, belief originates the good life, but good deeds are required for its continuance and effects, just as natural life begins with the soul but continues through the activity of its powers and organs.

The repeated use of the name Allah, rather than pronouns, points to the Source of all greatness and beauty, because testing creatures, knowing the unseen, choosing messengers, and human capacity to believe in Him are matters reserved exclusively to His divinity.
verses.180:
Al-Mizan relates niggardliness in spending wealth in God’s way to the respite granted to unbelievers: the miser delights in and boasts of accumulated riches, but what he takes as good is worse for him. Calling the wealth a grace granted by Allah exposes the meanness and blameworthiness of withholding it; it will become like an iron collar encircling the miser’s neck on the Resurrection Day.

Apparently, “and Allah’s is the heritage of the heavens and the earth” and “and Allah is aware of what you do” are circumstantial clauses connected with the Resurrection Day: on that day the heritage belongs to God and He is aware of their deeds. As a remote possibility, the first clause—and possibly the second as well—may instead qualify their being niggardly; the last clause may also stand independently.
verses.181:
Al-Mizan identifies those who said, “Surely Allah is poor and we are rich,” as the Jews, as indicated especially by the following reference to their killing prophets. They may have said this after hearing, Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan … (2:245), a possibility strengthened by the preceding condemnation of niggardliness; or, seeing the believers’ poverty and hunger, they may have taunted them that a rich Lord would have enriched His friends.

God’s “writing” their words means preserving and recording them, whether generally or in the scroll of deeds. Their killing of prophets “unjustly” was knowing and deliberate, not due to error, ignorance, or misunderstanding. Their blasphemous saying is joined to this killing because of its enormity. al-ḥarīq is the Hell-fire or flame, and has also been said to mean that which burns.

“What your (own) hands have sent before” means the deeds sent ahead, with hands mentioned as the usual instruments of sending. This and God’s not being unjust explain both the recording and requital of deeds: failure to record and recompense them would neglect the system of deeds and constitute immense injustice toward servants, from which God is far above.

The next verse continues the description of the same people: they claimed that Allah had ordered them not to believe a messenger unless he brought an offering consumed by fire. al-ʿAhd means an enjoining or order, and al-qurbān an offered sacrifice. The reply recalls earlier messengers, such as Zachariah and John, who came with clear evidences and the demanded sign, yet were slain by the Jews.

verses.184: Al-Mizan states that the verse consoles the Prophet over their rejection by recalling that earlier messengers were also rejected despite bringing clear evidences, scriptures, and the illuminating Book. al-Zubur is the plural of al-zabūr, a book of wisdom and sermons; the scriptures and illuminating Book include revelations such as Noah’s book, Abraham’s scriptures, the Torah, and the Injīl.
verses.185:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse promises good to the believer and threatens the rejector. Its declaration that every soul tastes death is universal, while al-tawfiyah denotes the full payment of recompense on the Resurrection Day. The verse is a sound argument for al-Barzakh, since full recompense on that Day implies a partial recompense beforehand.

al-Zaḥzaḥah, removal far from the Fire, conveys repeated, hasty pulling away; al-fawz is attainment of the desired object. al-ghurūr may be the verbal noun of gharra, “he deceived” or “deluded,” or the plural of al-ghārr, “deceiver.”
verses.186:
Al-Mizan explains that believers will repeatedly be tried in their wealth and persons and will hear hurtful speech from the People of the Book and the polytheists. Having first mentioned trials already endured and Jewish words that could weaken them, the verse foretells future afflictions in order to prepare them mentally and reconcile them to what they must bear.

They are commanded to be patient and to guard against evil, so that God may protect them from error and weakness of heart and they may become people of firm resolve. al-Iblāʾ means testing or trying. Adhan kathīran, rendered “much annoying talk,” metaphorically names the effect in place of its cause.
verses.187: Al-Mizan explains that God covenanted with those given the Book to make it known to people and not conceal it, but they neglected it and exchanged it for a small price. al-Nabdh means casting or throwing away; “they cast it behind their backs” is an idiom for leaving or neglecting something, the opposite of putting it before one’s eyes and directing one’s attention to it.
verses.188: Al-Mizan takes “what they have brought about” to mean the wealth God bestowed on them, accompanied by love of riches and niggardliness. Those who delight in this and seek praise for what they have not done will not be safe from chastisement; al-mafāzah means deliverance or safety. They were destroyed because their hearts adhered to falsehood and thus withdrew from the protection of truth. God’s closing declaration of His kingdom over the heavens and earth and power over all things may explain the reason for all that precedes.

verses.190: Al-Mizan holds that “creation” here most probably has a comprehensive sense: it includes how the heavens and earth came to be, their properties and characteristics, and such concomitants as motion, rest, change, and variation. Thus, the creation of the heavens and earth and the alternation of night and day encompass the great phenomena of creation, which are signs for men of understanding.
verses.191:
Al-Mizan explains that these believers remember God in every state—standing, sitting, or lying down—and, through observing the heavens, the earth, and the alternation of night and day, continually remember Him and reflect on creation. This reflection recalls to them the coming resurrection and recompense, so they seek God’s mercy and fulfilment of His promise.

Their use of hādhā, a singular masculine demonstrative, shows that they regard the many created things as one creation rather than attending to each thing’s particular name or identity. al-Bāṭil means that which has no aim or purpose. Since creation is not vain, they infer that God must gather people for recompense and inflict the disgraceful punishment of Hell upon the unjust. No one can avert the principle of chastisement; otherwise creation would be purposeless. Hence their prayer for protection from the Fire, whose entrants are disgraced and find no helpers.

verses.193:
Al-Mizan identifies the crier as the Messenger of God; “saying: Believe” explicates his call. The believers affirm that they believed him, accepting his warnings about sins, faults, dying in unbelief and transgression, and his exhortations toward forgiveness, mercy, and the promised Garden. They therefore ask God to forgive and cover their faults, let them die with the righteous, and grant the Garden and mercy promised through His messengers.

ʿAlā rusulika, literally “on Thy messengers,” means the promise God gave to the messengers and which they guaranteed to the believers on His behalf. Their request not to be disgraced on the Day of Resurrection means that God should not fail to fulfil this promise, for He does not break promises.

The commentary concludes that reflection on God’s signs gave these believers faith in God, the hereafter, and the mission of the messengers. The details brought by the Prophet, however, were learned through belief in and obedience to him. Thus they follow nature in what reflection on nature and creation can disclose, and accept the Prophet’s teaching in other matters.

verses.195:
Al-Mizan says that calling God “their Lord” indicates the immediacy and intensity of divine mercy. The unrestricted assurance that no worker’s deed, male or female, will be wasted establishes that there is no discrimination either among deeds or among workers.

The subsequent references to those who emigrated, were expelled from their homes, persecuted in God’s way, fought, or were slain enumerate deeds for which reward is described; the conjunctions do not require that one person combine every deed. The verse selects the virtues especially stressed in this chapter: preferring religion to homeland, patiently enduring hardship in God’s way, and fighting for religion.

Emigration apparently includes every kind of flight, whether from polytheism, family, or home. The term is unrestricted; expulsion from homes is then mentioned as one particular kind; and the later promise to cover al-sayyiʾāt, apparently minor sins in Qur’anic usage, indicates that they had already fled major sins by abstaining or repenting. A translator’s note adds that this use of al-sayyiʾāt is not invariable. Thus the emigration intended is more comprehensive.
verses.196: Al-Mizan says that the verse removes a possible misunderstanding: after describing the righteous believers’ condition and reward, it warns that the unbelievers’ affluence, luxury, riches, and fearless movement through the cities must not deceive. Though grammatically addressed to the Prophet, the warning is meant for others as well. Their enjoyment is brief and impermanent, and their final abode is Hell.

verses.198: Al-Mizan identifies those who fear their Lord with the righteous. Their promised reward consists of gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding there; entertainment (al-Nuzul)—food, drink, and other things served to a guest—from their Lord; and the assurance that what is with God is best for the righteous. This supports the preceding warning’s purpose of removing a possible but unspoken misunderstanding.
verses.199:
Al-Mizan explains that believing followers of the Book receive the better reward along with other believers. Happiness in the hereafter is not reserved for a nation or tribe: it depends upon belief in God and His messengers. If the People of the Book accept true belief, they are eligible for the same reward. The verse especially praises them by excluding the evils for which other Jews and Christians had been condemned: distinguishing among God’s messengers, concealing what they had covenanted to disclose, and selling God’s signs for a small price.

The commentary then argues that man and woman are two classes of the same human species. Since all the characteristics of the species found in man are also found in woman, differences in the relative strength of shared traits do not make woman less human. The potential perfections open to either are therefore open to the other, including spiritual perfection through belief, obedience, and deeds that bring one near to God. It presents “I will not waste the work of a worker among you, whether male or female, the one of you being from the other” as the fullest statement of this principle.

Al-Mizan contrasts this with the Bible, citing Ecclesiastes’ portrayal of woman as more bitter than death, with a heart of snares and nets and hands of fetters, and its claim to have found one man among a thousand but no woman. It further states that most ancient peoples regarded women’s deeds as unacceptable to God; that Greeks called woman an abomination from Satan’s handiwork; that Romans and some Greeks denied her an abstract immaterial human soul while affirming one for man; that a Christian council in France in 586 C.E. judged woman human but created to serve man; and that in England, a hundred years earlier, woman was not considered part of human society. It refers readers to works on ancient beliefs, mythology, and anthropology for further such views.
