Al-Mizan explains that the command to “be patient” is unrestricted: it includes patience in hardship, obedience to God, and abstention from disobedience. It concerns the individual. al-Muṣābarah, rendered as helping one another in patience, literally means vying in patience; it is collective steadfastness when people endure a common hardship and each person’s endurance is reinforced by that of the others. Such mutual action strengthens them, redoubles patience, and multiplies its effect. al-murābaṭah, “remain lined up,” is still broader: it means that people link their powers, faculties, and activities in all affairs of religious life, in ease as well as hardship. The translator notes that although the word later came to be used for troops being stationed, the commentary takes its original sense of being linked with one another. These commands are followed by fear of God because their aim is not merely partial worldly prosperity, but real and complete happiness and success in this world and the next.

Human beings are social by nature and have always lived in society. The Qur’an indicates this through humanity’s common origin, the division into nations and tribes for mutual recognition, differences in livelihood, and ties of blood and marriage. Yet society, like humanity’s other qualities connected with knowledge and will, did not arise complete; it advanced gradually from primitive to developed forms and continues to do so.

The earliest social group apparently was the family founded on marriage, since sexual satisfaction requires union rather than solitary action. From this developed the instinct of exploitation, by which one person compels another to serve his needs, and then forms of leadership: head of household, patriarch, tribal chief, and national ruler. Initially leadership belonged to the strongest and bravest, then to one who also possessed wealth and many children, and finally to one regarded as most capable in administration, diplomacy, and politics. The commentary associates this development with the rise and continued strength of idolatry. Society itself always existed, but people were not initially conscious of it as a distinct human reality; it grew alongside instincts such as exploitation and self-defence.

According to the Qur’an, prophethood made people fully aware of society and social bonds and called them to preserve them. Humanity was originally one simple community; when differences and disputes emerged, God sent prophets and revealed books to judge among people and restore social concord through ordained laws: Mankind was but one people; so Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good news and as warners, and He sent down with them the book with truth, so that it might judge between the people in that in which they had differed [2:213]. Likewise, the religion prescribed for Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muḥammad commands people to establish religion and not divide over it [42:13]. Thus religion secured sound social order. Noah was the first prophet given a law and a book; the laws of Noah and Abraham contained relatively few rules, and Moses’ law was the most extensive of the four mentioned, reportedly containing about six hundred rules. In any event, the distinct call to organized social life came through the prophets in the form of religion.

The commentary maintains that Islam alone deliberately grounds its whole structure in human society and never neglects the social aspect of any affair. Its shariah directs the immense variety of human actions and circumstances, while moulding its rules in a communal form. In this respect it surpasses the shariahs of Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus; systems such as idolatry, Sabiʾism, Manichaeism, and dualism stand still farther away. Historically, nations generally inherited social customs based on exploitation and united under kings or chiefs selected by lineage, locality, and similar factors. Even Rome and Persia were despotic orders centered upon Caesar and Khusraw. Philosophical writings on society remained merely theoretical and did not take practical shape.

The Prophet of Islam, through revelation, was therefore the first to summon humanity to treat social affairs as an independent concern and to seek good life together. The Qur’an orders believers to hold fast together to God’s cord, not divide, establish a body that invites to good and enjoins right and forbids wrong, follow the straight path rather than ways that scatter them, make peace between brethren, avoid quarrelling lest their strength depart, and cooperate in goodness and piety. Islamic society is accordingly founded on unity and harmony and on preserving its spiritual and material benefits.

Islam views human individuals as a plurality within a real unity. Just as bodily organs and faculties retain their particular identities yet serve one human being and produce benefits exceeding the sum of their separate effects, human beings, though many, are one in species and can unite. The more water is gathered, the stronger its effects become; similarly, a social whole possesses powers beyond those of isolated persons. Human kinship and marriage reveal this real connection between individuals. Because people contribute their existence, capacities, and characteristics to society, society acquires an independent entity and traits of its own. The Qur’an consequently speaks of nations as possessing appointed terms, books, perception, understanding, action, obedience or disobedience, messengers, and judgment. It therefore attends to the histories of nations as much as, or more than, those of individuals, unlike earlier historical writing, which chiefly recorded kings and nobles.

Society’s power ordinarily overcomes that of an individual when they conflict. Group will, especially in crowds and mobs, can suppress individual judgment; collective terror during retreat, riots, earthquakes, famine, or epidemics can do the same. Even customary practices and national dress can compel conformity and weaken independent perception. Hence individual moral training alone seldom succeeds where society’s atmosphere is opposed to virtue; only a few resist it. Islam accordingly builds such major obligations as ḥajj, prayer, jihād, spending in God’s way, and religious piety upon social life. It preserves that life through Islamic government, through the communal duty of inviting to good, enjoining virtue, and forbidding evil, and through a common goal: true happiness, nearness to God, and honor before Him. This goal acts as an unseen but vigilant supervisor even where human observers fail.

The commentary considers the objection that Islam’s social order was briefly realized and then became despotism, whereas Western civilization endured and rests upon the majority’s will. It grants that present circumstances may not favor Islamic law, but replies that this proves nothing: every social system began amid conditions hostile to it, often suffered setbacks, and either eventually prevailed through repeated struggle or perished when its conditions failed. This is true of religious and temporal systems alike, including democracy and communism. A system’s opposition to its environment therefore does not establish its error. Islam too is subject to social and physical conditions, but its position is not weaker than that of Noah, Abraham, or Muḥammad when each began alone amid disorder. The Messenger began with only a man and a woman supporting him, then established a society in which goodness and piety predominated, until later strife and intrigue transformed it. Even this brief and limited model spread over the earth in less than fifty years and permanently redirected human history.

Al-Mizan argues that ideological history must acknowledge Islamic civilization as the immediate and sufficient cause of contemporary worldly advancement, even if many European scholars deny Islam its due through religious prejudice or political expediency. Christianity cannot fairly be called the source of modern civic and social progress when Christ, as the commentary describes him, concerned himself with spiritual affairs rather than governmental and bodily affairs; Islam explicitly directs social life and mutual cooperation in every aspect. Islam has thus demonstrated that it can lead humanity to happiness and good life, and cannot be dismissed as an impracticable hypothesis. The commentary further holds that reflection on creation shows humanity will reach its destination: the universal dominance of true Islam and its complete authority over social order. It cites the divine promises that God will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him [5:54], make believing good-doers successors and establish their chosen religion [24:55], and give the earth to His righteous servants [21:105].

The decisive contrast, however, is between Islam’s following truth in belief and practice and modern civilization’s following the views and desires of the majority. Islamic happiness is rational and real: each human power is given its due in moderation, while bodily desire serves rather than obstructs knowledge of God through servitude. Islamic commandments rest on wisdom and intellect, prohibit what corrupts sound reason, and make society responsible for enforcing conduct, morality, and fundamental gnosis alongside the government’s functions. Such restrictions are naturally unwelcome to those immersed in desire and lust and require strenuous propagation, training, and vigilance.

Modern civilization, by contrast, makes material enjoyment its end and follows reason only when it does not oppose desire. Its laws follow majority pleasure and can effectively govern only outward acts; ethics and fundamental gnosis are left to acceptance or rejection unless they violate civil law. A society governed in this way tends toward lust and excessive anger, treats much that religion condemns as desirable, and may mock good morals and higher spiritual knowledge under the name of constitutional freedom. Sensuality reverses moral judgments, presenting what wisdom judges depravity as chivalry, manliness, or good manners. It uses intellect chiefly to facilitate enjoyment; nothing restrains desire except conflict with another enjoyment or the society’s own desire. The commentary regards modern civilization as a technically refined collective form of earlier idolatry. Its apparent agreement with popular nature is not peculiar to it: throughout history people have preferred social systems that flatter material attachment to religion’s call to truth.

The Qur’an, in the commentary’s view, plainly identifies Islam as the religion of truth and declares that most people dislike truth. It rejects government by majority desire because, were truth to follow their desires, the heavens, the earth, and all within them would perish [23:70–71]. History’s recurring human-made disasters confirm this. The claim that following the majority is natural confuses two meanings of majority. External events are governed by universal causality, and an effect occurring in most cases has a stable majority-pattern as an objective fact. Human nature follows real external things, and human perceptions are means to apprehend that reality. But truth belongs to the thing known, not to the number of people who believe something. Majority opinion may be true when it conforms to reality and false when it does not; it is not to be accepted merely because it is widespread. One who knows a thing to be true does not genuinely abandon it merely because all others deny it; apparent submission may arise from fear or embarrassment, not conviction. Nature therefore requires following what objectively occurs in all or most cases, not following what most people happen to think. The Qur’anic legislation is based on the good of the majority in this objective sense, as when it states purposes commonly realized by purification and fasting, not on majority opinion as such.

Technological strength and maximum exploitation of natural resources are not, for Islam, happiness. True human felicity joins bodily and spiritual well-being, material blessing, excellent character, and true divine gnosis, securing happiness in this life and the next; immersion in material pleasure while neglecting spiritual felicity is unhappiness. The commentary also says that observers err when they judge an advanced society by how its members treat one another internally. A person formed by collective thinking sees himself as inseparable from his society, whose good and harm are his own. Like bodily organs working together under one human identity, members of such a collective share its good and evil in relation to other societies. This is why the Qur’an may censure later generations of groups whose collective mentality identifies them with their predecessors’ sins, while still excepting righteous individuals whose hearts are not polluted by the social corruption.

Advanced societies must therefore be judged by their collective conduct toward weaker nations. The commentary sees the history of European collective life since the Renaissance as revealing a continuous aim of subjugating weaker peoples: by war, colonial intrigue, annexation, suzerainty, supposed protection of shared interests or independence, peacekeeping, repelling danger, or defending displaced groups. Such domination over lives, honor, property, thought, and will cannot be called goodness or happiness, even apart from religion’s definition of happiness. Human nature gives its members equal faculties; it cannot consistently authorize some to own and rule others. If this condition is called happiness, it is only ironically.

Every society is united by a common goal that becomes its one spirit. Nonreligious societies are held together by collective worldly enjoyment. A solitary person would face only the limits imposed by his own body, but social life requires law because unrestricted individual action produces conflict and the destruction of human life. Uncivilized societies follow inherited customs and gradually accept rules to protect themselves, though such rules lack a firm foundation and are subject to alteration and invalidation. Civilized societies more consciously establish laws that restrict wills and actions, remove conflict, and concentrate coercive authority in a center responsible for enforcement.

Law moderates desire and action by imposing limits. It leaves people free in matters outside its scope, which is proper once will and action have been regulated. Modern law therefore does not inherently concern itself with divine knowledge or ethics; these become dependent on law and can decline into outward rites without inner purity. Politics may then prohibit religion, zealously use it, or leave it neglected. Civil law also lacks a final guarantee: its ruler may convert collective authority into personal tyranny, ignore the law, and escape correction; moreover, crimes may remain unknown or outside the executive’s reach.

Islam holds that human life includes the hereafter, where nothing benefits except divine gnosis concentrated in monotheism. This gnosis requires noble moral traits and purification from base qualities, while such traits reach completion only in a healthy society founded on worship, submission to divine lordship, and social justice. Islam’s unifying social goal is therefore monotheism. It does not merely regulate intentions and outward actions, but adds worship, true knowledge of God, and noble character. Enforcement belongs first to Islamic government and then to society through education, practice, enjoining good, and forbidding evil. All parts form one integrated whole: monotheism permeates virtue, virtue animates required deeds, and ultimately all religious elements return to monotheism; descending into outward life, monotheism becomes good character and deeds, while ascending, deeds and good words return to it: To Him do ascend the good words; and the good deed lifts them up [35:10].

The weakness of Islam in a given period does not refute this system, because every law exists in the mind and is realized through human will. Secular law connects action with the majority’s present intention but does not preserve that intention. If collective will dies through spiritual decay, loses perception through frivolity, luxury, and material absorption, or is overpowered by a stronger will, law cannot protect society. Nor can it fully control secret crimes or acts beyond its jurisdiction. The commentary points to postwar European divisions as an illustration. Law fails because society has not secured the factor that preserves and strengthens collective will: high morality. Laws and traditions unsupported by noble character resemble a tree uprooted from the earth. Communism is presented as a natural offspring of democracy’s extreme inequality between wealth and deprivation, while world wars arise from the arrogance, mischief, and greed of supposedly civilized nations.

Islam, by grounding law in morality and thoroughly training people in noble traits, gives the law an inward guardian active in private as well as public, stronger than police or other external authority. Secular educational calls to morality cannot succeed, the commentary argues, because extreme luxury and extreme deprivation are both sources of evil while civil law permits them, and because societies that collectively oppress weaker societies contradict their own moral instruction. Further, morality requires a guarantor: monotheism, including belief in one God who created creatures for perfection and happiness, loves good, hates evil, gathers all for judgment, rewards good, and punishes evil. Without the Day of Judgment, the commentary sees no genuine reason for a person to forsake desire or sacrifice himself for another where no punishment, censure, or benefit to himself is expected. Patriotism, love of humanity, and posthumous praise are only unstable inclinations or conventions; one who believes death is annihilation cannot truly enjoy later praise. Monotheism and the Last Day alone make a person do good and refrain from evil whether observed, praised, exhorted, or not, knowing God sees every soul and that every deed will be present for recompense.

The commentary distinguishes the logic of sensuousness from the logic of understanding. Sensuousness seeks perceived worldly benefit and becomes inactive where it sees none. Understanding follows truth because what is with God is better and more enduring, regardless of worldly gain. ʿAntarah’s verse urges his soul to remain firm in battle because death brings praise and victory brings relief from the enemy; this courage depends on obtaining one of these personal benefits. The Qur’anic logic is expressed in: Say: “Nothing will afflict us save what Allah has ordained for us; He is our Patron; and on Allah should the believers rely.” Say: “Do you await for us but one of the two most excellent things? And we await for you that Allah will afflict you with punishment from Himself or by our hands. So wait; we too will wait with you.” [9:51–52]. Believers seek God’s promised reward for submission and adherence to His religion. If harmed or killed, they receive reward; if victorious, they receive both reward and worldly victory. Their enemies can expect success only if they defeat believers, whereas believers obtain one of two good outcomes.

Courage rooted in praise or deliverance fails whenever no personal benefit is expected: people may not know, admire, or distinguish faithfulness from betrayal, or destroying an enemy may bring no inward relief. The same logic underlies embezzlement, crime concealed from authorities, apathy toward truth, and rejection of moral purity when it seems to bring hardship. Islamic logic places worldly aims second to truth and divine reward. Every act or omission is performed for God’s pleasure and in submission to His ordained truth; God is the ever-watchful Witness whether people see, value, or praise an act or not. The commentary states that Islamic training was once so powerful that people came to the Messenger of God to confess secret sins and accept even capital punishment, seeking God’s pleasure and purification from sin.

Making the hereafter’s reward the primary social aim does not, Al-Mizan says, demand rejection of worldly ends or monasticism. Islam bases legislation on creation: the ordered chain of causes brings humanity into being and drives it toward its appointed end. People must develop life through free choice and striving in accordance with these causes, lest life become a destructive conflict between means and ends. Above all causes is God, their Creator and Manager, the Complete Cause; surrender to Him is monotheism, Islam’s sole foundation. Seeking God’s pleasure throughout life gives every cause its proper due without polytheism or heedlessness. Muslims have worldly and otherworldly, material and spiritual aims, but pursue material goals only as rationally required. Thus exclusive attachment to God does not oppose following the laws of life and nature, and seeking His pleasure does not conflict with other legitimate ends so long as it governs them. The claim that religion’s real end is merely social justice, and that anyone establishing justice belongs to religion even without belief or worship, falsely changes religion’s objective of monotheism into the secular aim of material enjoyment; these are opposite aims and cannot be transformed into one another.

Modern freedom derives from human will, without which perception, sensation, and humanity itself would be nullified. Yet because people are social, the same nature that gives will and action also requires law to define their limits and coordinate persons with one another. Modern civil law, founded on material enjoyment, thus means freedom from religious belief and moral restraint outside the sphere of civil law. Islam, however, bases law on monotheism and noble morals and gives guidance for every personal and social concern; it has no room for freedom in that modern sense. It frees human beings instead from serving anything other than God. It permits choice regarding lawful good provisions and the moderate enjoyments of life, but not an unbounded liberty that undermines religion.

The commentary rejects deriving freedom of belief from There is no compulsion in religion [2:256]. Since monotheism is Islam’s foundation, freedom to deny its principles would be like freedom from law in a civil order. Moreover, firmly rooted affirmative belief is not a voluntary action that can literally be permitted, prohibited, compelled, or made free. What law can regulate are acts arising from belief: propagating it, canvassing for it, publishing it, or undermining opposing belief and activity. Such acts may be forbidden when they conflict with the laws and foundational principles of a society. Islamic legislation rests on belief in God’s oneness, prophethood, and the Day of Judgment, beliefs shared by Muslims and the People of the Book named here as Jews, Christians, and Zoroastrians. Islamic freedom remains within this limit; freedom beyond it destroys religion’s foundation. A separate freedom to state a belief for debate and discussion remains to be explained.

Islam’s comprehensive regulation and protection of fundamental beliefs do not cause social stagnation. The dialectical-materialist objection confuses two kinds of knowledge. Technical knowledge, such as mathematics and physics, changes and develops, raises material life, and enables greater command of nature; Islam does not obstruct this process. Metaphysical knowledge concerning origin, resurrection, happiness, and misery has definite and final truths, though people can develop deeper and more detailed understanding of them. Its stability does not halt social development, just as stable general truths—that people need work to preserve life, live in society, inhabit a real universe, and possess bodily powers—do not halt it. The belief in one God, comprehensive prophetic law, and future recompense is such a foundational truth; subjecting it to dialectical rejection would bring decline rather than progress.

Changes in theories of social organization, such as monarchy, democracy, and communism, become necessary only where the existing order fails to bring society toward perfection. Their relation is one of wrong and right, not lower and higher stages of one necessary evolution. A society founded on social justice, training in useful knowledge and good action, and continuous advance toward happiness has no rational need to change its foundations merely for change’s sake. Likewise, the doctrine that all beliefs and values are relative and change with time, environment, and circumstance cannot be universally true. If it is itself an unrestricted, unchanging truth, then at least one universal truth exists; if it is only partly true, universal truths likewise exist. If every opinion must change, that doctrine too must change, which entails that some beliefs do not.

Modern life differs from earlier life chiefly in forms and instruments, not in its permanent human principles. People still need food, clothing, homes, transport, society, and sexual, commercial, technical, and professional relations. A primitive meal and the many refined foods of modern life remain food satisfying hunger. Thus general Islamic laws, laid down according to human nature and happiness, are not invalidated by new means, provided those means do not conflict with nature. If they do conflict with nature, Islam rejects them in every age. Rapidly changing public matters—currency, administration, defence, communications, transport, and municipal affairs—are entrusted to the ruler, who decides internal and external affairs, war and peace, finance, and related matters after consultation and according to society’s interest: and take counsel with them in the affairs; but when you have decided, then place your trust in Allah [3:159]. Such decisions are particular and change with circumstances; divine rules founded on the Book and sunnah are general and not subject to abrogation.

Authority over Islamic society belonged to the Messenger of God, whom believers had to obey, who judged by what God taught him, and who had a greater claim upon believers than they had upon themselves. His encompassing authority is evident from his life and from the totality of revelations concerning worship, transactions, politics, ethics, and social affairs. At the same time, the Qur’an commonly addresses its commands—prayer, fasting, jihād, spending, testimony, penalties, retaliation, unity, and establishment of religion—to believers collectively rather than only to the Prophet. Religion is therefore a collective responsibility: believers themselves must establish it, manage their society, and implement its law; none is exempt from this responsibility. The Messenger’s distinctive offices were delivering the message, guidance, purification, teaching the Book and Wisdom, and leading the ummah during his life.

This order is neither monarchy, in which a ruler treats God’s wealth as personal booty and people as slaves, nor a materialist social order such as democracy. Materially oriented societies are driven by exploitation, the arrogant desire to subjugate all things and people. Formerly this appeared as despotic monarchy; now the same spirit appears collectively under claims of civilization and development, as powerful nations oppress weaker ones. Islamic government is free from this ambition, as shown by the Prophet’s conquests and treaties. It also excludes class privilege. No person, estate, or group has precedence except the God-given distinction of piety. Ruler and ruled, leader and follower, superior and subordinate, free and slave, male and female, rich and poor, great and small are equal before the law. Nor is enforcement restricted to a distinct ruling class: each member is bound to call to good, enjoin right, and forbid wrong.

After the Prophet, most Muslims hold that the community chooses a caliph; Shīʿī Muslims hold that the caliph must be appointed by God and His Messenger and that the caliphs are the twelve Imāms. In the present period, when the Prophet has died and the twelfth Imām is in occultation, the authority of Islamic government lies with Muslims themselves. They must appoint a ruler according to the Prophet’s pattern of imāmah, not monarchy or imperialism. He must enforce the unaltered Islamic laws, while administering matters outside them through consultation appropriate to time and circumstance.

Islam rejects national separateness as the basis of social order. Nationalism emerged from nomadic tribal life and differences of climate, land, and region, which divided humanity into groups of differing language and color. Groups then possessed territory, called it homeland, loved it, and repelled outsiders. Although this arose from a natural need, it opposes humanity’s deeper need for unified social life, in which scattered powers join and are strengthened. National unity separates one country’s people from others, fractures humanity, and leads each national collective to exploit and subjugate other collectives. Islam therefore bases society on faith and belief rather than race, descent, homeland, or territorial borders. Even marital and inheritance rights rest on shared monotheistic belief rather than country.

The Islamic social form remains applicable whether Muslims rule or are ruled, prevail or are overcome, are visible or concealed, strong or weak. When dominant, they must establish religion and avoid division; when oppressed, they must revive and honor Islam as far as they can. Even a lone Muslim must adhere to the religion and implement it as far as possible, even if only through inward faith and gestural prayer. The provisions concerning al-taqiyyah—dissimulation of religion under compulsion or threatening harm—make this flexibility clear.

Islam seeks collectivity in every law capable of joint performance, with differing degrees of emphasis. Collective defensive jihād is directly required to the necessary extent. Fasting and ḥajj are obligatory for those able and unexcused, and consequently gather believers together; the two ʿīds and their prayers complete this pattern. The five daily prayers are obligatory, while their congregation is not; nevertheless, a congregational Friday prayer is obligatory within a radius of one farsakh. In other matters Islam strongly recommends communal observance even without directly making it obligatory, as with congregational performance of obligatory prayer, because it is a sunnah of the Prophet. The Messenger of God is reported to have threatened those who abandoned mosque prayer with having firewood placed at their doors and their houses burned over them. The commentary takes this as illustrating the duty to preserve the Prophet’s established practices by every possible means; detailed rulings belong to ijtihād based on the Book and sunnah.

Collectivity extends to Islam’s basic knowledge. Islam calls people to natural religion as manifest truth, and the shared principle that truth must be followed is the first basis for uniting minds. It excuses one for whom proof has not been established and the way has not been made clear, even if he has heard arguments. It therefore grants thinkers full scope to examine and reflect on religious cognition. Differences of understanding arise from several sources. They may come from differing psychological traits, since uprightness, justice, moderation, prejudice, tyranny, rashness, and misguidance affect intellectual capacity. Religious training can overcome this by producing virtues conforming to religious truth. They may come from sinful and anti-truth actions, lusts, temptations, and wicked thoughts that plant doubts and false ideas. Islam addresses this by continuously inviting to religion, enjoining right, forbidding wrong, and requiring dissociation from deviating persons and doubting groups. Believers must not join discourse that ridicules, casts doubt upon, or attacks divine signs, because such conduct comes from treating religion as play and being deceived by worldly life; its cure is sound training and constant remembrance of God.

Differences may also arise from external circumstances: people may live where true faith has not reached them, has reached them only superficially or in distorted form, or lack sufficient understanding. Islam’s remedy is universal propagation carried out patiently, politely, and with good manners. Invitation must be made with clear sight and in proportion to each hearer’s understanding. The commentary cites a report narrated by both sects in which the Messenger says: “We, the group of prophets, talk with people according to the measure of their understanding.” A group from every community should acquire proper understanding of religion and return to warn its people [9:122].

To prevent disagreements from weakening society, believers must unite upon the straight path and avoid other paths that scatter them. They must hold fast together to God’s cord, understood as the Qur’an, or as the Qur’an together with the Messenger. When confronted by a new doctrine or doubt, they should meditate collectively on the Qur’an; if they do not know, they should ask those who do. The Qur’an’s lack of discrepancy, its examples for the learned, and the command to ask the followers of the Reminder show that differences are resolved through Qur’anic reflection and reference to those qualified to reflect. Referring disputes to the Messenger, and to those vested with authority who can draw out the truth, likewise explains the truth and removes social discord.

Islam thus gives complete freedom of thought while safeguarding its particular divine cognitions. Muslims must collectively investigate religious realities and need not fear doubts arising in the course of inquiry. They should examine doubt in the light of the Qur’an and, if it remains, refer it to the Messenger or his successor for clarification. This differs from freedom to propagate a belief before such reference, since premature propagation produces division and damages healthy society. The commentary calls this the best social arrangement because it opens intellectual development while protecting personal freedom. Islam does not approve forcing belief, sealing hearts, suppressing thought through oppression, or ruling through whip, sword, anathema, excommunication, boycott, or banishment. It attributes such methods to Christianity, especially the Church between the fifth and sixteenth centuries. The commentary laments that Muslims have lost collective thought and freedom of belief by neglecting their duty to God; churchlike conduct has entered their society, producing discord and sectarianism.

Finally, Al-Mizan holds that the good end belongs to piety. Human nature seeks true happiness: a social life that grants the soul its share in both worldly and otherworldly existence. This is Islam, the religion of monotheism. Humanity’s deviations do not mean that nature has abandoned its destination; they result from errors of judgment and mistaken application. The goal set by creative nature must eventually be reached. The Qur’an’s description of natural devotion to the right religion, the emergence of corruption through human deeds so that people may return, the promised people beloved of God, and the inheritance of the earth by righteous servants all show, in the commentary’s view, that Islam will ultimately appear in its complete form and rule the world.

The objection that this is untested wishful thinking fails because Islam, in this sense, is humanity’s final destination whether or not people fully recognize it. Experience of other species shows every species moving toward the end suited to its being, and humanity is no exception. Nor was any previous religious or secular system first validated by experiment before its establishment: the laws of Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, Brahma, Buddha, Māni, democracy, and communism all arose and were implemented without prior testing. What establishes a social system is a group of people with conviction, high ideals, and unwavering determination, who do not tire, weaken, or entertain doubt about their eventual success, but persevere until they achieve their aim. This principle applies whether the goal is divine or Satanic.
